title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
Quick Guide

QUICK GUIDE TO THE PTB ABA EXAM STUDY MANUAL

A few things you should know to get the most out your PTB ABA Exam Study Manual.

- The content in this Manual is the 6th Edition Test Content Outline. We have done our best to be thorough and comprehensive, but you may find that you need a bit more information on some of the concepts, and less on others. Don't hesitate to refer to your textbooks for more detailed explanations.
- While this Manual is a comprehensive guide to preparing for the BCBA or BCaBA exams, it is a Study Manual. If you find that you are learning something for the first time, please reference the source material. There are NO shortcuts to becoming an awesome BCBA!
- The content is organized in order of the BCBA exam TCO. Be sure to pay attention to the title page of every section and the upper right-hand corner which calls out the specific Domain covered on that page.
- For candidates preparing for the BCaBA exam, each section title, includes the corresponding BCaBA exam TCO Domains.
- This is a study guide and in no way intended to be an instructional manual for the actual practice of ABA. It does however make a great reference tool once you get those hard-earned letters.
- The Manual uses many graphic elements such as icons, charts, and graphs, as well as a variety of call-outs. These visuals are intended to make the TCO content more salient and help you understand, organize, and retain the information being covered. Following is a helpful key for your reference.

| a.k.a. | Some ABA terms sound very different but share a similar meaning. These synonyms are referred to as AKAs (an acronym for "also known as"). You can find AKAs next to their related term, or look for the complete list of AKAs in the back of the Manual, starting on page 453. |
|---|---|
| [Acronym] | Acronyms (abbreviations typically using the first letter of the word) are featured throughout the Manual to help you organize and memorize concept lists in the ABA vocabulary. They are found on the left-hand column lists in the relevant concept. Sometimes, a silly sentence is included to create a little stimulus salience. The complete and organized acronym list may be found in the back starting on page 445. Try coming up with your own individualized acronyms and silly sentences to make this more memorable. |
| [*] | An asterisk is used to indicate when something is especially important or meaningful, suggesting you may want to make a mental (or physical) note. |
| [BCBA] | The Manual covers the TCO content for both the BCBA and the BCaBA exams. Each individual Domain section is introduced with a specific label that identifies the relevant BCBA TCO items and the corresponding BCaBA TCO items. However, the Manual is organized according to the BCBA TCO. |
| [BCaBA] | The Manual covers the TCO content for both the BCBA and the BCaBA exams. Each individual Domain section is introduced with a specific label that identifies the relevant BCBA TCO items and the corresponding BCaBA TCO items. However, the Manual is organized according to the BCBA TCO. |

| Breakdown | Occasionally, a more detailed breakdown is needed for specific concepts and strategies to help you better understand the topic and all of its nuances. |
| CAUTION: | If you see the caution tape, heed warning and pay close attention. This is intended to flag common misconceptions and pitfalls. |
| Definition: | This blue box is for TCO terms and their definitions. When you see this, it is probably something you should know. |
| ETHICS DEVIL WARNING | Meet the Ethics Devil. Although ethics (and the Code) is covered in Domain E, the Ethics Devil shows up throughout the Manual to point out all the ethical implications across the TCO. If you see the Ethics Devil, be sure to make note of the ethical considerations and warnings. |
| EXAM TIP | Exam-focused tips highlight exam question scenarios. Look for the Exam Tip icon next to the related terms or concepts. |
| FORMULA: | As a data-led science, ABA requires math, and math means formulas, all of which can be found in this Manual. Just look for this formula icon. |
| fyi. | FYI (an acronym for "for your information") is intended to give you a heads up on little tidbits of additional knowledge. |
| FUN FACT | Who doesn't love a fun fact? These gems of information are featured right next to the icon. |
| HINT | The Hint icon draws your attention to the salient features of a particular term or concept. It is intended to make the details more memorable, and help you make a correct discrimination on exam day. |
| Just in Case | Turns out, the BACB keeps a pretty tight lid on what they plan to include on the exam. Although the TCO is quite specific, sometimes we have to do some interpreting and guesswork. The Just in Case icon lets you know that we're not entirely sure if the subject matter is needed for exam day, but it may be important... Just in case. |
| my Notes | In addition to providing ample space in the columns, we have deliberately left an entire page blank at the start of each Domain. This is intended for ideas and notes, or however you see fit. We recommend you use it to organize your whiteboard prompts. |
| pro con | There are pros and cons with everything, even in behavior analysis. Whenever we find very specific literature about the pros and cons of a topic or concept, it is noted with the PRO and CON icons. If you don't see the icon, it doesn't mean that there aren't any pros and cons. It may just not be explicitly stated in the literature, or we chose not to include it in the Manual. |

| Icon | Description |
|:--- |:--- |
| [PROCEDURE] | Since ABA is a bunch of empirically-validated procedures, we have broken them down throughout the Manual. The Procedure icon lets you know that you're about to get a step-by-step overview. |
| [REFRESHER] | Sometimes, we have to call back to a previous section. When we revisit a concept, we give you a little refresher so that you can keep moving forward. |
| [REVIEW Qs DOMAIN] | At the end of each Domain, you will find review questions, framed as open-ended questions, matching, and true and false scenarios, intended to test your Domain-specific knowledge. You can find the answer keys in the back of the Manual starting with page 459. |
| [THINK:] | THINK (green) calls your attention to a simplified and contextualized version of a TCO topic. If a concept isn't clicking, the THINK prompt is added to make it more accessible and relatable. |
| [USE FOR] [NOT FOR] | If you have ever asked yourself, "What do I use this for?" when studying an ABA procedure, this is for you. This is a no-nonsense guide that spells out what a procedure can and cannot be used for. |
| [UMBRELLA TERMS] | A helpful way to organize concepts into categories of related terms that fall under specific umbrellas. You'll see these groupings next to the umbrella (hence the term). Being able to conceptualize and visualize the concepts that exist under the same umbrella will help you narrow the field of answer options on exam questions. |
| [CONCEPT 1] VS [CONCEPT 2] | Certain terms are easy to mix up, and it's not always simple to tell concepts apart. The versus icon is a side-by-side comparison that helps make the differences more apparent. |
| [yes] [no] | Sometimes we pose the questions and then we answer them. That's what these yes and no icons are for. We'd wait for your response, but mulling it over could take forever. |

title: ROADMAP TO EXAM DAY
body:
ROADMAP TO EXAM DAY
Plan your study schedule with this study planning guide and checklist.

[3 - 6 MONTHS PRIOR]

□ ACCEPTANCE
This exam is hard. There's no way to get around it. You might as well accept it. The good news is, the taste of success is so much sweeter knowing that you beat the odds.

P.S. This advice is true for retakers, too. Retaking the exam sucks, but there's no shame in needing another try (and you're far from alone). As hard as it may be, find acceptance and make a plan to move forward. As one former student so eloquently put it, "Get revenge on the test."

□ GET YOUR AFFAIRS IN ORDER
Complete your supervision hours, gather all the needed documents, transcripts, and paperwork to submit your application to the BACB. It's getting real.

□ SCHEDULE AN EXAM DATE
Having a set date will incentivize studying. Think of your exam date as the day you become a BCBA/BCaBA. That day is right around the corner!

□ PLAN YOUR STUDY ACTIVITIES
Now that you have purchased an awesome study manual that organizes the exam content for you, combine it with activities that include your own content, like notes and outlines. Use it with established tools like SAFMEDS or Flashcards. Don't have these handy? PTB has you covered with options for every learning style.

□ CREATE A STUDY SCHEDULE
PTB recommends studying 15-20 hours per week. Having a schedule will help you stay accountable. Treat your study sessions like appointments. If you have to cancel, then reschedule. This will also help with work-study-life balance.

□ START COMPREHENSIVE STUDYING
Join the PTB Big Exam Prep Workshop. Read the PTB ABA Exam Study Manual. Review source materials like textbooks and relevant journal articles. Listen and watch videos. Write out and outline the content. Create and study your flashcards, use the PTB FlashMEDS or Small Stack SAFMEDS. Take fluency drills and some mock exams too, for good measure.

□ BUILD EXAM TAKING SKILLS
If you want to pass the Big ABA exam, you have to build your memorization, comprehension, and application skills. Memorization will help a lot; understanding what you've memorized is extremely important; and being able to apply that knowledge to exam questions, well that's your only job on the Big day!

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
Roadmap to Exam Day
[THINK:] 3 - 6 MONTHS PRIOR
- RECRUIT A STUDY BUDDY
Connect with a fellow candidate to study and learn together, and teach and test each other on the material. Working with another person increases accountability, learning opportunities, salience, and is just more fun. Choose your study buddy wisely.
[THINK:] 1 MONTH PRIOR
- SIGN UP FOR THE PTB BIG EXAM PREP WORKSHOP
If you are nervous about all the content, managing your time, organizing your materials, or just feel that you would benefit from the accountability provided by a structured study workshop, join the PTB Big Exam Prep Workshop for up to 14 weeks of access to study materials and 6 weeks of weekly live classes. Participation will keep you on a study track for up to 14 weeks. Check it out or email PTB at help@passthebigabaexam.com with questions.
- TAKE CARE OF YOURSELF
We liken the exam to a marathon. If you have ever run a marathon (we haven't), then you know that taking care of your body is a Big part of a successful run. Making sure you sleep, eat a healthy diet, and get fresh air will help revive you and keep that brain working. Remember: you're training your brain. You have to feed it, warm it up, stretch it, and nurture it. We know that doesn't sound very 'behavioral' (sorry not sorry).
- KEEP UP THE INTENSIVE STUDYING
By now you should have a solid study routine in place. Keep that up in this final month, especially the study activities that you have found most helpful and motivating.
- PLAN YOUR WHITEBOARD
The whiteboard is meant to serve as scratch paper and response prompts. Take some time to plan the exact content that you will include. Memorize your whiteboard content, and practice filling it out from memory prior to mock exams. You'll be glad you did. By the way, creating the whiteboard is not a generic process. It should be individualized to you to include only what you need.
- TAKE MOCK EXAMS
Mock exams can be a really helpful resource to assess your readiness. If you haven't already done so, be sure to take a complete mock exam- one that mimics the actual BCBA exam. Be sure to use mock exams from trusted sources. Domain- specific mock exams can be helpful for more focused help. This is how application skills are established. Practice makes perfect.
Check out the selection of PTB Mock Exams, including mini mocks you can target by Domain, a complete mock that simulates the exam experience. Or, if you want a live review focused on specific Domains, check out the PTB MiniBig.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual | Roadmap to Exam Day
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual | Roadmap to Exam Day
-- | --

[1 MONTH PRIOR]

- **SIMULATE THE EXAM EXPERIENCE**
  When taking mock exams, create a Pearson VUE-like atmosphere. Set a timer to take a 175-question mock exam. If you plan to wear earplugs on the Big day, do so for the mock exam as well. Fill out that whiteboard and use it. Set up a divider to create the claustrophobic cubicle environment, and any other elements that may throw you off your game when sitting for the exam. All of this will help you better role-play the Big day.

- **MAKE SOME LIFESTYLE ADJUSTMENTS**
  This is a good time to start reducing and avoiding extra stressors, like Big life changes, new projects, new jobs, diets, partying and staying out late (even one glass of wine can make you tired and less productive the next day). Make sure to get plenty of sleep!

- **MIX THINGS UP**
  Mix up your study materials. Study out of order and out of context, to promote generalization. Studying in content order can actually prompt correct responses, so randomize and mix it up.

- **EXPLORE YOUR EXAM CENTER**
  Being prepared will offset exam anxiety so make sure you know where you're going, what you're bringing, and any particulars of your exam center. They all do vary, so investigate ahead of time. Confirm the address, parking information, indoor temperature, wardrobe policy, access to locker/food, earplugs, type/size of whiteboard, etc. Make sure you have the needed identification. You need two forms of valid identification. Both must show your full name exactly as it appears on your BACB account. Both must have your signature and be current. The primary identification must be government-issued and also include a photo.

[1 WEEK PRIOR]

- **TAKE A STUDY BREAK**
  Take some time away from studying before you burn out: dinner with friends, see a movie, or just veg out on the couch with your favorite TV show. It's OK to do something other than study!

- **STOP CRAMMING**
  If you've been committed to a study routine, you're probably in pretty good shape by now. The most effective way to use this last week is reviewing the areas that have been most difficult, scored lower on mock exams or previous Big exam attempts.

- **REVIEW STUDY MATERIALS**
  Your manual, flashcards, SAFMEDS or PTB FlashMEDS will come in handy right about now, for light review. No need to reference the denser textbooks and journal articles anymore.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual | Roadmap to Exam Day
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual | Roadmap to Exam Day

[EXAM DAY]

- EAT WELL
Eat a good breakfast and/or lunch. This is not the day to give up caffeine or carbohydrates. Make sure to eat some protein, too. You'll need your brain running on all cylinders.

- DOUBLE CHECK YOU HAVE ALL THE ITEMS YOU WILL NEED
Your IDs, water, snacks, documents, etc. Some testing centers allow you to access your snacks when you take a break.

- BE ON TIME/EARLY
Arrive at the test center 30 minutes prior to your appointment to allow sufficient time to park and check-in.

- DO A LAST PASS OF YOUR NOTES
Review your last glance notes and whiteboard plan.

- DON'T FREAK OUT
Exam centers are intimidating. They are very high security and this process may increase your anxiety. Be prepared for that. Ask your friends with exam experience about your mutual exam centers.

[DURING THE EXAM]

- USE YOUR WHITEBOARD
You get a whiteboard and a dry erase marker. Fill out that whiteboard. Write down every formula, acronym, hint, that you practiced, planned for, and remember. Even the easy stuff. Write it all down. If you followed our advice and rehearsed this ahead of time, this will hopefully be a piece of cake.

- TAKE A BREAK, OR A FEW
Even if it's a short one, you need to move your body and change your scenery (have a snack, use the restroom, stretch). It is crucial that you don't spend four hours looking at a computer screen. NOTE: the exam clock doesn't stop, so be mindful of the time.

- TAKE YOUR TIME, BUT HURRY UP
Leave time to review your answers at the end. Unless you are the type to second-guess and change correct answers, then don't. If you have used the PTB Self-Monitoring Test-Taking Form, then you will know this about yourself ahead of time, and plan accordingly.

- KNOW WHEN TO MOVE ON
Don't spend time on things you are confused about or can't remember. This will cause you to lose confidence. There is plenty of time to come back to a question. It is OK not to know everything. Even Skinner wouldn't know all the answers, or maybe he would. We don't really know. We never met him. Remember, you don't need to get 100%.

title: [DURING THE EXAM]
body:
[DURING THE EXAM]

- ☐ **TAKE A GUESS**
  Don't leave any question blank. You have a 25% chance of getting it right with a guess.

- ☐ **NARROW YOUR FIELD**
  For each exam question, eliminate the obvious wrong choices, made up words, items that fall under different umbrellas, and redundancies. Doing this will increase your odds.

- ☐ **LOOK AT THE LAST SENTENCE FIRST**
  This will help you to identify the call to action. Knowing what the question is asking, will help you identify important key words and eliminate useless information.

- ☐ **WATCH OUT FOR NEGATION WORDS**
  Pay attention to words like 'not', 'except', 'other than', in exam scenarios. These words negate what is being asked. Remember: a double negative equals a positive.

[AFTER THE EXAM]

- ☐ **GO GET YOUR RESULTS**
  Results are available immediately at the front desk of the testing center. Submit your exam, take a deep breath and go get the news.

[I BEAT THE ODDS / BCBA]

- ☐ **IMMEDIATELY BECOME A BCBA AND START ACTING LIKE A BOSS**
  Your certification is effective immediately and you'll find your certificant number in your BACB account within 24 hours.

  Update your email signature to include your BCBA certification. You will remember your first email using your new signature forever. You can even surprise your friends and family with your results by sending them an email with your new signature.

- ☐ **TELL YOUR BOSS YOU'RE READY FOR NEW BUSINESS CARDS WITH YOUR NEW CREDENTIAL**
  This is the most fun part. You may not even need business cards for your job, but you should absolutely get some to celebrate your certification.

- ☐ **SHARE YOUR GOOD NEWS WITH PTB**
  We want to know. Plus, you can help inspire other students who are on their journey. And, if you completed the PTB Big Exam Prep Workshop, PTB will pay for your first year membership with Association of Professional Behavior Analysts (APBA). To redeem, email help@passthebigabaexam.com with a photo of your BACB letter.

- ☐ **CELEBRATE**
  Enjoy the amazing feeling. You've worked hard and you earned this!

title: BCBA
body:
BCBA

A.1 Identify the goals of behavior analysis as a science (i.e., description, prediction, control).

BCaBA

A.1 Explain the goals of behavior analysis as a natural science (i.e., description, prediction, control).

THREE LEVELS OF SCIENTIFIC UNDERSTANDING

The goal of behavior analysis is to scientifically understand the variables that affect the behavior of living organisms across three levels of understanding.

[THINK:]
3 LEVELS OF SCIENTIFIC UNDERSTANDING

Description
Prediction
Control

1. Description:
- First level of scientific understanding.
- Describe the facts that are derived from observing behavior.
- Quantify and classify these observed events to test for possible relationships.
- **Example:** When we organize and categorize observations into ABC data.
- **THINK:** Organize information to make a prediction (hypothesis) for further exploration.

| A | B | C |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parent denied child access to a desired toy. | Child screamed and attempted to hit the parent. | Parent gave the child the desired toy. |

*ABC chart. Description.*

2. Prediction a.k.a. correlation, covariation:
- Second level of scientific understanding.
- With control, a primary goal of the science of behavior.
- Look at descriptions of events to make a hypothesis about function.
- Identify the probability of one event occurring when another event occurs.
- **Example:** When repeat ABC observations show a consistent relationship between the occurrence of two events, you can predict a function.
- **THINK:** Hypothesize about function.

| A | B | C | [Outcome] |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parent denied child access to a desired toy. | Child screamed and attempted to hit the parent. | Parent gave the child the desired toy. | Hypothesized function = Access. |
| Parent denied child access to a desired toy. | Child screamed and attempted to hit the parent. | Parent gave the child the desired toy. | |

*ABC chart: Prediction.*

title: THREE LEVELS OF SCIENTIFIC UNDERSTANDING (Cont'd)
body:
### THREE LEVELS OF SCIENTIFIC UNDERSTANDING (Cont'd)

[CAUTION]: Not necessarily proof that one event causes the other; an experimental demonstration is needed to prove the relationship.

3. **Control a.k.a. causation:**
- Third and highest level of scientific understanding.
- Experimental test of the prediction.
- Experimental demonstration that manipulating one event (the independent variable) results in a change in another event (the dependent variable), and this change can be attributable only to the independent variable.
- With prediction, a primary goal of the science of behavior.
- Establishes the functional relationship.
[THINK]: Proof. Test the hypothesis to confirm what has been predicted.
*Example:* The FA proved that hitting occurred when access was denied and was less likely to occur when access was available.

![Graph: Example of control.](https://i.imgur.com/w5y5y5y.png)

title: FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS
body:
### FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS

1. **Determinism:**
- The assumption that the world is an orderly, predictable and lawful place where all events occur as a result of cause and effect.
- Everything happens because of other events.
- In ABA, this is the assumption that behavior is caused by environmental stimuli.
*Example:* Human behavior is preceded by an antecedent. It does not typically occur spontaneously without cause.
[THINK]: Everything has a cause and nothing happens out of nowhere.

title: FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS (Cont'd)
body:
FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS (Cont'd)

5 PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS
DETERMINISM
EMPIRICISM
PARSIMONY
PRAGMATISM
SELECTIONISM

2. Empiricism:
- The assumption that knowledge is built on objective observation and measurement (data).
- Reliance on a detailed description of events and objective quantification (measurement).
Example: "I drink five sodas a day" vs. "I drink a lot of soda."
THINK: Evidence-based, experimental, data-based scientific approach.
THINK: Empiricism = Evidence = Facts = Data

3. Parsimony:
- The assumption that the simplest and already-established theory, requiring the fewest assumptions, must be ruled out before considering more complex explanations.
THINK: Explanations based on our science first.
Example: It's more parsimonious to attribute a client's behavior to a maintained consequence before blaming Mercury in retrograde.
Example: The infant cries when he is hungry because in the past, crying has resulted in getting a bottle, vs. the infant cries because Mercury is in retrograde.

4. Pragmatism:
- The assumption that what is discovered in research is only useful when there are practical positive outcomes (e.g., effective for a client).
- Relying on outcomes in an applied setting to verify the effectiveness of a procedure.
Example: Even though the research shows that a DRO is an effective strategy for eliminating undesirable behaviors, it wasn't effective with Janine, therefore her BCBA chose a procedure that had better outcomes for Janine.
THINK: If it works, don't fix it.
Example: The concepts of reinforcement, punishment, and prompt are pragmatic, because the terms can only be applied if there is a specific effect on behavior (e.g., behavior increases, decreases or is successfully evoked).

5. Selectionism:
- The assumption that behavior evolves and is maintained by consequences (function).
Example: Behavior that is followed by reinforcement is more likely to be maintained and to produce more sophisticated repertoires.
THINK: Selection by consequences.

title: FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS (Cont'd)
body:
FIVE PHILOSOPHICAL ASSUMPTIONS UNDERLYING THE SCIENCE OF BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS (Cont'd)

[USE FOR] Just in Case

Although the TCO doesn't list these terms, some literature also includes them as philosophical assumptions.

1. Experimentation:
- Basic strategy of most sciences.
- Requires manipulating variables (IVs) to see their effects on the behavior (DV).
- Controlled comparison of the DV under two or more conditions (IVs).
- Determine if one event caused another event.
- Requires that all variables be controlled except the DV.
THINK: Research, functional analysis/control.

2. Replication:
- One experiment is valuable, but it's not enough; we need reliability.
- Repeat experiments to determine their reliability.
- Determine usefulness of findings.
- Discover and correct mistakes.
THINK: Science is a self-correcting enterprise.

3. Philosophical doubt:
- A continuously critical eye on the results of studies/work with clients.
- Question even after reliable findings.
- Be open to being wrong.
THINK: Be a healthy skeptic and question the truth.

A.3 Explain behavior from the perspective of radical behaviorism.

A.3 Describe and explain behavior from the perspective of radical behaviorism.

RADICAL BEHAVIORISM

- B.F. Skinner contribution.
- Seeks to understand all human behavior, both public and private.
- Subscribes to the belief that one's private events (covert behavior) should be analyzed using the same behavioral principles as directly observable (overt) behaviors.
- Response to private events is as significant as response to public events (e.g., private stimuli can evoke and affect behavior).
- Responses to private events can be private or public.
Example: A sad memory is a private event that evokes crying which is a public response to the private event.
Example: A headache is a private event only experienced by the individual who is feeling it.

FUN FACT "Radical" because up to this point behavior was considered to be the directly observable stuff.

title: RADICAL BEHAVIORISM
body:
RADICAL BEHAVIORISM
(Cont'd)

[BOX: Private events: Covert events (stimuli) taking place inside the skin that are solely accessible or detectable by the individual experiencing the event (e.g., thoughts, pain, feelings, ideas, sensations). Influenced by function, just like public events.]

[CAUTION: Don't confuse radical behaviorism with mentalism.]

[BCBA] A.4 Distinguish among behaviorism, the experimental analysis of behavior, applied behavior analysis, and professional practice guided by the science of behavior analysis.

[BCaBA] A.4 Distinguish among behaviorism, the experimental analysis of behavior, applied behavior analysis, and professional practice guided by the science of behavior analysis.

FOUR BRANCHES OF
BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS

[BOX: 4 BRANCHES OF
BEHAVIOR ANALYSIS
Behaviorism
EAB
ABA
Professional Practice]

1. Behaviorism:
- Examines the philosophical, theoretical, historical, and methodological issues within the science of behavior.
- Contrasts mentalism which often has difficulty making predictions that could be tested using experimental methods.
- Environmental (not mentalistic) explanation of behavior.
- Today's behaviorism = Skinner's radical behaviorism.

2. Experimental analysis of behavior (EAB):
- Research on basic processes and principles; is conducted mainly in laboratories.
- Human and non-human subjects.
[THINK: Controlled settings.]

3. Applied behavior analysis (ABA):
- Applied research.
- An applied science that uses the behavior principles derived from EAB, to improve socially important behavior.
- Involves assessing the environmental influences on behavior, assessment-based intervention, and data-based decision-making.
- Behavior analysts that assess, monitor, analyze, revise (if needed), and communicate the effects of their work.
- Creates behavior-change tactics that can:
  - Increase behavior.
  - Teach and maintain behavior.
  - Make behavior sensitive to environmental events.
  - Generalize behavior.
  - Reduce challenging behavior.
- Technology for improving behavior.

ABA
Behavioral
Applied
Technological
Conceptually

1. Behavioral:
- The subject of interest is the behavior in need of improvement.
- Targeted behavior must be measurable.
- Ask whose behavior has changed (the client's or observer's).
[THINK:] We, as behavior analysts are behavioral because, in our work, the subject of interest is clearly defined, measurable and observable behavior.

2. Applied:
- Improve socially significant behaviors in real-world settings (e.g., social language, academic, daily-living, self-care, vocational, and/or recreational and leisure skills).
[THINK:] Improving individuals' everyday lives.
- Help significant others (e.g., parents, peers, employers) behave more positively towards the client.
[THINK:] We, as behavior analysts, are applied because our work takes place in applied settings, targeting the socially significant problem behaviors where they occur (home, school, park, etc.).

3. Technological:
- Requires that procedures are defined clearly and in detail so they are replicable (like a recipe) and can generate the same results repeatedly/reliably.
[THINK:] Direct and precisely replicable procedures.

- When an experimenter can control the occurrence and non-occurrence of the target behavior.
- Exhibit as much control as possible given the boundaries of the treatment setting and behavior.
- Believability - is there enough experimental control to prove a reliable functional relation?
[THINK:] We need to know the function to do our jobs!
[THINK:] Functional relation; control; causation; proof.
[THINK:] We, as behavior analysts, are analytic because, in our work, we assess for the function of behavior, and we base our treatments on that function.

6. Generality:
- Behavior change that persists across time in conditions that differ from the original intervention conditions (e.g., across other settings, behaviors, and people).
[THINK:] Generalization.
[THINK:] We, as behavior analysts, program for generalization to ensure the behavior changes we produce continue to occur in other settings, and with other people.

7. Effective:
- Practical improvement.
- Behavior change creates a socially significant difference in a person's life and in the lives of the people who live with and interact with them.
[THINK:] We, as behavior analysts, are effective because our work results in significant and measurable changes to an individual's life.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING:] Code Standard 2.01: Providing Effective Treatment:
Behavior analysts prioritize clients' rights and needs in service delivery. They provide services that are conceptually consistent with behavioral principles, based on scientific evidence, and designed to maximize desired outcomes for, and protect all, clients, stakeholders, supervisees, trainees, and research participants from harm. Behavior analysts implement non-behavioral services with clients only if they have the required education, formal training, and professional credentials to deliver such services.

B.1 Identify and distinguish among behavior, response, and response class.
B.1 Identify and distinguish among behavior, response, and response class.
BCBA
BCaBA

BEHAVIOR
- What living organisms say, do, think, and/or feel.
- The subject matter of behavior analysis.
- Large set of responses that share physical dimensions/functions.
- How living organisms interact with their environment.
- Action that has an effect on the environment.
- Includes movement within the skin, not observable by others.
- THINK: Verbs, activity, movement.
- THINK: Behavioral dimension of ABA.
- Example: Study behavior, clapping hands, thinking about an old boyfriend, shifting eye gaze in another direction.
- CAUTION: Not movement produced by an outside force, like being pushed by another person.
Repertoire: All the behaviors a person can do; a collection of learned skills related to a specific task or a specific setting.
Example: Language skills; daily routines; practicing ABA; cooking; study behaviors.

ENVIRONMENT
- An elaborate and always changing universe of events.
- In ABA, refers to stimulus conditions that are internal and external to the individual.
- Events that differ moment to moment.
- Influences behavior through stimulus changes.
- fyi. Behavior doesn't occur without an environment.

RESPONSE
- A single instance of behavior.
- Measurable unit of analysis in the science of behavior analysis.
- Example: If clapping one's hands at the end of a performance is a behavior, then each individual clap is a response.

RESPONSE CLASS
- A group of behaviors that have the same function.
- Important to us because behavior analysis looks at how behavior affects the environment, functionally.
- All the behaviors in a specific response class have the same effect on the environment.
- Similar behaviors that are strengthened or weakened collectively as a result of operant conditioning.

RESPONSE CLASS (Cont'd)
THINK: A group of behaviors that meet the same need. Example: Exam prep behaviors serve the same function but can look topographically different (e.g., reading this manual, watching videos, taking mock exams, attending workshops, filling out flashcards, SAFMEDS, etc.).

[FUN FACT] Responses in the same response class can look different. Members of some response classes may have widely varying forms (e.g., there are many ways to get dressed), but topographical variations among members of other response classes can be limited (e.g., an individual's signature, grip on a golf club, etc.).

IS IT A BEHAVIOR?
[EXAM TIP] Since behavior is the subject of interest for behavior analysts, it is important to be able to define it. Here are a few questions you can ask yourself to make better discriminations.

- Is it an action, a verb?
  THINK: Running, moving arm, crying, frowning, collecting change, thinking about the exam.
- Is it a label?
  THINK: Tired, happy, sad, interested-these are adjectives not verbs.
- Is it a condition/state?
  THINK: Hungry, anxious, depressed-these are adjectives not verbs.
- Does it pass the mentalism test? Mentalistic terminology rarely describes behavior.
  THINK: Experiencing anxiety, confusion, depression, or mindfulness.
- Does it pass the operational definition test?
  THINK: If you can't operationally define it so that it can be measured by a person, it's not behavior. Example: Feeling negative because you're jealous: Try to define it. You can't!
- Does it pass the dead man's test?
  THINK: If a dead man can do it, it ain't behavior. Example: Although being knocked down by a strong wind is not behavior (a dead man would also be blown over), moving arms and hands in front of your face, tucking and rolling, and yelling, "Whoa!" as you are being blown over are behaviors.
  THINK: Weekend at Bernie's (it's a funny movie).

title: STIMULUS (Cont'd)
body:
STIMULUS (Cont'd)

3. Exteroceptors: Receive stimulation from the five senses (i.e., hearing, seeing, touching, smelling, and tasting; external events). Most often studied by behavior analysts.
   Example: Smelling smoke, tasting BBQ, hearing a bird, touching a soft blanket.

STIMULUS CLASS

- A group of stimuli that may vary physically but share a set of common elements and have a common effect on a response class (behavior).
- Members of a stimulus class can share similarities in one or more dimensions (e.g., form, timing, function).
- Members of a stimulus class tend to evoke or abate the same behavior or response class.

[5 TYPES OF STIMULUS CLASSES]
- Formal
- Temporal
- Functional
- Feature
- Arbitrary

Fun times for family activities

FIVE DIFFERENT TYPES OF STIMULUS CLASSES:
1. Formal.
2. Temporal.
3. Functional.
4. Feature.
5. Arbitrary.

FORMAL STIMULUS CLASS

- A group of stimuli that share certain physical features (i.e., topographies).
  Example: Stimuli that are the same size, color, intensity, weight; or spatial positions in relation to other objects (e.g., prepositions: On top of the TV or to the left of the TV; adjectives: Things that are round, things that are red, etc.).
- Stimuli in this group can be socially mediated (e.g., requests from parents) or non-social (e.g., a bad smell; loud noise; locked door).
  THINK: A labeling program by feature, such as things that are green.

TEMPORAL STIMULUS CLASS

- A group of stimuli that are related by their place in time.
- Antecedents: Stimulus changes that exist or occur before a behavior of interest. Important for learning and motivation.
- Consequences: Stimulus changes that occur after a behavior of interest. Important for increasing or decreasing future behaviors.
- Antecedent and consequent stimuli determine what is learned.
  Example: SDs and MOs are part of a temporal stimulus class because they occur prior to behavior. Reinforcement and punishment are part of a different temporal stimulus class because these stimuli occur after a behavior.

FORMAL STIMULUS CLASS VS. FEATURE STIMULUS CLASS
A formal stimulus class includes different stimuli with a common feature, such as things that are big (e.g., skyscrapers, elephants, the ocean), or things that are round (e.g., tires, the sun, a bowl), etc.

[fyi] The respondent conditioning process can also include pairing a neutral stimulus (NS) with a conditioned stimulus (CS).
Example: Once the dog responds to the tone (CS), the tone can be paired with the researcher moving their hand to manipulate the tone (NS), and now the hand movement is also a conditioned stimulus that elicits salivation (conditioned response).

OPERANT BEHAVIOR

[HINT] O is for operant and ontogenic.

[PROCEDURE] Operant: An instance of behavior whose consequences modify and control the occurrence of that behavior in the future.
THINK: Learned behavior.

- A behavior established and maintained by a history of consequences.
- Voluntary and learned behavior, selected by consequences.
  THINK: Selectionism from the philosophical assumptions. (A.2)
- Ontogenic: Learned behaviors that result from an interaction with one's settings; operant behavior is the product of one's individual history.
- Encompasses both reinforcement and punishment.
- Defined by function (not topography).
- Product of operant conditioning.
  Example: Reading, singing, dancing, and remembering an old boyfriend are all behaviors learned through consequences.
  THINK: All the behaviors a person has learned to do.

[EXAM TIP] On exam questions, remember operant behavior is emitted and/or evoked. NOT elicited.

OPERANT
CONDITIONING

a.k.a. ABC, 3-term
contingency,
behavioral,
contingency, stimulus-
response-stimulus
(S-R-S) model.

- How operant behavior is born.
- A 3-term contingency known as the ABCs of behavior, which involves an occasion for a behavior ($A/S^D$), the behavior itself (B), and the consequence (C) that follows that behavior.
- Determines the future of that behavior's occurrence or nonoccurrence.
  Example: At the drive through Jenna is asked, "What would you like to order?" ($A/S^D$) Jenna places her order (B), which she receives and enjoys (C) so much so that she frequents this restaurant whenever she craves a cheeseburger.
  THINK: What behavior analysts do for a living.
  A -> B -> C

RESPONDENT-
OPERANT
INTERACTIONS

- Respondent and operant conditioning can occur simultaneously.
  Example: Mabel is at the office about to warm up her favorite leftovers. She places the food in the microwave, starts the timer, and goes back to her desk. A few minutes later, she hears the microwave timer beeping and begins to salivate. She walks to the microwave to get her food and eats her food.

RESPONDENT-OPERANT INTERACTIONS (Cont'd)

**The respondent part of this scenario:** The food being presented (unconditioned stimulus) elicits salivation (unconditioned response). The sound of the microwave timer beeping (neutral stimulus) has been paired with the presentation of food (unconditioned stimulus), which results in the microwave beep becoming a conditioned stimulus. And now the microwave beep elicits Mabel's salivation (conditioned response).

*ABC chart: Respondent breakdown.*

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | Food (US) + Beep (NS) | |
| | US + NS | UR | |
| | Food (US) + Beep (NS) | Salivation (UR) | X |
| | Beep (CS) | Salivation (CR) | X |

**The operant part of this scenario:** Mabel's hunger (MO), combined with the beeping of the microwave (SD), signals that her food is available. This evokes the behavior of taking the food out of the microwave (response), which leads to contacting the delicious food (reinforcer). This then leads to the likelihood of this behavior happening in the future when the same conditions are present (MO/SD).

*ABC chart: Operant breakdown.*

| MO | SD | B(R) | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hunger + Beep | Get food. | Enjoy food. | |

## CONSEQUENCE

- A stimulus change that comes after a behavior and changes the likelihood of that response occurring in the future.
- Critical part of operant conditioning.
- Only affects future behavior.
- THINK: Learning occurs through consequences.
- The three principles of behavior are based on consequences.

**THREE PRINCIPLES OF BEHAVIOR:**
1. Punishment
2. Extinction
3. Reinforcement

- Scientifically derived rules of nature.
- All ABA strategies are derived from these three principles.
- THINK: Conceptually systematic dimension of ABA. (A.5)

PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

[BCBA] B.4 Identify and distinguish between positive and negative reinforcement.

[BCaBA] B.4 Identify and distinguish between positive and negative reinforcement contingencies.

REINFORCEMENT CONTINGENCY

a.k.a. SR.

- The number one principle and major part of most behavior change procedures.
- Defined as a stimulus change that follows a behavior, that results in that behavior occurring more often in the future.
- A basic principle of operant conditioning.
- Can be either:
  - An organic process that is defined by an observed increase in behavior, following a specific consequence.
  Example: After eating her first delicious Girl Scout cookies, Adryan immediately ate another one.
  - OR, a procedure of applying a specific consequence to deliberately increase the occurrence of a target behavior.
  Example: To increase Dale's on-task behavior, his teacher gives him a token for each minute that he is able to stay engaged in an academic table-top activity, and the duration of on-task behavior increases.
- Reinforcement depends on motivation (MOs alter the current value of stimulus changes as reinforcement).
  Example: Faith will only hold a cup of water under the faucet tab when she is thirsty.

[CAUTION]: The IMMEDIACY of the reinforcer is critical.
[THINK]: Temporal relation.

A response becomes more frequent in the future if previously followed by a reinforcer or an increase in a reinforcer within:00 -:03 seconds. Delayed consequences aren't technically reinforcement, but they can still influence behavior (e.g., rule-governed behavior (B.18)).

WHAT DOES REINFORCEMENT DO?
- Makes antecedent-stimulus conditions relevant.
- Promotes stimulus control by making responding in the presence of the SD more likely (and not in the presence of the SΔ).
- Increases future responding.
- Maintains behavior that is already occurring.
[THINK]: Intermittent reinforcement (B.9).
- If a consequence causes the behavior to continue in the same way, this is also reinforcement.
  Example: When Matt is thirsty and sees a water fountain, he drinks water from the fountain. This relieves his thirst, so he continues to drink water if he sees a fountain when he is thirsty.

[EXAM TIP]: On test questions look for an increase in behavior, otherwise it's not a reinforcement contingency.

NEGATIVES REINFORCEMENT CONTINGENCY (Cont'd)

[EXAM TIP]
On test questions, look for scenarios that describe relief, escape, or avoidance and an increase in future behavior.

--- Breakdown ---
**Behavior:** Rubbing aloe vera on a sunburn.
**Consequence:** Relief from pain. (Something removed(-).)
**Future:** Rubbing aloe vera on sunburn increases.

2 TYPES OF NEGATIVE REINFORCEMENT

1. ESCAPE

2. AVOIDANCE
- Discriminated Avoidance
- Free-Operant Avoidance

Umbrella terms: Two types of negative reinforcement.

ESCAPE CONTINGENCY
- When a behavior leads to the termination of an ongoing aversive stimulus or unpleasant situation. So it's a good thing!
[THINK]: It's already happening and you need to get out of it.
**Example:** Turning down the volume of loud music (escape from loud music).

--- Breakdown ---
**Behavior:** Turning down the volume.
**Consequence:** Escape from loudness. (Loudness removed (-).)
**Future:** Turn down volume when music is too loud.

**Example:** Walking out of a boring lecture (escape from a boring lecture).

--- Breakdown ---
**Behavior:** Walking out of lecture.
**Consequence:** Escape from boredom. (Boredom removed (-).)
**Future:** Walk out when lectures are boring.

AVOIDANCE CONTINGENCY
- When a response prevents or postpones the presentation of an aversive stimulus/unpleasant situation. So it's a good thing!
- More common than escape!
[THINK]: Get away from it before it comes.

Domain B: B.5

BCBA B.5 Identify and distinguish between positive and negative punishment contingencies.
BCaBA B.5 Identify and distinguish between positive and negative punishment contingencies.

PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY
a.k.a. SP.
- A stimulus change following a behavior that results in that behavior occurring less often or not at all in the future.
- A basic principle of operant conditioning.
- Defined by its effect on behavior (function), not its form.
- Just because something is perceived as aversive doesn't make it punishment- future behavior must decrease!
Example: A reprimand, which is generally considered aversive or punishing, can only be considered "punishment" if it decreases the behavior that it follows.
THINK: Future behavior must decrease or it's not a punishment contingency.
Example: You get a speeding ticket and, as a result, your speeding decreases in the future.

DISCRIMINATIVE EFFECTS OF PUNISHMENT (S^DP)
- When a behavior occurs less often (or not at all) in certain conditions.
THINK: S^P but instead of signaling the availability of reinforcement, it's the availability of punishment that is being signaled. And since nobody likes punishment, behavior decreases in the presence of this signal.
Example: All the kids at Milton Middle School know about Mrs. Sinade. She is incredibly strict and if someone breaks a rule, she always sends them to the office for detention or writes a note home to the students' parents. This is why all the kids in her class are on their best behavior. If Mrs. Sinade is around, there is a decrease in bad behavior from everyone.

PUNISHER (SP) VS AVERSIVE STIMULUS
A stimulus change that decreases the future frequency of the behavior that immediately precedes it.
Just an unpleasant stimulus that may or may not impact future behavior.
Graphic: Punisher vs. aversive stimulus.

title: IS A THREAT A TYPE OF PUNISHMENT?
body:
## IS A THREAT A TYPE OF PUNISHMENT?

- No. Threat ≠ punisher.
- A threat precedes behavior, a punisher follows behavior.
- Both threats and punishers can decrease behavior.
- Threats are antecedent events: When a threat results in the non-occurrence or termination of a behavior, it's because the threat functions as an MO that evokes alternative behaviors to avoid the threatened consequence.

Example: The teacher threatened her class that whomever didn't complete their classwork would get extra homework; as a result, everyone completed their classwork.

> **Breakdown**
> Antecedent: Threat is delivered.
> Behavior: Students complete their work instead of engaging in off-task behavior.
> Consequence: Avoid extra homework.
> Future: No impact.

- Punishment is a consequence that follows the undesired behavior and, if effective, decreases the future occurrences of that behavior.

Example: The teacher gave extra homework to all the students that engaged in off-task behavior and didn't complete their classwork before the end of the day. The next day all the kids decreased their off-task behavior.

> **Breakdown**
> Antecedent: Unknown.
> Behavior: Students engaged in off-task behavior.
> Consequence: Extra homework.
> Future: Decrease in off-task behavior.

title: POSITIVE PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY
body:
# POSITIVE PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY
a.k.a. Type I punishment, SP+.

- When the addition of a stimulus immediately following a behavior results in a decrease in the future frequency of that behavior.
- THINK: Something aversive is added and future behavior decreases.

Example: Texting while walking makes you trip and sprain your ankle and, as a result, you decrease texting while walking in the future, to prevent the aversive stimulus of tripping and getting hurt.

> **Breakdown**
> Behavior: Texting while walking.
> Consequence: Tripping and falling. (Added stimulus (+).)
> Future: Texting and walking decreases.

Example: A mom shouts, "No!" after her son hits her. The hitting behavior decreases in the future because hearing "No!" shouted was aversive for her son.

title: POSITIVE PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY (Cont'd)
body:
POSITIVE PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY (Cont'd)

[Breakdown]
**Behavior:** Hitting.
**Consequence:** Reprimanded with "no". (Added stimulus (+).)
**Future:** Hitting decreases.

[EXAM TIP]: On exam questions, there must be a decrease in future behavior or it's not a punishment contingency.

NEGATIVE PUNISHMENT CONTINGENCY
a.k.a. Type II punishment, penalty principle, penalty contingency, SR-.

- When a response is followed immediately by the removal (or a decrease in the intensity) of a preferred/appetitive stimulus, and this results in a decrease in the future frequency of similar responses under similar conditions.
[THINK:]: Something desirable is taken away and future behavior decreases.
**Example:** Bob is at a restaurant by himself. He isn't finished with his meal, but leaves his table to go to the restroom. When he returns, his food is gone. (The waiter thought Bob had left and removed his plate.) In the future, Bob no longer leaves his table unattended when dining alone unless he is done.

[Breakdown]
**Behavior:** Leaving the table unattended.
**Consequence:** Plate of food removed. (Removal of desired item (-).)
**Future:** Leaving the table decreases.

- Future behavior must decrease or it's not a punishment contingency.

REINFORCEMENT VS. PUNISHMENT
[EXAM TIP]: How to tell if it is positive or negative, reinforcement or punishment in exam question scenarios.

FOUR-STEP FORMULA TO HELP YOU MAKE THE CORRECT DISCRIMINATION

| | |
|:--- |:--- |
| **STEP 1:** Identify: Behavior of interest. | E.g., shouting, running, asking a question. |
| **STEP 2:** Identify: Consequence. (Was something added or removed?) | Something added (+) = Positive. Something removed (-) = Negative. |
| **STEP 3:** Identify: Change in behavior. (Did the behavior increase or decrease?) | Behavior increased (↑) = Reinforcement. Behavior decreased (↓) = Punishment. |
| **STEP 4:** Summarize steps 2 and 3. | (+)(↑) = Positive reinforcement. (-)(↑) = Negative reinforcement. (+)(↓) = Positive punishment. (-)(↓) = Negative punishment. |

[BCaBA]

**B.6 Identify and distinguish between automatic and socially mediated contingencies.**

AUTOMATIC
REINFORCEMENT
CONTINGENCY

- When behavior is evoked, shaped, or maintained by environmental variables that are delivered without another person's mediation.
- Reinforcement that occurs without the social mediation of others.
[THINK]: Reinforcement is delivered to oneself by oneself.
- Can be delivered two ways:
  1. Reinforcement is the product of the behavior itself and produces natural sensory consequences (sounds good, looks good, tastes good, smells good, feels good to the touch), (e.g., scratching one's own itch, singing, pacing, etc.).
  2. Reinforcement is the product of the behavior's effect on the environment (e.g., organizing your closet, cooking dinner, turning on the air conditioner, etc.).

- Default meaning: When repetitive behaviors without clear function, that can seem non-purposeful, produce sensory feedback (self-stimulation).

- **COMMON MISCONCEPTION:** Repetitive, idiosyncratic and stereotypic behaviors are often referred to as producing automatic reinforcement. But, what looks like automatic reinforcement (e.g., loud vocalizations) may also have some socially mediated contingencies, like attention or escape from a demand.

[REFRESHER]: Remember: Behavior is defined by its function not its topography!

**POSITIVE AUTOMATIC REINFORCEMENT:**
- When a behavior is followed immediately by the presentation or addition of a stimulus, which increases the future frequency of that and similar behaviors under similar conditions.
- An individual's own behavior results in the addition of something desirable.

title: CONDITIONED REINFORCERS (CR)
body:
CONDITIONED REINFORCERS (CR)
a.k.a. Secondary reinforcer, learned reinforcer.

- Neutral stimuli that have been paired with one or more unconditioned or conditioned reinforcers and, as a result, begin to function as reinforcers.
- A stimulus or event that is present with (or immediately before) a previously established reinforcer, and gains the ability to act as a reinforcer on its own.
THINK: Stimulus-stimulus pairing.
THINK: Learning history required.
- The ability of a conditioned reinforcer to change behavior has to do with an individual's history with that stimulus.
- Product of ontogeny
Example: For a client to enjoy their ABA therapy, it often suggested that the RBT pair themselves with primary reinforcers (e.g., yummy snacks). By being associated with the snacks, the RBT becomes a conditioned reinforcer.
CAUTION: Don't confuse the pairing process of establishing conditioned reinforcers with respondent conditioning. Yes, both involve pairing, but the outcome is different. With conditioned reinforcers, a neutral stimulus becomes a reinforcer; with respondent conditioning, a neutral stimulus becomes an eliciting antecedent stimulus.

GENERALIZED CONDITIONED REINFORCERS (GCSR)
a.k.a. Generalized reinforcer, nonspecific reinforcer.

- A type of conditioned reinforcer that has been paired with an unlimited number of unconditioned and conditioned reinforcers.
- Doesn't depend on an MO for its effectiveness.
- So generalized that it is likely to be reinforcing at any time and to anyone. This makes it valuable and useful!
- People don't typically get satiated on GCSRs.
THINK: Money, tokens, social praise are most often associated with GCSRs.
Example: Money (or tokens in a token economy system) are reinforcing for everyone and at any time because of their pairing with almost any reinforcer.
CAUTION: A token board isn't considered a GCSR unless used as an economy system in which tokens act like money and can be exchanged (like money).

BCBA B.8 Identify and distinguish between unconditioned, conditioned, and generalized punishers.
BCaBA B.7 Identify and distinguish between unconditioned, conditioned, and generalized reinforcers and punishers.

UNCONDITIONED PUNISHERS (UCP)
- A stimulus change that decreases the frequency of any behavior that immediately precedes it, irrespective of the organism's learning history with the stimulus.

title: SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
body:
### SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
*(Cont'd)*

> **Continuous reinforcement (CRF):** Reinforcement is delivered every time the target behavior occurs. (**a.k.a.** FR 1.)

[USE FOR] The acquisition phase of novel behaviors.

**Example:** (Naturally occurring.) Flipping a light switch results in the light coming on every time.

**Example:** (Applied.) At the start of functional communication training, each communicative request is met with the specific item requested.

**THINK:** Ask and you shall receive!

> **Intermittent schedules of reinforcement (INT):** When some (but not all) instances of the target behavior are reinforced.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

RATIO SCHEDULES (Cont'd)
- [THINK:] Correct responses produce reinforcement.
- The response rate determines how quickly reinforcement is received.
- "Self-controlled" reinforcement because the client must deliver the correct number of responses to contact reinforcement.
- Produces higher rates of responding because faster responding means reinforcement comes sooner, and slower responding delays reinforcement.
- Not a time-based schedule.
- [USE FOR] Programs in which higher rates of responding are important; response maintenance.
- Large response requirements = More rapid response rates.

[CAUTION: Can negatively affect topography because going fast can hurt the quality of the response.]

- If the ratio is too large and responding decreases, decrease response requirements.

FIXED RATIO (FR)
- A ratio schedule in which a fixed number of responses have to occur before a response produces reinforcement.
- THINK: A specific count of responses is reinforced.

PATTERN OF RESPONDING PRODUCED BY FR SCHEDULES:
- Produces consistent pattern of responding after the first correct response.
- Typically produces a high rate of response.
- Low ratio requirements produce a lower response rate, while higher requirements produce a higher response rate.
- THINK: Responding speeds up with high ratio requirements to speed up access to reinforcement.
- Response requirements that are too high could decrease the rate of response, unless raised gradually over an extended period of time.
- Produces a post-reinforcement pause.

[Post-reinforcement pause: A pause in responding following reinforcement, after which responding speeds up again.]

- THINK: Pause to enjoy the reinforcement.
- The pause is affected by the size of the ratio (how many correct responses are needed) and the magnitude of reinforcement.

- Large ratios = Long pauses
- Short ratios = Short pauses
- Large magnitude = Short pause
- Small magnitude = Long pause

| FIXED RATIO (FR)
(Cont'd) | - After the pause, steady responding resumes.
[USE FOR] Reinforcing academic activities, trial-based learning programs; social initiations; programs with a certain amount of necessary product, etc.
**Example:** On an FR 7 schedule, reinforcement is delivered after the client has emitted 7 correct responses.
**Example:** (Naturally occurring.) Entering your four-digit pin at the ATM machine is an FR 4 schedule. Once four correct responses have been emitted, reinforcement (access to money) becomes available.
**Example:** (Applied.) On an FR 25 schedule, students must complete a 25-problem worksheet before getting free play time.

**FR PROTOTYPE**

``` Responses ^ | _/ | _/ B |<---- _/ | _/ A |<--_/ | _/ | |/ v +----C---------> Time ```

**KEY**
**A.** Post-reinforcement pause.
**B.** High rate of response "run."
**C.** Reinforcer delivered after the nth response.

*Graph: Fixed ratio.* | | [HINT] This is the only graph with steps. | | | VARIABLE RATIO (VR) | - A ratio schedule in which the requirement changes after delivery of reinforcement.
- A variable number of responses have to occur before the reinforcer is delivered.
- The indicated number refers to the average number of responses needed to deliver the reinforcer. In a VR 3 schedule, the requirement of responses varies, with an average of 3 responses.
**Example:** If Jenny replies to Andy's text messages on a VR 3 schedule, then she could reply to his 1st text, then his 2nd, then his 5th, then his 3rd, then his 4th, (1 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 4 = 15/5 = 3).
- Typically a computer-generated schedule. Because math is hard.
- Variable schedules are seldom used correctly in applied settings because math is hard and people usually end up guessing. The chance delivery of reinforcement lacks systematic implementation and makes the schedule ineffective.

[fyi,] The strongest basic schedule of INT reinforcement.

- **Pattern of responding produced by VR schedules:**
- Produces quick, consistent and steady rate of response.
- Does not produce a post-reinforcement pause (as FR schedules do). Why? It may be due to the uncertainty of when a response will produce reinforcement. | © 2012 - 2024, Pass the Big ABA Exam

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

VARIABLE RATIO (VR)
(Cont'd)

- Responding remains steady because the next response may produce reinforcement.
- Like FR schedules, low ratio requirements produce a lower response rate, while higher requirements produce a higher response rate.

[USE FOR] Maintaining behavior, since it's uncertain how many responses are needed to contact reinforcement when behavior tends to persist.

[THINK:] Slot machines in Las Vegas.

Example: On a VR 7 schedule, reinforcement is delivered after 7 correct responses have been emitted, then 9, then 8, then 5, and then 6 correct responses.

Example: (Applied.) A teacher gives a packet of five worksheets. Each sheet has a different number of math problems. The student starts with the first sheet which has 10 math problems. Once the student completes the 10 problems they get a check mark. The next sheet has six math problems. Once the student completes the six problems the teacher delivers another check mark. On the third sheet, there are three math problems that the student must complete to get a check mark. This continues for the next two worksheets with the opportunity to earn a total of five check marks, which are redeemable for computer time.

VR PROTOTYPE

[HINT] This graph has a super-fast and steep slope.

(Diagram of VR graph showing responses over time, labeled with A and B)

KEY
- A: High, steady rate of responding.
- B: Reinforcer delivered after meeting response contingency.

Graph: Variable ratio.

INTERVAL SCHEDULES

[HINT] Time and one correct response produces reinforcement.

- A schedule in which a certain amount of time must pass before reinforcement is available for one response.
- Rate of response is not important.

[THINK:] "Time-controlled" reinforcement.
- Preferred by staff because easier to implement, not requiring as much attention.

title: INTERVAL SCHEDULES (Cont'd)
body:
INTERVAL SCHEDULES (Cont'd)
- Preferred by clients because it requires less work. It's a win-win. THINK: Reinforcement is contingent on an interval of time, plus one correct response.
- Rate of response or pauses in responding don't matter because reinforcement comes with time passage and only one correct response.
- To increase response rate (and maintain high responding), shorten the interval. To decrease response rate, increase the interval.
fyi. Produces lower response rates than ratio schedules.
USE FOR → Programs for which a low response rate is acceptable.

COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS:
- Passage of time = Access to reinforcement. Nope! A correct response is also needed.
- The behavior must occur during the entire interval to produce reinforcement. Nope! The time just has to pass, and then only one correct response is needed.

EXAM TIP
In test question scenarios, interval schedules will have time criteria (e.g., hours, minutes, days, etc.).

FIXED INTERVAL (FI)
- A fixed amount of time must elapse before reinforcement is available for the first correct response that is emitted after the fixed period of time.
- There is no deadline for correct responding.
- Correct responses that occur during the interval are not reinforced. The next interval starts when reinforcement is delivered for the previous interval.
THINK: Constant time criteria.
- Pattern of responding produced by FI schedules:
  - Slow start but accelerating rate of response toward the end of the interval (with maximum rate at the end of the interval).
  - Interval duration influences the rate of response; larger intervals produce lower rates of response and shorter intervals produce higher rates of response.
  - Produces an FI scallop.

FI scallop: When the rate of response gradually accelerates toward the end of an interval. (Called this because of the rounded curves in the graph that resemble scallops.)

Example: When client reports are turned in, ABA supervisors get off to a slow start on the next report, but as the due date approaches, the rate of response increases to meet the deadline.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

**FIXED INTERVAL (FI)**
**(Cont'd)**

- Produces post-reinforcement pause, during the early part of the interval.
- Example: After completing all of her clients' reports for the first quarter, Janie paused all report writing activities until closer to the end of the 2nd quarter, because reinforcement isn't available until then.
- Larger FI requirement = Longer post-reinforcement pauses and vice versa.

[USE FOR] Academic task schedules; classroom rule schedules.

**Example:** On an FI 15 schedule, reinforcement is delivered for the 1st correct response that occurs after 15 minutes have passed.
**Example: (Naturally occurring.)** A paycheck is directly deposited into a bank account on the 1st and 15th of every month. It is only after the deposit is made that the funds can be used.
**Example: (Applied.)** A teacher gives a test once a week to assess weekly progress. Since the test is given at the same time each week, students don't study very hard at the beginning of the week but then really begin cramming in the days (and hours) before the test is given.

**THINK:** Last minute cramming.

**FI PROTOTYPE**

[Diagram: FI PROTOTYPE showing a graph with Responses on the y-axis and Time on the x-axis, featuring a fish icon and points labeled A, B, and C]

**KEY**
**A:** Post-reinforcement pause.
**B:** Increase in response rates.
**C:** Reinforcer delivered after the first correct response after interval.

Graph: Fixed interval.

[HINT] This graph has the scallops.

**VARIABLE INTERVAL (VI)**
- A variable (average) amount of time must elapse before reinforcement is available for the first correct response that is emitted after that period of time.
- Time requirements between reinforcement are randomized, and can change for all responses, but center around the specified number in the schedule.

**THINK:** Pop quizzes.
- Variable intervals should be systematically established, but seldom are in applied settings.
- Typically a computer-generated schedule in the lab. Because math is hard.

title: VARIABLE INTERVAL (VI)
body:
VARIABLE INTERVAL (VI)
(Cont'd)

- Variable schedules are seldom used correctly in applied settings - because math is still hard - and the chance/non-systematic delivery of reinforcement makes the schedule ineffective.
- Pattern of responding produced by VI schedules:
  - Constant, stable rate of response (few hesitations between responses).
  - Low-to-moderate rate of response.
- [fyi] Produces very few pauses in responding.
- Average interval duration influences the rate of response: Larger intervals produce lower rates of response and shorter intervals produce higher rates of response.

[USE FOR] Maintenance programs, when consistent responding is important.

**Example:** On a VI 7 schedule, reinforcement is available for the first correct response that occurs after 7 seconds, then 9, then 8, then 5, and then 6 seconds.

**Example:** (Applied.) Mr. Hiller loved a surprise pop quiz, and averaged one every 9 days (VI 9). His students, well aware of this tendency, studied very consistently, to make sure they were ready whenever a quiz popped up.

**VI PROTOTYPE**

[HINT] This graph is very similar to the VR graph (both have straight lines). But, the VI graph isn't steep (like the VR graph).

*(Graph showing Responses vs Time with a linear upward slope, labeled A at a response tick and B at a reinforcer arrow)*

**KEY**

A: Steady response rate.
B: Reinforcer delivered.

*Graph: Variable interval.*

BASIC SCHEDULES OF INTERMITTENT (INT) REINFORCEMENT

**4 BASIC SCHEDULES OF INTERMITTENT (INT) REINFORCEMENT**

| | FIXED RATIO (FR) | VARIABLE RATIO (VR) | FIXED INTERVAL (FI) | VARIABLE INTERVAL (VI) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **COUNT VS. TIME** | Count | Count | Time | Time |
| **RESPONSE PATTERN** | Consistent | Consistent | Slow Start | Consistent |

title: LIMITED HOLD (LH)
body:
LIMITED HOLD (LH)
- Adding a limited hold to an interval schedule limits the amount of time the reinforcement remains available following the end of the FI or VI interval.
  THINK: Limited time to respond.
- If the client doesn't respond within the time limit, they do not earn the reinforcement.
  Example: On VI 5 LH:30 seconds, five minutes must pass before a correct response can contact reinforcement, but only if that response is emitted within:30 seconds of the interval ending.
  [USE FOR] Decreasing response latency; building fluency; increasing academic engagement.

BASIC INTERMITTENT SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT
FOUR VARIATIONS OF BASIC INTERMITTENT SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT:
1. Lag schedule of reinforcement
2. Progressive ratio (PR) schedule of reinforcement
3. Delays to reinforcement schedule
4. Differential reinforcement of rates of responding (DRH, DRD, DRL). (G.2)

[BOX: 4 VARIATIONS OF BASIC INTERMITTENT SCHEDULES
Lag
Progressive ratio
Delays
Differential]

1. Lag schedule of reinforcement:
- A schedule in which reinforcement is delivered for a response that is different in topography, sequence, etc., from a previously reinforced response.
  [USE FOR] Increasing response variability (generalization); expanding language skills and verbal behavior repertoires; building problem-solving skills; enhancing academic and social skills.
  THINK: Do something different.
  Example: When Tim labels any shade of purple (from eggplant to lavender), he always says, "Purple" (which isn't wrong), but to program for variability his teacher uses a lag schedule of reinforcement, and reinforces any response other than purple.
  Example: When teaching intraverbals (categories), Carissa asked Matty to name different foods. To increase variability, she only provided reinforcement when he named a food that he had not given in a previous trial.

2. Progressive ratio (PR) schedule of reinforcement:
- The schedule is thinned after each successive reinforcement opportunity independent of the client's behavior, until the client's responding stops (the breaking point).

[BOX: Breaking point: When the participant stops responding. The primary measure of interest in a progressive schedule because it helps to assess the strength of a reinforcer.
THINK: How far will the reinforcer go?]

title: BASIC INTERMITTENT
body:
BASIC INTERMITTENT
SCHEDULES OF
REINFORCEMENT
(Cont'd)

- A variation of the FR schedule.
- Systematically and incrementally increase fixed ratio requirements until the end of a session... or until the breaking point is reached.

Example: A tact program began on an FR 3 schedule. The client received a mini-sized candy bar after three correct responses. The schedule was then thinned to an FR 6 schedule, and so on, in increments of three. The client stopped responding when the schedule advanced to an FR 15. The staff noted that a mini candy bar is effective for up to 12 correct responses.

[USE FOR] Reinforcer assessment (F.5) and intervention.

[CAUTION]: Not a quick way to check the strength of reinforcers; high ratio demands can be aversive; not a lot of known benefits to using this schedule, therefore it's questionable whether this schedule should be used with protected populations.

3. Delays to reinforcement schedule:
- A schedule in which reinforcement for correct responding is delayed.
- Delay cues are used to signal the timing of reinforcement delivery.

Example: After learning to ask for a break instead of eloping, Jolene's team decided to thin the scheduled reinforcement (extinction, B.11). This caused elopement to return (resurgence, H.4). In order to eliminate elopement again, asking for a break was once again reinforced but on a delayed schedule.

[USE FOR] Teaching tolerating delays to gratification; functional communication training; promoting cooperative work; offsetting resurgence.

4. Differential reinforcement of rates of responding (DRH, DRD, DRL).
Differential reinforcement procedures are discussed in G.2.

BCBA B.10 Identify and distinguish among concurrent, multiple, mixed, and chained schedules of reinforcement.

COMPOUND SCHEDULES
OF REINFORCEMENT

[4 COMPOUND
SCHEDULES
Concurrent
Multiple
Chained
Mixed

Call me! Call me!]

- Formed when two or more basic reinforcement schedules are combined.
- Can include combinations of intermittent schedules (FR, VR, FI, VI), continuous schedules (CRF), differential reinforcement of rate responses (DRL, DRH), and extinction (EXT).

FOUR COMPOUND SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT:
1. Concurrent schedules of reinforcement.
2. Multiple schedules of reinforcement.
3. Chained schedules of reinforcement.
4. Mixed schedules of reinforcement.

### MIXED SCHEDULES OF REINFORCEMENT (MIX)

[HINT]
- 1 Behavior.
- No Sᴰ.
- In any order.

- Two or more basic schedules of reinforcement are presented successively and independently, in any order, for one behavior.
- Identical to multiple schedules, except without the Sᴰ to signal which schedule is currently in effect.

[THINK:] Un-signaled, separate, and random.

[USE FOR] Promoting generalization.

**Example: Mix FR 4/FI 1 (min.) schedule:** When running a labeling program with Patrick, you randomly alternate between providing reinforcement after every four correct responses, or after one minute has passed and he provides a correct response. Patrick is not aware of which schedule is in effect at any time during the program.

title: OPERANT EXTINCTION (EXT)
body:
### OPERANT EXTINCTION (EXT)
**a.k.a.** Extinction.

[3 EXTINCTION VARIATIONS]
- Positive reinforcement
- Automatic reinforcement
- Negative reinforcement

- A procedure in which a maintaining reinforcer for a target behavior is discontinued.

[THINK:] No reinforcement means the behavior isn't effective. So why do it?

- Third principle of ABA.
- Results in the reduction of frequency, duration and intensity of a target behavior.

[CAUTION: Extinction is NOT a punishment procedure.]

- Critical to know the function of the behavior to use extinction.
- Functional Analysis prior to treatment ensures the efficacy of extinction and should be used to prescribe the correct type of extinction.

[USE FOR] Decreasing and eliminating behavior.

#### THREE EXTINCTION VARIATIONS (Based on function):
1. **Positive reinforcement extinction:**
   - Withholding attention or access, when the target behavior occurs.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: OPERANT EXTINCTION (EXT) (Cont'd)
body:
OPERANT EXTINCTION (EXT) (Cont'd)

- Socially mediated.
THINK: Ignoring; not granting access to desired items.
Example: Camille hates to see her 4-year-old, non-vocal daughter cry, which she typically does when she is denied access to potato chips. So Camille usually gives in. An assessment confirmed that crying was in fact maintained by access to tangibles and an extinction procedure was put into place. This involved teaching Camille to be consistent and ensuring that her daughter's crying never resulted in access to potato chips. Now when her daughter cries, Camille (unlike in the past) does not give her chips and crying for chips has ceased to exist.
Reducing behaviors with an attention or access to tangibles function
USE FOR → tangibles function

2. Automatic reinforcement extinction (a.k.a. sensory extinction):
- Withholding access to automatic reinforcement.
THINK: Preventing sensory consequences.
Example: Jamie flips the light switch on and off repeatedly to watch the lights flicker, so her BT disconnected the lightbulbs to stop the lights flickering when she flips the switch.
USE FOR → Behaviors with an automatic reinforcement function.

3. Negative reinforcement extinction (a.k.a. escape extinction):
- Withholding access to escape/preventing an escape contingency.
THINK: Preventing escape from demands (e.g., follow through).
Socially mediated.
Example: Pam claims to have a headache and leaves work early whenever there is a big work project due. Historically her boss has allowed this, but he's fed up. Now, when she tries to leave early he doesn't allow it, and she has stopped trying.
USE FOR → Behaviors with an escape function.
EXAM TIP
On exam questions about extinction, remember that the target behavior must still occur. Reinforcement, however, is withheld. What is being extinguished is not the behavior- it's the reinforcement!
CAUTION: Common exam mistakes:
- Extinction ≠ Ignoring: Unless the target behavior is maintained by attention.
- Extinction ≠ Reduction of behavior: Just because the behavior decreases doesn't necessarily mean its extinction (it could be punishment too)!
- Extinction ≠ Behavior prevented: It's the reinforcer that is prevented.
- Extinction ≠ Forgetting is when a behavior decreases due to the passage of time, without an opportunity to emit the behavior.

title: RESPONDENT EXTINCTION
body:
### RESPONDENT EXTINCTION

- Remember Pavlov? We talked about him in B.3. He's the guy who discovered respondent conditioning. Well, turns out he did more than that.

[REFRESHER] Respondent conditioning occurs when neutral stimuli (NS) achieve the capacity to elicit respondent behaviors (reflexes) that are typically elicited by specific unconditioned stimuli.

- **Respondent extinction:** Pavlov also found that the established conditioned reflex (CR) would eventually weaken if a conditioned stimulus (CS) is presented without the unconditioned stimulus (US) for a given period of time.
[THINK:] Tone presented without meat.
- Involves unpairing the conditioned stimulus (CS) and the unconditioned stimulus (US), and the conditioned stimulus (CS) becomes a neutral stimulus (NS) again.
[THINK:] Unpairing antecedents.
**Example:** When Pavlov unpaired the tone and the food by presenting the tone many times without the food, the tone lost its eliciting power and no longer elicited the dog's salivation because it returned to its neutral status (NS).

#### RESPONDENT CONDITIONING

NS + US ------------> CS

#### RESPONDENT EXTINCTION

US | CS ------------> NS

*Graphic: Respondent pairing and unpairing.*
