title: CHANGING CRITERION
body:
CHANGING CRITERION
DESIGN
(Cont'd)

- It is critical that partial reversals are included to strengthen experimental control (e.g., A-B-C-D-C-D-E-F-E).
- Functional relation shown by: How quickly and closely the level of responding changes to conform to each new criterion and remains stable in the specific criterion. If data points do not fall around the criterion lines, that means there is very little experimental control.
[THINK:] The smaller the vertical distance between the criterion line and that phase's data points, the more experimental control.

[USE FOR] Changing some dimension of a behavior that the client is already doing; to assess how criteria can control responding.

[EXAM TIP] For exam questions, remember that a changing criterion design will have one IV and one DV. It cannot be used to evaluate programs that teach/shape a novel behavior, only programs that shape a specific dimension of a behavior.

Example: A researcher may use this design to assess how a person's behavior changes when provided with reinforcement contingent upon 10 responses per minute, then 20 responses per minute then 30 responses per minute and so on.

[pro]
- Doesn't require a reversal of conditions.
- Enables an experimental analysis within the context of a gradually improving behavior.
- Good for evaluating instructional techniques.

[con]
- Can't compare treatments.
- Target behavior must be in participant's repertoire.
- Not appropriate for analyzing the effects of a program designed to teach or shape a new behavior.

**GUIDELINES FOR USING CHANGING CRITERION DESIGN:**
1. Consider length of phases:
   - Each phase serves as a baseline, so must be long enough to achieve stable responding.
   - If a behavior takes longer to change, the length of the phase must be increased.
   - The lengths of each phase must be varied.
2. Consider the magnitude of criterion changes:
   - The size of the changes between each criterion should vary to show strong functional relations.
   - Changes in size must be large enough to be detectable, but not so large as to be unachievable.
   - If data is stable, smaller-sized alterations can be used; with highly variable data, larger changes between phases will be needed to demonstrate change.
   - Avoid artificial limits on the amount of responding possible within each phase.

title: BCBA D.8 Identify rationales for conducting comparative, component, and parametric analysis.
body:
BCBA D.8 Identify rationales for conducting comparative, component, and parametric analysis.

BCaBA D.6 Distinguish among and implement comparative, component, and parametric analyses.

COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS
- A study that compares two or more IVs to assess which IV is most effective.
- Directly compares independent treatments that are not presented together as part of a treatment package.
THINK: Multielement design, multiple treatment reversal design.
[USE FOR] Comparing and selecting interventions.
Example: Using a multielement design to compare the efficacy of NCR vs. DRO to reduce a behavior.

COMPONENT ANALYSIS
a.k.a. Composite analysis, sequential withdrawal.
- A systematic assessment of two or more independent variables/components that make up a treatment package.
THINK: Assess the parts of a treatment package.

[BOX] Treatment package (a.k.a. behavioral package): A multi-component behavior intervention plan. (Common for complex behaviors.)

- Analyzes and considers the interplay of the different components:
  - Additive effects: When the effects of the individual components of a treatment package do not impact each other.
  - Multiplicative effects: When the effect of one component of a treatment package is dependent on the presence of another component.
  - Necessity: When a component is needed for a treatment package to be effective.
  - Sufficiency: When a component is as effective as the treatment package.

TWO METHODS FOR CONDUCTING COMPONENT ANALYSES:
1. Drop-out component analysis:
  - The treatment package is presented and components of the package are systematically removed.
  - If, when a component is removed, the treatment becomes ineffective, a necessary component has been identified.
  - The removal of components can tell us which ones are necessary to meet and maintain treatment goals.
  - Can be problematic if combining components masks the effectiveness of individual components, making it difficult to determine the necessity and sufficiency of individual components.

title: 6.01 CONFORMING WITH LAWS AND REGULATIONS IN RESEARCH
body:
6.01 CONFORMING WITH LAWS AND REGULATIONS IN RESEARCH
- Behavior analysts plan and conduct research in a manner consistent with all applicable laws and regulations, as well as requirements by organizations and institutions governing research activity.
- Researchers should be aware of and follow the applicable laws of their state and/or country.

[THINK:] The Code's definition of research: Any data-based activity, including analysis of preexisting data, designed to generate generalizable knowledge for the discipline. The use of an experimental design does not by itself constitute research.

6.02 RESEARCH REVIEW
- Behavior analysts conduct research, whether independent of or in the context of service delivery, only after approval by a formal research review committee.

[THINK:] The Code's definition of research review committee: A group of professionals whose stated purpose is to review research proposals to ensure the ethical treatment of human research participants. This committee might be an official entity of a government or university (e.g., Institutional Review Board, Research Ethics Board), an independent committee within a service organization, or an independent organization created for this purpose.

6.03 RESEARCH IN SERVICE DELIVERY
- Behavior analysts conducting research in the context of service delivery must arrange research activities such that client services and client welfare are prioritized. In these situations, behavior analysts must comply with all ethics requirements for both service delivery and research within the Code. When professional services are offered as an incentive for research participation, behavior analysts clarify the nature of the services, and any potential risks, obligations, and limitations for all parties.

6.04 INFORMED CONSENT IN RESEARCH
- Behavior analysts are responsible for obtaining informed consent (and assent when relevant) from potential research participants under the conditions required by the research review committee. When behavior analysts become aware that data obtained from past or current clients, stakeholders, supervisees, and/or trainees during typical service delivery might be disseminated to the scientific community, they obtain informed consent for use of the data before dissemination, specify that services will not be impacted by providing or withholding consent, and make available the right to withdraw consent at any time without penalty.

title: 6.04 INFORMED
body:
6.04 INFORMED
CONSENT IN RESEARCH
(Cont'd)

[DEFINITION BOX]
The Code's definition of research participant: Any individual participating in a defined research study for whom informed consent has been obtained.

[DEFINITION BOX]
The Code's definition of informed consent: The permission given by an individual with the legal right to consent, before participating in services or research, or allowing their info to be used or shared:
Service/research: Providing the opportunity for an individual to give informed consent for services or research involves communicating about and taking appropriate steps to confirm understanding of: 1) the purpose of the services or research; 2) the expected time commitment and procedures involved; 3) the right to decline to participate or withdraw at any time without adverse consequences; 4) potential benefits, risks, discomfort, or adverse effects; 5) any limits to confidentiality or privacy; 6) any incentives for research participation; 7) whom to contact for questions or concerns at any time; and 8) the opportunity to ask questions and receive answers.

The Code's definition of assent: Vocal or nonvocal verbal behavior that can be taken to indicate willingness to participate in research or behavioral services by individuals who cannot provide informed consent (e.g., because of age or intellectual impairments). Assent may be required by a research review committee or a service organization. In such instances, those entities will provide parameters for assessing assent.

6.05 CONFIDENTIALITY
IN RESEARCH
- Behavior analysts prioritize the confidentiality of their research participants except under conditions where it may not be possible. They make appropriate efforts to prevent accidental or inadvertent sharing of confidential or identifying information while conducting research and in any dissemination activity related to the research (e.g., disguising or removing confidential or identifying information).

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

6.06 COMPETENCE IN
CONDUCTING
RESEARCH

- Behavior analysts only conduct research independently after they have successfully conducted research under a supervisor in a defined relationship (e.g., thesis, dissertation, mentored research project).
Behavior analysts and their assistants are permitted to perform only those research activities for which they are appropriately trained and prepared. Before engaging in research activities for which a behavior analyst has not received training, they seek the appropriate training and become demonstrably competent, or they collaborate with other professionals who have the required competence. Behavior analysts are responsible for the ethical conduct of all personnel assigned to the research project.

6.07 CONFLICT OF
INTEREST IN RESEARCH
AND PUBLICATION

- When conducting research, behavior analysts identify, disclose, and address conflicts of interest (e.g., personal, financial, organization related, service related). They also identify, disclose, and address conflicts of interest in their publication and editorial activities.

6.08 APPROPRIATE
CREDIT

- Behavior analysts give appropriate credit (e.g., authorship, author-note acknowledgment) to research contributors in all dissemination activities. Authorship and other publication acknowledgments accurately reflect the relative scientific or professional contributions of the individuals involved, regardless of their professional status (e.g., professor, student).

6.09 PLAGIARISM

- Behavior analysts do not present portions or elements of another's work or data as their own. Behavior analysts only republish their previously published data or text when accompanied by proper disclosure.

6.10 DOCUMENTATION
AND DATA RETENTION
IN RESEARCH

- Behavior analysts must be knowledgeable about and comply with all applicable standards (e.g., BACB rules, laws, research review committee requirements) for storing, transporting, retaining, and destroying physical and electronic documentation related to research. They retain identifying documentation and data for the longest required duration. Behavior analysts destroy physical documentation after making deidentified digital copies or summaries of data (e.g., reports and graphs) when permitted by relevant entities.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

6.11 ACCURACY AND USE OF DATA

- Behavior analysts do not fabricate data or falsify results in their research, publications, and presentations. They plan and carry out their research and describe their procedures and findings to minimize the possibility that their research and results will be misleading or misinterpreted. If they discover errors in their published data, they take steps to correct them by following publisher policy. Data from research projects are presented to the public and scientific community in their entirety whenever possible. When that is not possible, behavior analysts take caution and explain the exclusion of data (whether single data points, or partial or whole data sets) from presentations or manuscripts submitted for publication by providing a rationale and description of what was excluded.

## ETHICAL AND PROFESSIONAL ISSUES

E.1 Identify and apply core principles underlying the ethics codes for BACB® certificants (e.g., benefit others; treat others with compassion, dignity, and respect; behave with integrity).

E.2 Identify the risks to oneself, others, and the profession as a result of engaging in unethical behavior.

E.3 Develop and maintain competence by engaging in professional development activities (e.g., read literature, seek consultation, establish mentors).

E.4 Identify and comply with requirements for collecting, using, protecting, and disclosing confidential information.

E.5 Identify and comply with requirements for making public statements about professional activities (e.g., social media activity; misrepresentation of professional credentials, behavior analysis, and service outcomes).

E.6 Identify the conditions under which services or supervision should be discontinued and apply steps that should be taken when transitioning clients and supervisees to another professional.

E.7 Identify types of and risks associated with multiple relationships, and how to mitigate those risks when they are unavoidable.

E.8 Identify and apply interpersonal and other skills (e.g., accepting feedback, listening actively, seeking input, collaborating) to establish and maintain professional relationships.

E.9 Engage in cultural humility in service delivery and professional relationships.

E.10 Apply culturally responsive and inclusive service and supervision activities.

E.11 Identify personal biases and how they might interfere with professional activity.

E.12 Identify and apply the legal, regulatory, and practice requirements (e.g., licensure, jurisprudence, funding, certification) relevant to the delivery of behavior-analytic services.

title: BCaBA
body:
### BCaBA
E.1 Identify and apply core principles underlying the ethics codes for BACB® certificants (e.g., benefit others; treat others with compassion, dignity, and respect; behave with integrity).

**ETHICS CODE FOR BEHAVIOR ANALYSTS (CODE)**
- The Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts is connected to everything that is studied under the Test Content Outline (TCO). In fact, you may have already noticed that we have connected many Code standards to specific areas of the TCO throughout this manual. There are more connections and interpretations that can be made.

[EXAM TIP]
A great way to study Domain E is to connect Code items to specific TCO items, which will organize how ethics is involved in everything you'll be tested on.

**Scope of the Code:**
The Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts applies to behavior analysts in all professional activities across settings and delivery modes (e.g., in person, in writing, via phone, email, text message, video conferencing, even on social media when you're presenting yourself as a BCBA or BCaBA).
- Direct service delivery.
- Consultation.
- Supervision.
- Training.
- Management.
- Editorial and peer-review activities.
- Research.
- Any activity within the ABA profession.

> **The Code's Definition of Behavior Analyst:** An individual who holds BCBA or BCaBA certification or who has submitted a complete application for BCBA or BCaBA certification; refers to those required to act in accordance with the Code.

[EXAM TIP]
Pay close attention to the Code's definition of behavior analyst. You may be surprised to find that YOU are a behavior analyst and that the Code already applies to you, even before you earn the certification.

**The Code does not apply to:**
- Behavior analysts' personal behavior unless the behavior poses a potential risk to the health and safety of clients, stakeholders, supervisees, or trainees.

**CORE PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING THE CODE**
Principles with which to interpret and apply the standards outlined in the Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts.

title: CORE PRINCIPLES
body:
CORE PRINCIPLES
UNDERLYING THE CODE
(Cont'd)

**Using the core principles:**
- The Code is not a complete list of all the possible ethics-related topics that could ever come up.
- If concerning behavior can't be found in one of the standards, the four core principles can help determine if a behavior can be described as misconduct.
- When two or more standards in the Code seem to be working against each other, the core principles can be used to make decisions.

[EXAM TIP]
Connect the core principles to the relevant Code standards and think about what each principle looks like in practice. This will help when you are asked to link core principle to specific exam scenarios.

[4 CORE PRINCIPLES
Benefit others
Compassion,
dignity, and respect
Integrity
Competence]

**FOUR CORE PRINCIPLES:**
1. Benefit others.
2. Treat others with compassion, dignity, and respect.
3. Behave with integrity.
4. Ensure competence.

**1. BENEFIT OTHERS: MAXIMIZE BENEFITS AND DO NO HARM BY:**
- Protecting the welfare and rights of clients above all others.
  THINK: Evaluate situations from the perspective of the client, always considering what might be good vs. harmful to them.
- Protecting the welfare and rights of individuals with whom we professionally interact.
  THINK: You have an obligation to protect people like caregivers, supervisees, trainees, and collaborating professionals (e.g., SLPs, PTs, teachers).
- Focusing on looking for the short- and long-term effects of professional activities.
- Actively identifying and addressing the potential negative impacts of one's own physical and mental health (e.g., personal life, stressors, depression, medical concerns, etc.) on professional activities and your ability to meet professional expectations.
  THINK: Watch for times in your life when personal situations impact things at work in a way that could be harmful.
  **Example:** A sudden significant stressor in your life (like caring for a loved one) might deprive you of sleep, and interfere with your ability to meet deadlines or make nuanced decisions at work.
- Actively identifying potential and actual conflicts of interest, and working to resolve them in a manner that avoids or minimizes harm.
- Actively identifying and addressing factors (e.g., personal, financial, institutional, political, religious, cultural) that might lead to conflicts of interest, misuse of position, or other negative impacts on professional activities.
  THINK: Watch for things in your personal life that might make it more difficult for you to see that you or others are making decisions that could be unethical and/or harmful to others.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: CORE PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING THE CODE (Cont'd)
body:
CORE PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING THE CODE (Cont'd)

Example: Personal financial difficulties could lead you to make work decisions that are based more on the need for income vs. what is best for the client.
- Effectively and respectfully collaborating with others in the best interest of clients, always placing clients' welfare first.

2. TREAT OTHERS WITH COMPASSION, DIGNITY, AND RESPECT BY:
- Behaving equitably towards others, regardless of factors such as age, disability, ethnicity, gender expression/identity, immigration status, marital/relationship status, national origin, race, religion, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, or other basis proscribed by law.

[NOTE: Equitable does not mean that everyone gets the same thing. It means that everyone gets what they need to have an equal chance of success.]

- Respecting others' privacy and confidentiality.
- Respecting and actively promoting clients' self-determination (control of one's own life) to the best of our abilities, particularly when providing services to vulnerable populations. Acknowledge that personal choice in service delivery is important by providing clients and stakeholders with info to make informed choices about services. [THINK: Sometimes, what a client or stakeholder wants does not align with what we personally or professionally want for them, but we should always strive to create opportunities for promoting the individual's choice and self-determination. Prioritize what they want, over what we want.]

3. BEHAVE WITH INTEGRITY BY:
- Fulfilling responsibilities to our scientific and professional communities, society in general, and the communities we serve by:
  - Behaving in an honest and trustworthy manner.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.01: Being Truthful: Behavior analysts are truthful and arrange the professional environment to promote truthful behavior in others. They do not create professional situations that result in others engaging in behavior that is fraudulent or illegal, or that violates the Code. They also provide truthful and accurate information to all required entities (e.g., BACB, licensure boards, funders) and individuals (e.g., clients, stakeholders, supervisees, trainees), and they correct instances of untruthful or inaccurate submissions as soon as they become aware of them.]

- Not misrepresenting ourselves, our work, or others' work; not engaging in fraud.
- Following through on obligations.
- Holding ourselves accountable for our work and that of our supervisees/trainees, and correcting errors in a timely manner.

title: CORE PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING THE CODE (Cont'd)
body:
CORE PRINCIPLES UNDERLYING THE CODE (Cont'd)

- Being knowledgeable about and upholding BACB and other regulatory requirements.

[CAUTION]: Not knowing about a requirement is not a defense.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 1.16: Self-Reporting Critical Information: Behavior analysts remain knowledgeable about and comply with all self-reporting requirements of relevant entities (e.g., BACB, licensure boards, funders).

- Actively working to create professional environments that uphold the core principles and standards of the Code.
- Respectfully educating others about our ethics requirements and the mechanisms for addressing professional misconduct.
[THINK]: Don't assume that others know about ethics requirements, and always be respectful/tactful when sharing Code information. Example: A marketing team in an organization might not know or understand that our Code prohibits us from soliciting testimonials from current clients for the sake of advertising. We'll need to explain that this is unethical for us, but remember that it is not unethical for them, so don't sound preachy or judgmental.

4. ENSURE COMPETENCE BY:
- Remaining within the profession's scope of practice.
[THINK]: Being aware of what practices are within the scope of practice for behavior analysis-based services, and which are outside the scope (i.e., those not based on the principle of behavior analysis).
- Remaining current and increasing knowledge of best practices and advances in ABA, and participating in professional development.
- Remaining knowledgeable and current about interventions (including pseudoscience) that may exist in our practice areas and pose a risk of harm to clients.
- Being aware of, working within, and continually evaluating the boundaries of our competence.
- Working to continually increase our knowledge and skills related to cultural responsiveness and service delivery to diverse groups.

[BCBA] E.2 Identify the risks to oneself, others, and the profession as a result of engaging in unethical behavior.

[BCaBA] E.2 Identify the risks to oneself, others, and the profession as a result of engaging in unethical behavior (e.g., misuse of social media, misrepresentation of one's credential, making confidential information public).

THE RISKS OF UNETHICAL BEHAVIOR
HARMFUL CONSEQUENCES FOR CLIENTS AND STAKEHOLDERS:
- Physical or emotional harm.
- Inadequate training results in poor quality of service delivery.
- Unfair or inequitable client treatment.

THE RISKS OF
UNETHICAL BEHAVIOR
(Cont'd)

- Ineffective programming.
- Missed due dates that impact services.
- Delays in progress, regression, worsened current concerns.
- Loss of opportunities for self-determination and choice.
- Exploitation of vulnerable people.
- Inappropriate multiple relationships confound treatment.

- Breeched privacy.
- Traumatic therapeutic experience.
- Loss of trust in ABA or other supportive services.
- Avoidance of future services.

NEGATIVE PROFESSIONAL CONSEQUENCES FOR THE PRACTITIONER:
- Strained relationships with colleagues and supervisors.
- Loss of professional opportunities.
- Fewer collaborators and/or ineffective collaborative experiences.
- Loss of employment/pay reduction.
- Negative implication for the individual's organization.
- Negative impacts (disciplinary action) on certification or licensure.

[BOX: 2 CORRECTIVE ACTIONS
Professional
development
Mentorship]

1. Corrective actions: Disciplinary actions imposed by the BACB for ethical violations.
- Professional development: Certificants or applicants are required to receive professional development activities (e.g., continuing education units or university course credits) relevant to their violation.
- Mentorship: Certificants or applicants are required to receive mentorship from an approved individual for a specified period of time on professional development related to their violation.
- Other required action: Certificants or candidates are required to fulfill a combination or variety of actions intended to correct ethical deviations.

[BOX: 5 SANCTIONS
Invalidation
Revocation
Suspension
Practice
Supervision]

2. Sanctions: Disciplinary actions, imposed by the BACB, that place a restriction on an individual's ability to practice. These consequences are published on the BACB website in the subject's Registry record until the sanction requirements are completed.
- Certificate invalidation: When eligibility requirements were not met and the subject obtained eligibility unethically and illegitimately.
- Certificate revocation: An individual's certification is terminated. After the revocation period, the individual can apply for post-revocation re-entry and a committee decides to approve or deny.
- Certification or eligibility suspension: An individual's certification may not be used for a specified period of time, or an eligible candidate cannot apply for certification for period of time.

title: DEVELOP AND MAINTAIN
body:
DEVELOP AND MAINTAIN COMPETENCE (Cont'd) Ways to maintain/expand professional competence: - **ABA conferences:** Connect with the leaders and innovators in our field as they present their most recent work, hear about recent research and practice developments, and connect with like-minded people. (We especially love APBA, CalABA, BABA and WIBA.) - **Current literature:** Stay informed about updates to procedures and concepts by reading peer-reviewed journal articles from professional publications such as the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis (JABA), Behavior Analysis in Practice (BAP). - [fyi:] Individuals registered/certified with the BACB can access many journals through their BACB gateway account. - **Workshops:** Continue to strengthen your skills and learn new ABA practices not in your current repertoire, such as: Acceptance Commitment Therapy (ACT), Organizational Behavior Management (OBM), Pivotal Response Training (PRT), cultural competency. - **Mentorship:** Connect with and learn from expert models (e.g., career development, new skills, networking, personal growth, etc.). - **Community of practice:** Have regular meetings with peers and help each other maintain and develop skills, share resources, and cheer each other on. It is your ethical responsibility to know the requirements for maintaining your certification. CONTINUING EDUCATION REQUIREMENTS | Length of Recertification Cycle: | Two years. | | --- | --- | | Number of Required CEs per 2-Year Cycle: | BCBA: 32 units per cycle.
BCaBA: 20 units per cycle. | | Number of Required CEs in Ethics: | Four units per cycle. | | Number of Required CEs in Supervision:
If supervising BCBA/BCaBA candidates; or
ongoing certification of BCaBAs | Three units per cycle. | Table: Continuing education requirements. - [fyi:] Effective January 2027, these requirements will change to 4 units in ethics, 4 units of supervision (if applicable), and 2 units in diversity, equity, and inclusion. The length of the recertification cycle and total required units will remain the same. SCOPE OF COMPETENCE: ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: **Code Standard 1.05: Practicing within Scope of Competence:** Behavior analysts practice only within their identified scope of competence. They engage in professional activities in new areas (e.g., populations, procedures) only after accessing and documenting appropriate study, training, supervised experience, consultation, and/or co-treatment from professionals competent in the new area. Otherwise, they refer or transition services to an appropriate professional.

title: DEVELOP AND MAINTAIN COMPETENCE (Cont'd)
body:
### DEVELOP AND MAINTAIN COMPETENCE (Cont'd)

[BOX: The Code's definition of scope of competence: The professional activities a behavior analyst can consistently perform with proficiency (e.g., specific interventions, behaviors, age-groups, diagnoses, etc.).]

- It is your responsibility to evaluate your scope of competence on an ongoing basis.
- Before working in a new area, get the appropriate training.
- Take on new roles or clients ONLY in those areas where you have appropriate training and experience.

[CAUTION: Don't confuse scope of competence with scope of practice.]

[DIAGRAM: SCOPE OF COMPETENCE VS SCOPE OF PRACTICE]

**Example:** Tia is a BCBA, working in early intensive behavior intervention for nearly three years. Her direct supervisor conducts the FAs, then Tia creates the plans and works with staff to implement treatment. While her supervisor was on leave, the agency received a referral for a child who engages in eye-gouging and needs treatment immediately. This seemed like an urgent situation, so Tia read a few articles on functional analysis and conducted the FA for this child. This is an ethical violation: Conducting an FA is outside of Tia's scope of competence.

**Example:** Jane's client's mother was having a hard time dealing with her daughter's recent autism diagnosis; the mother's stress was compounded by her recent divorce. Jane could see that this woman needed emotional support and decided to spend 30 minutes of her weekly parent training time to support her psychologically. Jane, who works with her client as a BCBA, also has a Master's in counseling psychology, so she thought she could be helpful. This is an ethical violation: Engaging in psychotherapy is outside of the scope of practice of behavior analysis.

*Graphic: Scope of competence vs. scope of practice.*

[CAUTION: A common misconception is that becoming certified means being an expert in all things behavior analysis. The exam is based on the knowledge of an entry-level behavior analyst.]

title: BCBA
body:
BCBA
E.4 Identify and comply with requirements for collecting, using, protecting, and disclosing confidential information.

CONFIDENTIAL INFORMATION

[THINK:] ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 2.03: Protecting Confidential Information: Behavior analysts take appropriate steps to protect the confidentiality of clients, stakeholders, supervisees, trainees, and research participants; prevent the accidental or inadvertent sharing of confidential information; and comply with applicable confidentiality requirements (e.g., laws, regulations, organization policies). The scope of confidentiality includes service delivery (e.g., live, teleservices, recorded sessions); documentation and data; and verbal, written, or electronic communication.

**What counts as confidential information?**
- It's your responsibility to know, because confidentiality is often specific to your context of practice.
- A good rule of thumb is to understand protected personal information (PII), sometimes referred to as personally identifiable information (PII). PPI/PII is any information about a person that could lead you (or others) to identify that individual (e.g., social security number, name, email address, phone number).
[THINK:] When in doubt, ask if something counts as PPI/PII. And if it does, make sure you protect that information.

**Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA):**
- Federal law that requires client privacy rights and establishes rules about the transition/storing client protected health information (PHI).
- Applies to covered entities (CEs) (i.e., agencies/companies) only.
- Requires all staff to be trained in HIPAA policies and specific protocols.

**The Family Educational Rights and Act (FERPA):**
- Federal law that protects the privacy of student education records.
- Applies to all schools that receive funding under an applicable program of the U.S. Department of Education.
- Gives parents certain rights with respect to their children's education records, and these rights transfer to the student when he or she reaches the age of 18 or attends a school beyond the high school level.

[THINK:] ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 2.05: Documentation Protection and Retention: Behavior analysts are knowledgeable about and comply with all applicable requirements (e.g., BACB rules, laws, regulations, contracts, funder, and organization requirements) for storing, transporting, retaining, and destroying physical and electronic documentation related to their professional activities. They destroy physical documentation after making electronic copies or summaries of data (e.g., reports and graphs) only when allowed by applicable requirements. When a behavior analyst leaves an organization, these responsibilities remain with the organization.

Please Do Not Duplicate

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

PUBLIC STATEMENTS (Cont'd)

- If you can answer a very specific question about a client in a public forum (like in a social media post or in a public training), well, then it is very likely that confidential information has been shared. Also, you have no way of verifying that consent was received before the question was posed.

[REFRESHER] Remember that once something has been posted on the internet, it never disappears. (Deleting a post doesn't delete the screenshots that others have taken of it.)

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 5.04: Public Statements by Others: Behavior analysts are responsible for public statements that promote their professional activities or products, regardless of who creates or publishes the statements. Behavior analysts make reasonable efforts to prevent others (e.g., employers, marketers, clients, stakeholders) from making deceptive statements concerning their professional activities or products. If behavior analysts learn of such statements, they make reasonable efforts to correct them. Behavior analysts document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.

- If your company's marketing team gets your credentials wrong or says that you have skills that you actually don't, it is your responsibility to reach out and respectfully discuss the ethical issue and a path for correcting it.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 5.05: Use of Intellectual Property: Behavior analysts are knowledgeable about and comply with intellectual property laws, including obtaining permission to use materials that have been trademarked or copyrighted or can otherwise be claimed as another's intellectual property as defined by law. Appropriate use of such materials includes providing citations, attributions, and/or trademark or copyright symbols. Behavior analysts do not unlawfully obtain or disclose proprietary information, regardless of how it became known to them.

- You must be careful when using titles, logos, and other information that does not belong to you. This applies to public statements you may make, resources you create and might share, and information you may use in presentations, reports, or other professional writing (e.g., blog posts).
- An example of illegally getting or sharing "proprietary information," even if you didn't know it was illegal or that you shouldn't have it: If someone posts test questions that they took from the BACB exam, or from a published mock exam that has copyright protection.

title: PUBLIC STATEMENTS (Cont'd)
body:
PUBLIC STATEMENTS (Cont'd)

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 5.06: Advertising Nonbehavioral Services: Behavior analysts do not advertise nonbehavioral services as behavioral services. If behavior analysts provide nonbehavioral services, those services must be clearly distinguished from their behavioral services and BACB certification with the following disclaimer: "These interventions are not behavioral in nature and are not covered by my BACB certification." This disclaimer is placed alongside the names and descriptions of all nonbehavioral interventions. If a behavior analyst is employed by an organization that violates this Code standard, the behavior analyst makes reasonable efforts to remediate the situation, documenting all actions taken and the eventual outcomes.]

Example: Jane, an independent practicing BCBA, is also a meditation coach. On her business webpage, under "Jane McAllistair, MS, BCBA," it says: "I provide applied behavior analysis services to young children with disabilities and their families, as well as meditation coaching and wellness retreats." Jane did not include the required disclaimer. This is problematic because she did not clearly separate the two services that she provides, nor did she clearly link her credentials to the right service. Failing to separate her two professional identities could lead to people believing that her meditation coaching services fall under her BCBA certification. It might be best for Jane to have two separate websites: One for the behavior analysis-based services, and one for the nonbehavioral service, where she leaves off "BCBA" from her list of credentials and includes the required disclaimer.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 5.07: Soliciting Testimonials from Current Clients for Advertising: Because of the possibility of undue influence and implicit coercion, behavior analysts do not solicit testimonials from current clients or stakeholders for use in advertisements designed to obtain new clients. This does not include unsolicited reviews on websites where behavior analysts cannot control content, but such content should not be used or shared by the behavior analyst. If a behavior analyst is employed by an organization that violates this Code standard, the behavior analyst makes reasonable efforts to remediate the situation, documenting all actions taken and the eventual outcomes.]

[The Code's definition of testimonial: Any solicited or unsolicited recommendation in any form, from a client, stakeholder, supervisee, or trainee, affirming the benefits received from a behavior analyst's product or service. From the point at which a behavior analyst asks an individual for a recommendation, it is considered solicited.]

- Even if you did not post the testimonial, you have a responsibility to make efforts to educate others about the ethical issue and resolve it.

PUBLIC STATEMENTS (Cont'd)

- If a caregiver posts information about their experience on a site that you do not control, that does not count as a testimonial. But, if you become aware of it, you may not link to it or copy and paste it on your website. If you do, then that statement effectively becomes a testimonial.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 5.08: Using Testimonials from Former Clients for Advertising: When soliciting testimonials from former clients or stakeholders for use in advertisements designed to obtain new clients, behavior analysts consider the possibility that former clients may re-enter services. These testimonials must be identified as solicited or unsolicited, include an accurate statement of the relationship between the behavior analyst and the testimonial author, and comply with all applicable privacy and confidentiality laws. When soliciting testimonials from former clients or stakeholders, behavior analysts provide them with clear and thorough descriptions about where and how the testimonial will appear, make them aware of any risks associated with the disclosure of their private information, and inform them that they can rescind the testimonial at any time. If a behavior analyst is employed by an organization that violates this Code standard, the behavior analyst makes reasonable efforts to remediate the situation, documenting all actions taken and the eventual outcomes.

ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 5.09: Using Testimonials for Nonadvertising Purposes: Behavior analysts may use testimonials from former or current clients and stakeholders for nonadvertising purposes (e.g., fundraising, grant applications, dissemination of information about ABA) in accordance with applicable laws. If a behavior analyst is employed by an organization that violates this Code standard, the behavior analyst makes reasonable efforts to remediate the situation, documenting all actions taken and the eventual outcomes.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 5.10: Social Media Channels and Websites: Behavior analysts are knowledgeable about the risks to privacy and confidentiality associated with the use of social media channels and websites and they use their respective professional and personal accounts accordingly. They do not publish information and/or digital content of clients on their personal social media accounts and websites. When publishing information and/or digital content of clients on their professional social media accounts and websites, behavior analysts ensure that for each publication they (1) obtain informed consent before publishing, (2) include a disclaimer that informed consent was obtained and that the information should not be captured and reused without express permission, (3) publish on social media channels in a manner that reduces the potential for sharing, and (4) make appropriate efforts to prevent and correct misuse of the shared information, documenting all actions taken and the eventual outcomes. Behavior analysts frequently monitor their social media accounts and websites to ensure the accuracy and appropriateness of shared information.

- Code Standards, 3.14, 3.15, and 3.16 are about ensuring that you avoid and minimize any possible harm to a client or supervisee when there is a disruption, interruption, transfer, or discontinuation of services.
- It doesn't matter that some of these things can be out of our control and unplanned. You are still required to proactively work to avoid and minimize these situations and any subsequent issues.
- THINK: Antecedent management strategies.

[CAUTION] ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 3.14: Facilitating Continuity of Services:
Behavior analysts act in the best interests of the client to avoid interruption or disruption of services. They make appropriate and timely efforts to facilitate the continuation of behavioral services in the event of planned interruptions (e.g., relocation, temporary leave of absence) and unplanned interruptions (e.g., illness, funding disruption, parent request, emergencies). They ensure that service agreements or contracts include a general plan of action for service interruptions. When a service interruption occurs, they communicate to all relevant parties the steps being taken to facilitate continuity of services. Behavior analysts document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.

title: TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)
body:
TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)

- Consider these antecedent strategies:
  - Giving proper notice for planned events.
  - Having backup plans for surprise events, like having enough staff for coverage or colleagues who can support (with short-term contracts).
  - Service agreements (Code, 3.04) should describe a general plan for how disruptions or interruptions will be addressed, which can help you navigate a scenario.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 3.15 Appropriately Discontinuing Services: Behavior analysts include the circumstances for discontinuing services in their service agreement. They consider discontinuing services when: (1) the client has met all behavior-change goals, (2) the client is not benefiting from the service, (3) the behavior analyst and/or their supervisees or trainees are exposed to potentially harmful conditions that cannot be reasonably resolved, (4) the client and/or relevant stakeholder requests discontinuation, (5) the relevant stakeholders are not complying with the behavior-change intervention despite appropriate efforts to address barriers, or (6) services are no longer funded. Behavior analysts provide the client and/or relevant stakeholders with a written plan for discontinuing services, document acknowledgment of the plan, review the plan throughout the discharge process, and document all steps taken.

- This standard gives you conditions under which discontinuation might be appropriate. So, make sure to include them in the service agreement.
- Six possible conditions under which discontinuation might be appropriate:
  1. The client has met all behavior-change goals.
  2. The client is not benefiting from the service.
  3. The behavior analyst and/or their supervisees or trainees are exposed to potentially harmful conditions that cannot be reasonably resolved.
  4. The client and/or relevant stakeholder requests discontinuation.
  5. The relevant stakeholders are not complying with the behavior-change intervention despite appropriate efforts to address barriers.
  6. Services are no longer funded.

[EXAM TIP]: On exam questions:
- Look for one or more of these conditions to evaluate ethical discontinuation.
- Consider the language "...be reasonably resolved." Look for reasonable efforts to resolve issues, or failure to describe actions for a reasonable resolution, when evaluating ethical discontinuation.

title: TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)
body:
## TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]
**Code Standard 3.16: Appropriately Transitioning Services:** Behavior analysts include in their service agreement the circumstances for transitioning the client to another behavior analyst within or outside of their organization. They make appropriate efforts to effectively manage transitions; provide a written plan that includes target dates, transition activities, and responsible parties; and review the plan throughout the transition. When relevant, they take appropriate steps to minimize disruptions to services during the transition by collaborating with relevant service providers.

- What is a proactive step you could take throughout services that would likely lead to a smooth transition? Yep! Maintain your documentation systems well!
- What might count as collaborating with other relevant service providers? Maybe offering to have an overlap/transition meeting, allowing them to observe (remote or in person) a session?

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]
**Code Standard 3.07: Third-Party Contracts for Services:** When behavior analysts enter into a signed contract to provide services to a client at the request of a third party (e.g., school district, governmental entity), they clarify the nature of the relationship with each party and assess any potential conflicts before services begin. They ensure that the contract outlines (1) the responsibilities of all parties, (2) the scope of behavioral services to be provided, (3) the likely use of the information obtained, (4) the behavior analysts' obligations under the Code, and (5) any limits about maintaining confidentiality. Behavior analysts are responsible for amending contracts as needed and reviewing them with the relevant parties at that time.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]
**Code Standard 3.08: Responsibility to the Client with Third-Party Contracts for Services:** Behavior analysts place the client's care and welfare above all others. If the third-party requests services from the behavior analyst that are incompatible with the behavior analyst's recommendations, that are outside of the behavior analyst's scope of competence, or that could result in a multiple relationship, behavior analysts resolve such conflicts in the best interest of the client. If a conflict cannot be resolved, the behavior analyst may obtain additional training or consultation, discontinue services following appropriate transition measures, or refer the client to another behavior analyst. Behavior analysts document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.

[fyi.] If you are required to transition a client per **Code Standard 3.08**, then make sure you are meeting **Code Standards 3.14: Facilitating Continuity of Services; 3.15: Appropriately Discontinuing Services; and 3.16: Appropriately Transitioning Services.**

title: TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)
body:
TRANSITIONING CLIENTS AND SUPERVISEES (Cont'd)

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 3.09: Communicating with Stakeholders About Third-Party Contracted Services: When providing services at the request of a third party to a minor or individual who does not have the legal right to make personal decisions, behavior analysts ensure that the parent or legally authorized representative is informed of the rationale for and scope of services to be provided, as well as their right to receive copies of all service documentation and data. Behavior analysts are knowledgeable about and comply with all requirements related to informed consent, regardless of who requested the services.

The Code's definition of third-party: Any individual, group of individuals, or entity, other than the direct recipient of services, the primary caregiver, the legally authorized representative, or the behavior analyst, who requests and funds services on behalf of a client or group of clients. Some examples include a school district, governmental entity, mental health agency, among others.

[THINK:]: A therapeutic relationship involves two-parties: The client party and the treatment team party. Anyone who doesn't fit into one of the two-parties, but is somehow associated with the client receiving services, is a third party.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 3.13: Referrals: Behavior analysts make referrals based on the needs of the client and/or relevant stakeholders and include multiple providers when available. Behavior analysts disclose to the client and relevant stakeholders any relationships they have with potential providers and any fees or incentives they may receive for the referrals. They document any referrals made, including relevant relationships and fees or incentives received, and make appropriate efforts to follow up with the client and/or relevant stakeholders.

[THINK:]: "Making referrals" might include referring a client to a different behavior analyst if you can no longer serve them.

[fyi,]: If you are required to refer a client to another provider, per Code Standard 3.13, then make sure you are meeting Code Standards 3.14: Facilitating Continuity of Services; 3.15: Appropriately Discontinuing Services; and 3.16: Appropriately Transitioning Services.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 2.19: Addressing Conditions Interfering with Service Delivery: Behavior analysts actively identify and address environmental conditions (e.g., the behavior of others, hazards to the client or staff, disruptions) that may interfere with or prevent service delivery. In such situations, behavior analysts remove or minimize the conditions, identify effective modifications to the intervention, and/or consider obtaining or recommending assistance from other professionals. Behavior analysts document the conditions, all actions taken, and the eventual outcomes.

[BCaBA] E.7 Identify types of and risks associated with multiple relationships, and how to mitigate those risks when they are unavoidable.

MULTIPLE RELATIONSHIPS

- The Code's definition of multiple relationship: A co-mingling of two or more of a behavior analyst's roles (e.g., behavioral and personal) with a client, stakeholder, supervisee, trainee, research participant, or someone closely associated with or related to the client).

- The Code's definition of conflict of interest: An incompatibility between a behavior analyst's private and professional interests, resulting in risk or potential risk to services provided to, or the professional relationship with, a client, stakeholder, supervisee, trainee, or research participant. Conflicts may result in a situation in which personal, financial, or professional considerations have the potential to influence or compromise professional judgment in the delivery of behavioral services, research, consultation, supervision, training, or any other professional activity.

title: MULTIPLE
body:
MULTIPLE
RELATIONSHIPS
(Cont'd)

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.11: Multiple Relationships: Because multiple relationships may result in a conflict of interest that might harm one or more parties, behavior analysts avoid entering into or creating multiple relationships, including professional, personal, and familial relationships with clients and colleagues. Behavior analysts communicate the risks of multiple relationships to relevant individuals and continually monitor for the development of multiple relationships. If multiple relationships arise, behavior analysts take appropriate steps to resolve them. When immediately resolving a multiple relationship is not possible, behavior analysts develop appropriate safeguards to identify and avoid conflicts of interest in compliance with the Code and develop a plan to eventually resolve the multiple relationship. Behavior analysts document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.]

[fyi]: Code Standard 1.11 does not state that being in a multiple relationship is an immediate ethics violation. BUT: There are always risks with multiple relationships, and therefore, they should be avoided and continually monitored for.

[CAUTION: There is misconception that if both sides acknowledge and monitor a multiple relationship... well, that removes the multiple relationship and any possible conflicts. That is not true - the multiple relationship and the potential for conflicts always exist.]

[EXAM TIP]
On exam questions, look for the specific steps for navigating a multiple relationship that cannot be ended immediately:
1. Identify that a multiple relationship has developed and what the conflicts and risks are. (Talk with the other person/people involved.)
2. Take action to minimize those risks.
3. Make a plan to resolve the multiple relationship as soon as possible (e.g., reassign duties, clients, supervisees, or trainees or find a different provider and facilitate a transition).
4. Document all of the steps taken.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.12: Giving and Receiving Gifts: Because the exchange of gifts can invite conflicts of interest and multiple relationships, behavior analysts do not give gifts to or accept gifts from clients, stakeholders, supervisees, or trainees with a monetary value of more than $10 USD (or the equivalent purchasing power in another currency). Behavior analysts make clients and stakeholders aware of this requirement at the onset of the professional relationship. A gift is acceptable if it functions as an infrequent expression of gratitude and does not result in financial benefit to the recipient. Instances of giving or accepting ongoing or cumulative gifts may rise to the level of a violation of this standard if the gifts become a regularly expected source of income or value to the recipient.]

They also comply with practice requirements (e.g., attestations, criminal background checks) imposed by the BACB, employers, or governmental entities.]

- Interpersonal skills include being timely when communicating with clients, caregivers, and others in your professional activities.

BCBA
E.9 Engage in cultural humility in service delivery and professional relationships.

BCaBA
E.7 Identify types of and risks associated with multiple relationships, and how to mitigate those risks when they are unavoidable.

CULTURAL HUMILITY

Cultural humility: An ongoing process of self-reflection and lifelong learning that involves recognizing and addressing one's own prejudices and implicit and explicit biases. It requires a continuous, critical examination of one's behavior, beliefs, and assumptions, particularly in interactions with individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds.

Engaging in cultural humility involves:
- The process of active self-reflection on all of our professional activities; taking skills that are needed to build and sustain professional relationships and activities within those relationships, like rapport building, collaborating on assessments and interventions, setting and evaluating goals, and soliciting and giving feedback.
- Always seeking to increase the awareness and empathy that people have complex, intersecting, and valuable cultural identities that are likely different from ours.

Please Do Not Duplicate

title: CULTURAL HUMILITY (Cont'd)
body:
CULTURAL HUMILITY (Cont'd)
- Recognizing, understanding, and reflecting on one's own prejudices and biases (both implicit and explicit), as well as taking a critical look at one's own behavior and acknowledging how it is informed by those prejudices and biases.
- Continually learning about, considering, responding to, and celebrating other peoples' cultures, cultural identities, and learning histories is a lifelong process.

**BCBA** E.10 Apply culturally responsive and inclusive service and supervision activities.
**BCaBA** E.10 Apply culturally responsive and inclusive service and supervision activities.

CULTURAL RESPONSIVENESS

[BOX: Cultural responsiveness: The practice of engaging with individuals and communities in a way that fully honors and acknowledges their unique cultural backgrounds, experiences, and perspectives.]

- Cultural responsiveness focuses on taking action that centers the individual strengths and needs of others, as related to their intersecting cultural identities.
- Taking a culturally-responsive approach in your professional activities can lead to healthier professional relationships, increased self-determination and autonomy, better matched interventions and services, and providing more accurate (and accepted) feedback.

[BOX: ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.07: Cultural Responsiveness and Diversity: Behavior analysts actively engage in professional development activities to acquire knowledge and skills related to cultural responsiveness and diversity. They evaluate their own biases and ability to address the needs of individuals with diverse needs/backgrounds (e.g., age, disability, ethnicity, gender expression/identity, immigration status, marital/relationship status, national origin, race, religion, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status). Behavior analysts also evaluate biases of their supervisees and trainees, as well as their supervisees' and trainees' ability to address the needs of individuals with diverse needs/backgrounds.]

**Engaging in culturally-responsive practice:**
- View differences as strengths.
- Create a safe/brave learning environment that invites collaboration, innovation, and autonomy.
- Promote equity in services to clients, caregivers, supervisees, and trainees by gathering information about individuals and using it to inform your services. This shows up everywhere, including:
 1. Client intake.
 2. Client and stakeholder interviewing.

4. Designing supervision and training activities.

[fyi.] Code Standard 1.07 requires that you evaluate your own biases AND those of your supervisees and trainees and their abilities to engage in culturally-responsive practices.

ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.09: Non-harassment: Behavior analysts do not engage in behavior that is harassing or hostile toward others.

- Whether or not something is "harassing" or "hostile" should be determined by the recipient, so taking a culturally-responsive perspective here is critical.
  [THINK]: Just because something would not (or does not) bother you, does not mean that it won't (or did not) bother someone else.
  Example: Offensive or derogatory jokes, racial slurs, micro-aggressions, inappropriate sexual behavior, unwelcome comments about personal characteristics (e.g., hair style, body size, religion or religious garments), offensive or derogatory images.

BCBA

E.11 Identify personal biases and how they might interfere with professional activity.

PERSONAL BIASES

ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: Code Standard 1.10: Awareness of Personal Biases and Challenges: Behavior analysts maintain awareness that their personal biases or challenges (e.g., mental or physical health conditions; legal, financial, marital/ relationship challenges) may interfere with the effectiveness of their professional work. Behavior analysts take appropriate steps to resolve interference, ensure that their professional work is not compromised, and document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.

- Pay close attention to anything that could negatively impact your own professional behavior.
  [THINK]: Benefit others.
  [THINK]: Do no harm by putting the needs of the client first.
- Engage in ongoing, honest self-reflection of your personal biases and challenges.
- Know what your behavior looks like under stress.
- Identify precursor indicators that your professional behavior is being influenced by your biases or challenges.
- Evaluate your own behavior.

[EXAM TIP] For exam questions, be familiar with the steps outlined in Code Standard 1.10:
1. Maintain awareness.
2. Take steps to resolve the interference.
3. Make sure there are no negative impacts on your work activities.
4. Document steps and outcomes.

SUPERVISION REQUIREMENTS

There are specific requirements when overseeing the work or training of others providing behavioral services, or working toward their BACB certification, or when assessing performance of those individuals.

[PROCEDURE] 3 SUPERVISORY ROLES
- Supervisor
- Assessor
- Trainer

THREE SUPERVISORY ROLES:
1. Supervisor: Oversees individuals providing behavior services (i.e., RBTs, BCaBAs, behavior technicians) and individuals working toward obtaining certification.
2. Assessor: Directly conducts or oversees the assessments of individuals pursuing RBT certification or maintaining their RBT.
3. Trainer: Develops and/or provides the RBT 40-hour training and/or oversees individuals who provide the RBT 40-hour training.

SPECIFIC SUPERVISION REQUIREMENTS:
- Assessing RBTs:
  - BCBA or BCaBA certified.
  - Complete the 8-hour supervision training.
- Supervising RBTS:
  - BCBA or BCaBA certified.
  - Complete the 8-hour supervision training.
  - Receive ongoing CEUs in supervision.
  - Employed at the same organization as the RBT requirements coordinator.
  - Must have sufficient client knowledge.
  - RBT requirements coordinator:
    - Responsible for ensuring that multiple supervisors in an organization provide appropriate supervision to RBTs.
    - Must have sufficient client knowledge.
- Supervising BCBA and BCaBA trainees:
  - Complete the 8-hour supervision training.
  - Receive ongoing CEUs in supervision.
  - Remain familiar with fieldwork requirements and types (e.g., hours, duration, acceptable activities, etc.).

body:
SUPERVISORY
RESPONSIBILITIES

First-year BCBAs can supervise trainees under the guidance of a consulting supervisor.

- Consulting supervisor:
  - Active BCBA, certified at least five years.
  - Complete the 8-hour supervision training.
  - Receive ongoing CEUs in supervision.
- Supervising BCBAs:
  - Complete the 8-hour supervision training.
  - Receive ongoing CEUs in supervision.

**Supervising BCBA and BCaBA trainees:**
- Ensure that the trainee abides by all ethical and legal requirements.
- The supervisor and trainee both must understand and be in compliance with all fieldwork requirements and the Code.
- Confirm that the trainee has met all requirements before the outset of supervised fieldwork.
- Demonstrate technical, professional, and ethical behavior.
- Ensure that activities are in the best interest of the client, not for the purpose of meeting the fieldwork requirements.
- Provide supervision within defined areas of competence.
- Take on a volume of supervisory activity that allows effectiveness.
- Delegate tasks that trainees can reasonably be expected to perform.
- Provide conditions for the trainee to acquire skills safely and ethically.
- Ensure that activities are behavior analytic, effective, and ethical, and meet BACB requirements.
- Develop and execute the supervision contract.
- Provide ongoing, documented and timely performance feedback.
- Obtain ongoing evaluation of your effectiveness as a supervisor.

**Supervising RBTs:**
- Be familiar with the RBT Ethics Code.
- Ensure that supervisee abides by all ethical and legal requirements.
- Understand and be in compliance with all BACB requirements relating to RBT supervision.
- Select, design, and oversee RBT performing specific required activities (e.g., preference assessments, discrete-trial teaching, session notes, etc.).
- Provide ongoing supervision (the number of required supervision hours is based on a specified percentage of hours worked providing behavioral services each month).

LEGAL, REGULATORY,
AND PRACTICE
REQUIREMENTS

[CAUTION] ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: **Code Standard 1.02: Conforming with Legal and Professional Requirements:** Behavior analysts follow the law and the requirements of their professional community (e.g., BACB, licensure board).

LEGAL, REGULATORY, AND PRACTICE REQUIREMENTS (Cont'd)

- Not knowing a legal or professional requirement is NOT a defense!
- You are required to avoid creating situations that could result in someone else failing to conform with legal and professional requirements (Code Standard 1.01).
- Make sure that you, and your supervisees and trainees, have the most up-to-date information from the BACB and any other relevant regulatory bodies, like a state licensure board.

[EXAM TIP]: Read up on the BACB newsletter for clarifications and changes to requirements. Staying current is an ethical responsibility, which means you could be tested on recent updates. These can be found in the BACB newsletter.

[*] Register for the BACB newsletter for reliable news on any changes.

LAWS, RULINGS AND STATEMENTS THAT PROTECT CLIENTS' RIGHTS

> Code's definition of clients' rights: Human rights, legal rights, rights codified within behavior analysis, and organization rules designed to benefit the client.

ETHICAL PRINCIPLES OF PSYCHOLOGISTS AND CODE OF CONDUCT:
- American Psychological Association; adopted by ABAI.
- Five general ethical principles:
 1. Beneficence (doing good) and non-maleficence (do no harm).
 2. Fidelity and responsibility.
 3. Integrity.
 4. Justice.
 5. Respect for an individual's rights and dignity.

HANCOCK VS. AVERY:
- A federal court ruling that protects a client by limiting the duration of, and placing conditions on the use of, a time-out procedure.
- An inmate sued a prison for cruel and unusual punishment (after being forced to spend long periods in solitary confinement).

INDIVIDUALS WITH DISABILITIES ACT (IDEA):
- A federal law that gives students with disabilities the right to have a:
 - Free, appropriate public education.
 - Individualized education plan (IEP).
 - Guarantees the student's parents have rights (e.g., in IEP meetings, the right to request due process if an agreement isn't reached).

MANDATED REPORTING:
- Laws that apply to professionals who regularly interact with children and vulnerable adults (such as those with disability, mental illness, advanced age).

title: LAWS, RULINGS AND STATEMENTS THAT PROTECT CLIENTS' RIGHTS (Cont'd)
body:
LAWS, RULINGS AND STATEMENTS THAT PROTECT CLIENTS' RIGHTS (Cont'd)

Example: Behavior analysts, Registered Behavior Technicians, teachers, pediatricians, group home staff, nursing home staff, etc.
- Legally mandated reporters are required to report suspected abuse, neglect, financial exploitation to child protective services or other relevant authorities.
- Laws vary state to state, so be sure to acquaint yourself with your state's laws in regards to mandated reporting.
- Failing to report can result in civil penalties and/or criminal prosecution.

THE RIGHT TO EFFECTIVE EDUCATION:
- A statement generated from a report by the Association for Behavior Analysis International Task Force that outlines recommendations for effective education, derived from the principles that have been demonstrated to improve all student learning and performance.
- Requires that assessment and educational treatments:
 1. Are based on research demonstrating effectiveness.
 2. Address functional relations between behavior and environment.
 3. Are monitored and evaluated on a systematic and ongoing basis.
 4. Only be considered when likely to be effective, based on empirical evidence and assessment results.

THE RIGHT TO EFFECTIVE BEHAVIORAL TREATMENT:
- A statement that was developed by the Association for Behavior Analysis International Task Force, explaining their position on a client's right to effective behavioral treatment as a set of guiding principles designed to protect individuals from harm as a result of either the lack of, or the inappropriate use of, behavioral treatment.
- Entails rights of individuals receiving ABA services.
- Six basic client rights:
 1. Therapeutic environment.
 2. Overriding goal: Personal welfare.
 3. Treatment by a competent behavior analyst.
 4. Acquisition of functional skills.
 5. Ongoing evaluation and assessment.
 6. Most effective treatments available.

STATEMENT ON RESTRAINT AND SECLUSION:
A statement generated by a task force authorized by the Executive Council of the Association for Behavior Analysis International.
- Defines and explains the uses of restraint, seclusion, and time-out procedures.
- Requires informed consent, oversight, and monitoring.
- Addresses what constitutes the necessity for emergency procedures.

title: LAWS, RULINGS AND STATEMENTS THAT PROTECT CLIENTS' RIGHTS (Cont'd)
body:
LAWS, RULINGS AND STATEMENTS THAT PROTECT CLIENTS' RIGHTS (Cont'd)

- Three main areas:
  1. Welfare of client is the first priority.
  2. Right to choose: Clients have the right to be involved in decisions about treatment.
  3. Principle of least restrictiveness.

WYATT VS. STICKNEY:
- A federal court ruling establishing that involuntarily institutionalized individuals with mental illness or intellectual disabilities have the constitutional right to personal treatment with minimum standards of care, which includes the right to individualized treatment plans, safe and sanitary living conditions, and adequate staffing.
- Sought to transition individuals from large institutions to community-based care settings.
- Includes three elements:
  1. Humane psychological and physical environment:
     - Eliminated unnecessary medication, physical restraint and isolation, experimental research, and unwanted treatment procedures (e.g., lobotomy and shock treatment).
     - Access to adequate food, medical care, clothing, exercise, and religious worship.
  2. Qualified staff to implement effective treatment.
  3. Individualized treatment plans.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 2.06: Accuracy in Service Billing and Reporting: Behavior analysts identify their services accurately and include all required information on reports, bills, invoices, requests for reimbursement, and receipts. They do not implement or bill nonbehavioral services under an authorization or contract for behavioral services. If inaccuracies in reporting or billing are discovered, they inform all relevant parties (e.g., organizations, licensure boards, funders), correct the inaccuracy in a timely manner, and document all actions taken in this circumstance and the eventual outcomes.

title: ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS IN ASSESSMENT
body:
ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS IN ASSESSMENT

Prior to the initiation of any assessment activities, behavior analysts must provide an opportunity for clients and/or stakeholders to give informed consent.

**The Code's definition of client:** The direct recipient of the behavior analyst's services. At various times during service provision, one or more stakeholders may simultaneously meet the definition of client (e.g., the point at which they receive direct training or consultation). In some contexts, the client might be a group of individuals (e.g., with organizational behavior management services).

**The Code's definition of stakeholder:** An individual, other than the client, who is impacted by and invested in the behavior analyst's services (e.g., parent, caregiver, relative, legally authorized representative, collaborator, employer, agency or institutional representatives, licensure board, funder, third-party contractor for services).

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 2.11: Obtaining Informed Consent: Behavior analysts are responsible for knowing about and complying with all conditions under which they are required to obtain informed consent from clients, stakeholders, and research participants (e.g., before initial implementation of assessments or behavior-change interventions, when making substantial changes to interventions, when exchanging or releasing confidential information or records). They are responsible for explaining, obtaining, reobtaining, and documenting required informed consent. They are responsible for obtaining assent from clients when applicable.

**Code's definition of informed consent for information use/sharing:** The permission given by an individual with the legal right to consent before participating in services or research, or allowing their information to be used or shared. Providing the opportunity for an individual to give informed consent to share or use their information involves communicating about: 1) the purpose and intended use; 2) the audience; 3) the expected duration; 4) the right to decline or withdraw consent at any time; 5) potential risks or benefits; 6) any limitations to confidentiality or privacy; 7) whom to contact for questions or concerns at any time; and 8) the opportunity to ask questions and receive answers.

title: THREE REQUIRED ELEMENTS TO ENSURE INFORMED CONSENT:
body:
### THREE REQUIRED ELEMENTS TO ENSURE INFORMED CONSENT:
1. The client has the CAPACITY to make an informed decision:
    - Understands nature of the procedure, risks, and relevant information.
    - Has adequate mental processes for gaining knowledge.
    - Has the ability to select and express choice.
    - Has the ability to engage in a rational process of decision-making.
    - If a client's disability prevents informed decision-making, then a legally authorized representative can make decisions on their behalf.
2. Consent to participate must be VOLUNTARY, given in the absence of coercion, duress, or any undue influence. Participants must know that they can withdraw at any time.
3. The client and/or their legally authorized representative must have KNOWLEDGE about their participation (e.g., purpose of services, time commitment, procedures, risks and benefits, adverse effects, limits to confidentiality or privacy, point of contact, and alternative choices).
    - Information must be delivered in clear, nontechnical language and there should be time for questions and answers.
[THINK:] Being informed means being able to answer questions about the procedure in their own words.

[The Code's definition of legally authorized representative: Any individual authorized under law to provide consent on behalf of an individual who cannot provide consent to receive services or participate in research.]

RELEVANT SOURCES OF INFORMATION IN RECORDS (Cont'd)

3. Historical records:
- Past ABA assessments and programs.
- Early childhood records, treatments, developmental milestone reports, etc.
- Non-ABA interventions (e.g., speech, OT, etc.).
- History of relevant behavioral incidents.
- Psychological evaluations, test results, etc.
- Therapy or counseling reports, notes, goals, and progress.
- Relevant legal history (e.g., custody agreements, guardianship, etc.).

BCBA F.2 Identify and integrate relevant cultural variables in the assessment process.

CULTURAL VARIABLES
- Cultural contingencies shape behavior, and should be considered in the assessment process.
- Culture can be defined as, "the extent to which a group of individuals engage in overt and verbal behavior reflecting shared behavioral learning histories, serving to differentiate the group from other groups, and predicting how individuals within the group act in specific setting conditions." (Sugai et al. 2012, p.200.)
- Cultural identity: The occurrence of specific stimuli and response classes that are connected to a person's race, socioeconomic class, age, religion, sexual orientation, ethnicity, disability, nationality, and geographic context.
[THINK: A client's personal values, learned reinforcers, characteristics, and unique circumstances. What is important to this person?]
- Understanding cultural variables helps guide the assessment process and results in improved quality of services for diverse populations.
- Behavior analysts who lack the experience and knowledge to serve a culturally diverse client should take the time to learn about the client's cultural behaviors, values, and norms as well as gain direct exposure to culturally similar experiences and people. (If not possible, client should be referred to somebody with specific knowledge/experience.)
- Assessors should collaborate with cultural experts to better understand the cultural perspectives of their clients.

CONSIDERATIONS FOR IDENTIFYING AND INTEGRATING RELEVANT CULTURAL VARIABLES IN THE ASSESSMENT PROCESS (E.10):
1. Establishing the assessment team:
- In addition to the clinical team, there should be collaboration with family, community members, and professionals to learn about the client's culture and for awareness of sociocultural explanations of client behavior.

[CAUTION: Don't forget to get consent first! (Code, 2.11)]
