title: 2. Ensuring assessor's cultural responsiveness:
body:
## 2. Ensuring assessor's cultural responsiveness:

- An assessor should consider their own cultural values, preferences, characteristics, and circumstances. A culturally aware assessor can identify the reinforcement and punishment contingencies that have been established by themselves, their colleagues, their family, and any other social group they may belong to or identify with.
- Assessors should learn about the client's cultural values, preferences, characteristics, and circumstances. Not doing so can result in treatment recommendations that don't align with (or even interfere with) the client's cultural values.
- Assessors should receive cultural awareness training and reflect on how culture might impact their belief system.
- Assessors should self-assess their understanding of cultural diversity and their biases, and how that affects relationships with clients. (E.11)

> **[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING] Code Standard 1.07: Cultural Responsiveness and Diversity:**
> Behavior analysts actively engage in professional development activities to acquire knowledge and skills related to cultural responsiveness and diversity. They evaluate their own biases and ability to address the needs of individuals with diverse needs/backgrounds (e.g., age, disability, ethnicity, gender expression/identity, immigration status, marital/relationship status, national origin, race, religion, sexual orientation, socioeconomic status). Behavior analysts also evaluate biases of their supervisees and trainees, as well as their supervisees' and trainees' ability to address the needs of individuals with diverse needs/backgrounds.

title: 3. Communication:
body:
## 3. Communication:

- Communication should be easily understood and culturally aware.
- Assessors should consider how their spoken and written language will be perceived by a client; avoid culturally inappropriate language and behavior analytic jargon. This can lead to confusion, and impact participation in the assessment and recommended procedures.

> **[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING] Code Standard 2.08: Communicating About Services:**
> Behavior analysts use understandable language in, and ensure comprehension of, all communications with clients, stakeholders, supervisees, trainees, and research participants. Before providing services, they clearly describe the scope of services and specify the conditions under which services will end. They explain all assessment and behavior-change intervention procedures before implementing them and explain assessment and intervention results when they are available. They provide an accurate and current set of their credentials and a description of their area of competence upon request.

- Assessment paperwork should be at the level of literacy and comprehension of the language for the individual completing it.
- If there is limited language comprehension, to avoid embarrassing or intimidating the individual, get information orally and/or have another person complete the paperwork and/or provide forms in the native language, or get an interpreter.

title: CULTURAL VARIABLES (Cont'd)
body:
CULTURAL VARIABLES (Cont'd)

4. Choosing assessment activities:
- Select assessment methods with consideration of cultural factors, preferences, and norms.
- Modify assessment activities to better fit the cultural values, norms, and preferences of the client (e.g., translating materials, using culturally relevant examples and visuals, etc.).
- Clients should not be expected to conform to an assessor's cultural values or scientific expectations.
- Assessment practices should be rooted in an assessor's clinical expertise and their knowledge of a client's preferences and learning histories.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 2.13: Selecting, Designing, and Implementing Assessments: Before selecting or designing behavior-change interventions behavior analysts select and design assessments that are conceptually consistent with behavioral principles; that are based on scientific evidence; and that best meet the diverse needs, context, and resources of the client and stakeholders. They select, design, and implement assessments with a focus on maximizing benefits and minimizing risk of harm to the client and stakeholders. They summarize the procedures and results in writing.

5. Defining target behaviors:
- In addition to identifying target behaviors, examine (and understand) the functional relationships between behavior and culture.
- Use positive language to define problem behaviors so that definitions don't feel accusatory.
- Use forms of communication that are sensitive to cultural differences (e.g., eye contact, wait time, meanings of words, non-vocal body language, personal space, and quality of voice).

6. Data collection:
- Family members should be involved in developing data collection protocols, determining the time, date, and location of data collection, and deciding who will be present for data collection.
- Methods should be adapted to the family's interaction and style.
- Prior to data collection, assessors should understand the client's cultural perspectives, literacy, communication, and language background.

7. Analyzing data:
- Assessments should go beyond identifying motivating operations, antecedents, behaviors, and consequences; they should also incorporate an assessment of cultural preferences and norms.
- Assess the socio-cultural variables that could help explain occurrences of target behavior.
- Consult clients and their families about cultural variables that may influence assessment results.

F.4 Implement assessments of relevant skill strengths and deficits, and contextual fit (e.g., client values, cultural variables, social validity, environmental resources).

ASSESSING SKILLS AND BEHAVIORS

The purpose of a functional behavior assessment (FBA) is to identify a client's strengths and areas of need, to guide the development of goals and effective interventions.

> **Functional behavior assessment (FBA):** The systematic methods and activities (indirect assessment, direct assessment, and functional analysis) used by behavior analysts to gather information about the function of problem behavior, the results of which are used to guide goal setting and interventions for decreasing target behavior and increasing desirable behavior.

**FBA METHODS FUNNEL**

Yields *least* precise information

**INDIRECT FUNCTIONAL BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT**

**DIRECT FUNCTIONAL BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENT**

**FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS**

Yields *most* precise information

*Graphic: FBA methods.*

- Practitioners must design FBA packages that will lead to the most comprehensive and complete information.
- To produce the best outcomes, an FBA can combine a variety of assessment activities (i.e., structured interview, rating scales, direct observation, functional analysis).
- The most important part of an FBA is gathering reliable and valid data, and the analysis of that data.

**WAYS TO COLLECT CLIENT INFORMATION IN AN ASSESSMENT (FBA):**
- Record review. (F.1)
- Indirect assessments. (F.3)
- Direct assessments. (F.3)
- Preference and reinforcer assessments. (F.4)
- Descriptive assessments. (F.5)
- Functional analysis. (F.6)

title: INDIRECT ASSESSMENT
body:
INDIRECT ASSESSMENT

- Assessor relies on the recall and truthfulness of the people who know the client best.
[THINK:] Talk to the client's people.
- Ensures an understanding of the natural events that correlate with the behaviors of interest.
- Initial insight into the variables that may be maintaining target behavior.
- Can be a combination of interviews, checklists and rating scales.

[USE FOR] Gaining a personal and historical perspective, gathering preliminary insights for descriptive assessments; forming a hypothesis of behavior function; identifying preferences and potential reinforcers; identifying best direct observation times, and formulating potential functional analysis conditions.

[CAUTION] Direct methods should be used to evaluate the accuracy of indirect assessment results.

- Doesn't require client observations.
[pro] - Helpful in the early stages of assessment to begin narrowing down the focus and identify priorities.
- Requires less training.

- Informants are not always correct or objective, even if they intend to be (memories are faulty, and cognitive biases are real).
[con] - Less reliable than direct assessments, minimal (subjective) information about the function of behavior.
- Can be misused by assessors to prescribe treatment.
- Assessors don't come into contact with the actual target behavior.
- Derived from what individuals can recall or perceive as important.

[3 INDIRECT ASSESSMENTS]
- Interview
- Checklists
- Rating scales

TYPES OF INDIRECT ASSESSMENTS:
- Behavioral interview.
- Behavior checklists.
- Rating scales.

BEHAVIORAL INTERVIEW
- The first step in learning about potential target behaviors, and the client's and stakeholders' primary concerns.
- Assessors can interview the client directly, unless the client can't be interviewed and/or information is needed from significant others.

title: BEHAVIORAL INTERVIEW (Cont'd)
body:
BEHAVIORAL INTERVIEW (Cont'd)

[pro]
- Doesn't require client observations.
- Helpful in early stages of assessment.
- Gives stakeholders a chance to share their concerns.
- Helpful in assessing stakeholder expectations, cultural norms and values.

[con]
- Informants are not always correct or objective.
- Less reliable than direct assessments.
- Can be misused by assessors to prescribe treatment.
- No contact with actual target behavior.
- Derived from what individuals can recall or perceive as important.
- Type of questions and how they are asked may bias responses.
- Informants may provide misleading info to meet interviewer expectations.
- Informants may not understand certain questions or be reluctant to disclose information.

BEHAVIOR CHECKLISTS
- An assessment in the form of checklists that gathers descriptions of the specific behaviors of interest, and the antecedents and consequences that affect the frequency, duration, or intensity of behavior.

[USE FOR] Assessing challenging behavior (e.g., tantrums, aggressions) and specific skills (e.g., turn-taking, hand-washing).

[PROCEDURE]
1. A functional assessment checklist is given to a relevant stakeholder.
2. Responders are asked to check off the relevant information as it pertains to the target behavior, environmental variables (e.g., potential antecedents and consequences, times of day, what the behavior looks like, etc.).
3. When combined with rating scales, may include information about likelihood of the behavior in specific conditions, times of day, magnitude, etc.
4. When combined with interview questions or structured interviews, stakeholders are asked for narrative descriptions of the behavior and any other needed specific details.

[pro]
- Doesn't require client observations.
- Helpful in early stages of assessment.
- Require less training for the assessor.

[con]
- Minimal (subjective) information about the function of behavior.
- Can be misused by assessors to prescribe treatment.
- No contact with actual target behavior.

title: RATING SCALES
body:
RATING SCALES

- Gathers quantifiable information about a behavior's occurrence and related environmental variables.
  THINK: Likert scale.
  [USE FOR] Generating a hypothesis of function; generating preliminary information; assessing severity; identifying important details for planning descriptive assessments.
  [PROCEDURE]
  1. Informants are asked to make estimations about the conditions in which target behavior occurs.
  2. Numerical values are assigned to an informant's ratings, to be analyzed.
  3. The scores in each rated condition are used to form a hypothesis of the function of a behavior.
  4. The condition with the highest rating is hypothetically correlated to the problem behavior.
  Example: If a score reflects that a target behavior is always preceded by attention being diverted from the client, an attention function hypothesis can be made.
- Uses a multi-point scale to rate, ranging from strongly agree to strongly disagree, or 0-10, etc.
- If more information is needed, can be combined with interviews and checklists.
  THINK: Customer satisfaction scales.
  Example: On a scale of 1-10, how excited are you to become a BCBA?
  Example: On a scale ranging from strongly disagree to strongly agree, is the target behavior always preceded by someone asking the client to stop playing video games and come to work?

[pro]
- Quantified data can be compared across time, settings and raters for reliability.
- Avoids biased measurement and interpretation.

[con]
- Results can be unreliable (i.e., poor interrater agreement).
- Validity and Accuracy are typically low.

Examples of published rating scales (combine interview, rating scales, and checklists):
1. Vineland Adaptive Behavior Rating Scale (VABS-3).
2. Motivation Assessment Scale (MAS).
3. Motivation Analysis Rating Scale (MARS).
4. Problem Behavior Questionnaire (PBQ).
5. Functional Analysis Screening Tool (FAST).
6. Questions About Behavioral Function (QABF).
7. Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) (2 versions).
8. Adaptive Behavior Scale-School (ABS-S).

title: DIRECT ASSESSMENTS | Assessment procedures that provide measurable and valid information about target behavior.
body:
DIRECT ASSESSMENTS | Assessment procedures that provide measurable and valid information about target behavior.

SIX DIRECT ASSESSMENT METHODS:
1. Standardized tests.
2. Criterion-referenced assessment.
3. Curriculum-based assessment.
4. Ecological assessment.
5. Direct observation. (F.5)
6. Discrepancy analysis.

STANDARDIZED TESTS | - An assessment that compares results, in general, to the population for whom the specific test was designed.
Example: The Wide Range Achievement Test-5 (WRAT-5) assesses general grade level performance.
- Results are plotted on specific tables and charts.
[USE FOR] Comparing an individual's performance to normative levels in specific categories (e.g., grade, age, etc.).
- There are different variations and evaluation processes from which to yield important client information:
    - Norm-referenced: An individual's performance is compared to a norm group, using a bell curve to represent normal distribution, and showing where the individual's results "fall on the curve."
    - Percentile ranks: Average scores are labeled as the 50th percentile, and results reflect deviation from the average score. An individual's performance percentile means they scored equal to or better than X% of others who took the same test.
Example: Scoring in the 75th percentile means a person scored equal to or better than 75% of the test participants.
    - Grade equivalent score: A learner's raw score (number of items answered correctly) is compared to the expected grade level performance of a norm group.
Example: Scoring 3.2, means performing at early third grade level.
    - Age equivalent score: A learner's raw score is compared to the expected age level performance of a norm group.
Example: Scoring 5.5, means performing at the age of 5.5 years.
- Results are not meaningful for identifying specific skills or behavior, and therefore not useful in determining the direction of intervention.
Example: Scores below a normative performance level, don't give information about specific skill deficits.
[con] - Often requires a licensed professional to administer. (BCBA is a certification, not a license.)
Example: Iowa Tests of Basic Skills, Peabody Individual Achievement Test-R/NU, Wide Range Achievement Test-5 (WRAT-5), SAT, BACB Exams, Graduate Record Exam (GRE), General Education Development (GED), etc.
section_heading: DIRECT ASSESSMENTS | Assessment procedures that provide measurable and valid information about target behavior.

title: CRITERION-REFERENCED ASSESSMENT (CRA)
body:
CRITERION-REFERENCED ASSESSMENT (CRA)
- An assessment of client performance across recognized and commonly accepted developmental milestones.
- [USE FOR] Measuring developmental progress or lack thereof.
- Scoring requires that assessors indicate that a specific skill was present, absent, or emerging.
- Example: A three-year-old should be able to run and jump easily, walk upstairs unassisted, and ride a tricycle. An assessor would look for these skills and report on current performance.
- [pro] Better than standardized tests for identifying information about specific skills and generating behavior-change goals.

CURRICULUM-BASED ASSESSMENT (CBA)
- An assessment of student progress on specific weekly tasks and lessons.
- Produces very specific information about the student.
- [USE FOR] Measuring weekly progress through a planned curriculum, to assess ongoing progress of motor, language, cognition, self-help, and academic skills in an academic setting.
- Data reflect mistake patterns, relative progress, independent performance, semi-independent performance, no performance.
- Measures progress, or lack thereof, as skills are taught (e.g., daily or weekly), but can also summarize longer periods of time (e.g., quarter, semester, year, etc.).
- Example: Weekly spelling tests or math quizzes, final exams, etc.

ECOLOGICAL ASSESSMENT
- An objective assessment of the complex environmental relationships within different aspects of an individual's life (e.g., work, home, school).
- [USE FOR] Identifying the most pressing behavioral concerns and possible solutions; identifying settings in which a client engages in challenging behavior.
- Assessors gather a lot of information about the client and the environments in which the client lives and works.
- Relies on direct observations, interviews, and record review.
- Potential areas of assessment include: Physiological conditions, physical arrangements (e.g., lighting, noise, seating arrangements), interactions with others, home environment, and reinforcement history.
- [pro] A comprehensive, objective, and broad look at an individual's life.
- [con] Time consuming, especially if observers aren't specific about needed information.
- [con] Takes a lot of time and resources, and there are privacy concerns.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: DIRECT OBSERVATION
body:
DIRECT OBSERVATION
- An assessment where client behavior is observed directly and repeatedly in its natural environment.
[USE FOR] Identifying behaviors for assessment and/or treatment, gathering behavior measures for assessment, and measuring baseline levels.
- Should include a variety of settings, people, and behaviors, to ensure a higher-quality assessment with more valid results.
- Frequency, rate, duration, latency, and time sampling can be used to measure target behavior during direct observation.

[pro] - Objective data collection, good way to get baseline data, and gain insight into potential FA conditions.

[con] - Can produce limited or skewed information; not as reliable as direct measurement or an FA.
Example: If behavior is only observed in one environment, it can paint a misleading picture of its occurrence.

TYPES OF DIRECT OBSERVATIONS: (F.5)
- ABC continuous recording.
- ABC narrative recording.
- Scatterplot recording.

DISCREPANCY ANALYSIS
a.k.a. Normative comparison.
- A comparison of a client's behavior to same-age, typically developing peers to determine if a challenging behavior is at problematic levels or appropriate for age or context.
[THINK:] Social validity of behavior change.
[USE FOR] Assessing if behavior is problematic or normative.
- A socially valid performance expectation is determined by a normative sample for a specific behavior or skill, to be used as comparison for client performance.
Example: It is normative (typical) for a two-year-old child to emit protest responses, therefore a goal to eliminate protest behaviors for a two-year-old girl with autism is not an appropriate target.

[pro] - Prevents unreasonable goal expectations.

[BCBA] F.4 Design and evaluate preference assessments.
[BCaBA] F.5 Implement preference and reinforcer assessments.

STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT (SPA)
A variety of procedures used to identify:
- The stimuli that a person typically prefers (selects and engages with).
- The relative preference of preferred stimuli (low to high).
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT (SPA) (Cont'd)
body:
STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT (SPA) (Cont'd)

- Changes in preferences when demands are placed, during states of deprivation, or changes in schedules of reinforcement.
- The highly preferred stimuli that can act as effective reinforcers. (Most important for a successful behavior change program.)

GUIDELINES FOR SELECTING AND USING PREFERENCE ASSESSMENTS:
- Make sure there is ample time and available resources.
- Assessors should be trained and know how to identify stimuli for assessment, conduct the procedure with an actual client, and interpret and score the results. (Code, 1.05)
- Methods are flexible and data from multiple methods can be combined.
- Identify current MOs (B.16) prior to an assessment.
- If time is limited, use brief methods and test fewer stimuli.
  - Brief is better because it's faster, but not if it doesn't provide useful predictions about preferences and would, therefore, delay things.
- Stay flexible and assess continuously because preferences change.
- Categorize items for quicker assessment (e.g., food, toys, games).
- Verify that preferred stimuli are available and will be effective as reinforcers.

[ICON: Devil character]

3 STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENTS
Asking
Free-operant
Trial-based

THREE BASIC STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT METHODS:
- Asking your clients and others about stimulus preferences.
- Free-operant observations.
- Trial-based methods.

ASKING ABOUT STIMULUS PREFERENCES
- An assessor asks the client or stakeholders about the client's specific preferences, or offers the client a pre-task choice.
- A quick and easy method to identify client preferences.

1. Asking the client:
- Spoken or written open-ended question (e.g., "What toys do you like to play with?").
- Ranking: The client ranks a list of objects in order of preference. For clients with limited language, nods or points are accepted as making a choice. Best to use actual items over pictures or icons.
2. Asking people who know the client:
- Significant others, stakeholders, parents, caregivers, teachers, siblings, friends, etc. provide information about the client's preferences.
- Gather information using structured interviews, rating scales, and/or checklists (e.g., RAISD: Reinforcer Assessment for Individuals with Severe Disabilities).
3. Offering the client a pre-task choice:
- Preferences are identified using other assessment methods and presented as choices prior to a task.
Example: Before an instruction is given, the client is asked, "What do you want to earn for doing the task, swing or jump rope?"

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

FREE-OPERANT STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT

- Observing and recording what stimuli and/or activities the client chooses to engage in during a period of unrestricted access to numerous stimuli.

[USE FOR] Identifying the relative preferences of stimuli that exist in the client's natural environment, or which stimuli can be introduced as potential preferences and reinforcers.

[THINK:] What does the client do in his spare time?

[pro]
- Takes minimal time.
- Good for larger items and activities (table top is limited to smaller items).
- Less likely to evoke problem behavior.

[con]
- Identifies fewer potential reinforcers unless assessment is repeated without the most preferred item.

**TWO TYPES OF FREE-OPERANT STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENTS:**

1. **Naturalistic free-operant observation:**

   [PROCEDURE]
   1. Conducted in the client's everyday environment (e.g., home, school).
      [THINK:] Free-time space.
   2. Client is given noncontingent access to all of the stimuli in their natural environment for an interval of time.
   3. The assessor unobtrusively records the count and duration the client selects and spends time with each stimulus.
   4. Longer duration of engagement = More preferred item.
   5. Results are organized in a preference hierarchy on a bar graph.

2. **Contrived free-operant observation:**

   [PROCEDURE]
   1. The client's environment is arranged with a variety of easily accessible stimuli (chosen for the client).
   2. The client is given noncontingent access to all of the stimuli for an interval of time. (Can be a 5-minute interval for a brief version.)
   3. The assessor unobtrusively records the count and duration of time the client spends with each item.
   4. Longer duration of engagement = More preferred.
   5. Results are organized in a preference hierarchy on a bar graph.

© 2012 - 2024, Pass the Big ABA Exam

title: TRIAL-BASED STIMULUS
body:
TRIAL-BASED STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT

- An assessment of preferred stimuli across a series of trials.
- Responses are measured by looking at client behavior across three
measures:
1. Approach: Measure of detectable movement toward the stimulus
(e.g., eye gaze, head turn, hand reach).
2. Contact: Measure of client touching or holding the stimulus.
3. Engagement: Measure of the total time or percentage of intervals
in which the client interacts with an item.
- More approaches, touches, and/or engagement = Higher preference.
- Preferred stimuli are labeled: High preference (HP); medium
preference (MP); low preference (LP).

[BOX: 3 TYPES OF TRIAL
BASED STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT
METHODS
Paired
Multiple
Single]

THREE TYPES OF TRIAL-BASED STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT
METHODS:
1. Paired stimulus preference assessment.
2. Multiple stimulus preference assessment.
3. Single stimulus preference assessment.

PAIRED STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT

a.k.a. Forced choice.

- Two or more stimuli are presented at the same time, and the client's
choices are recorded.
THINK: Forced to choose between two stimuli.

[CAUTION: To use this assessment method, clients should be able to
make choices.]

[PROCEDURE]
1. Potentially preferred items are organized into pairs, ensuring that
each item is matched (paired) with each other item.
2. In each trial, the client is asked to choose only one item from each
presented pair.
3. Approach responses are recorded for the chosen item.
4. Data reflect the percentage of approach for each chosen item.
5. Items are ranked by preference or categorized in terms of high
(e.g., 80% engagement) to low preference (e.g., 50% or less).
6. Results are organized in a preference hierarchy on a bar graph.

[pro]
- Can identify many potential reinforcers in a possible hierarchy.
- Convenient for assessing larger-sized stimuli.
- More efficient than the single stimulus method for ranking
preferences.
- Good for clients who cannot scan an array of more than two items.

[con]
- Time consuming because every possible pair must be presented.
- Item position may result in choice bias if not controlled for.
- More time consuming than multiple stimulus without replacement
and free-operant observations.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: MULTIPLE STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT
body:
MULTIPLE STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT
- Three or more stimuli are presented at the same time, and the client's choices are recorded.
[THINK:] Multiple stimuli to choose from.
[CAUTION:] Can only be used with clients who are able to make choices.

TWO TYPES OF MULTIPLE STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT:
1. Multiple stimulus with replacement (MSWI):
[PROCEDURE]
1. An assessor presents a grouping of three or more stimuli and asks the client to choose one item. (E.g., "Which one do you want most?" or "Choose one.")
2. The item/activity that the client chooses remains in the array and those not chosen are replaced with new items/activities.
3. An assessor presents the new group of items, which includes new items and the original (chosen) item, and again asks the client to choose one item.
4. At the end of each trial, the array will always have the same number of stimuli that the assessor starts with. The assessor should be changing the placement of items to control for position-biased responding.
5. This process can be repeated multiple times, for the same stimuli or for new stimuli.
Example: An assessor presents a client with an array of three different color balls and says, "Choose one." The client chooses a red ball. The chosen ball remains in the array, and the unchosen balls are replaced with two different color balls. The client is again asked to, "choose one." This time, the client chooses a lavender ball. The lavender ball remains in the array, and the others are replaced with another new set of new balls. This continues until the assessor is out of balls.

[pro]
- Can identify many relative preferences and potential reinforcers.
- Good for ranking potential reinforcers.

[con]
- Can take a lot of time to complete.
- Item positions may result in choice bias.
- Can limit assessment to fewer and smaller items appropriate for tabletop.
- More time consuming than multiple stimulus without replacement and free-operant observations.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: MULTIPLE STIMULUS
body:
MULTIPLE STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT
(Cont'd)

2. Multiple stimulus without replacement (MSWO):

[PROCEDURE]
1. An assessor presents a grouping of three or more stimuli and asks the client to choose one item (e.g., "Which one do you want most?" or "Choose one").
2. The item/activity that the client chooses is removed from the array, and the remaining items are rearranged for the next trial.
   THINK: The chosen stimulus is out!
3. The assessor presents the leftover stimuli and again asks the client to choose one item.
4. At the end of the assessment the assessor is left with one unchosen item.
5. This process can be repeated multiple times, for the same stimuli or for new stimuli.
Example: Rusty presents his client with five Pokemon cards and says, "Choose one." The client chooses one card, which Rusty removes from the array. He doesn't replace it. Rusty says, "You're now left with four cards," and presents the array (which is now missing the selected card). The client chooses a second card from the remaining cards, which Rusty removes and doesn't replace. There are now three cards left. Rusty again presents the choices and the client picks another card. Again, the chosen card is removed and not replaced. For the final trial, the client must choose between the remaining two. The client makes his choice and Rusty is left with one card.

[pro]
- Can identify many potential reinforcers in a short amount of time.
- Creates a clearer hierarchy with a smaller number of stimuli.
- Takes less time than multiple stimulus with replacement.

[con]
- Item positions may result in choice bias.
- Can limit assessment to fewer and smaller items appropriate for tabletop.
- More time consuming than free operant observations.

SINGLE STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT

a.k.a. Successive
choice.

- Stimuli are presented one at a time, and the client's response to each individual stimulus is recorded.
  THINK: One at a time.
- Most basic method for assessing preference.

[USE FOR]
Clients who have a hard time choosing between two or more items/activities, and/or are unable to scan an array of two or more items.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Potential stimuli are gathered across all domains (i.e., visual, auditory, vestibular, tactile, olfactory, gustatory, and multisensory).
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: SINGLE STIMULUS
body:
SINGLE STIMULUS
PREFERENCE
ASSESSMENT
(Cont'd)

2. Initially, all items are made available for a short time so that the
client can sample each.
3. The assessor presents each item on its own and records the
client's interest and engagement (e.g., duration of holding,
touching, playing, looking).
4. Each item is presented several times, sequentially.
5. Assessor records approach (e.g., movement toward item),
avoidance or rejection, and duration of engagement.
6. The percentage of approach is recorded.
7. Results are organized in a preference hierarchy on a bar graph.

[pro]
- Can identify many potential reinforcers.
- Can be conducted with larger-sized items.

[con]
- Doesn't assess relative preferences, unless duration of engagement
is also measured.
- Can result in false positives.

REINFORCER
ASSESSMENTS

a.k.a. Reinforcer
analysis.

[4 TYPES OF
REINFORCER
ASSESSMENTS
Concurrent
In-the-moment
Multiple schedule
Progressive ratio]

FOUR TYPES OF REINFORCER ASSESSMENTS:
1. Concurrent schedule reinforcer assessment.
2. In-the-moment reinforcer analysis.
3. Multiple schedule reinforcer assessment.
4. Progressive ratio reinforcer assessment.

CONCURRENT
SCHEDULE
REINFORCER
ASSESSMENT

- Assesses the effectiveness of reinforcers, when two or more
contingencies operate on two or more behaviors, at the same time,
yet independent of each other.
- Two or more potential reinforcers are set to compete against each
other to see which will produce a larger increase in responding when
presented as a consequence.
THINK: Concurrent schedules of reinforcement. (B.10)

[USE FOR]
Assessing the relative effectiveness of high-preference
(HP) and low preference (LP) stimuli as reinforcers; and
the effectiveness of low preference (LP) stimuli as
reinforcers when delivered contingently in the absence of
high-preference (HP) stimuli.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: CONCURRENT
body:
CONCURRENT
SCHEDULE
REINFORCER
ASSESSMENT
(Cont'd)

[PROCEDURE]
1. Target behaviors and corresponding reinforcers and schedules are established for each behavior. The schedules are discriminated for the client (either verbally or visually).
2. The client is able to choose between competing contingencies (i.e., chooses a behavior to engage in, knowing the specific reinforcement each behavior will produce).
   THINK: Choice.
3. Assessors compare the rates of the competing target responses to assess which stimuli/schedule produce the higher rate of responding.
   THINK: Behavior goes where reinforcement flows.
4. If a client allocates a greater proportion of responding to one component of the concurrent schedule over the other, the stimulus used as a consequence for that component is the more effective reinforcer.
   - Relative effectiveness (high vs. low preferences) is connected to the proportion of responding in each component.
5. Stimuli that produce higher response rates are rated as more effective reinforcers.
   THINK: Matching law. (B.23)

Example: To test the relative effectiveness of an iPad vs. television as a reinforcer, a client (who doesn't enjoy reading) can choose to read 25 pages to earn 20 minutes of iPad time, or read 10 pages to earn 10 minutes of television. The client chose to read 25 pages. Although reading 25 pages requires more response effort than 10, the value and amount of iPad time proves to be a stronger reinforcer.

Example: To test the relative effectiveness of binge-watching Love on the Spectrum vs. a glass of wine as reinforcers, a student is given a choice of: Reading the "White Book" for two straight hours to earn a glass of wine; or taking a full-length mock exam to earn binge-watching Love on the Spectrum for the rest of the evening. The student chooses reading, which reflects the value of a (probably) much-needed glass of wine.

IN-THE-MOMENT
REINFORCER ANALYSIS
- Basing an item's reinforcing effectiveness on a client's immediate response when the presumed reinforcer is presented, rather than on a future increase in response rates.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Preferred stimuli are identified from past preference and reinforcer assessments.
2. During programming, trainers have presumed reinforcers on hand.
3. When the client emits a target response, trainers make an in-the-moment decision about which previously established reinforcer to deliver.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: IN-THE-MOMENT
body:
IN-THE-MOMENT
REINFORCER ANALYSIS
(Cont'd)

[THINK:] An in-the-moment judgment call.
4. Reinforcers are chosen with consideration of: The client's current affect (laughing, tired, neutral face, frowning, crying); a client's previous approach, engagement, and contact with the item; previous performance data for specific stimuli; and preferences observed in the past.

**Example:** After several stimulus preference assessments, Devin's therapist has many presumed reinforcers to use in session (e.g., mini cupcakes, Starburst, gum balls, little figurines, and baseball cards). Prior to running a matching program, the therapist lays out a few preferred items, and notices that Devin is smiling and staring at the little figurines. After his first correct match, Devin is given a figurine to play with. The therapist uses the figurines for about 10 correct matching trials, after which he notices Devin eyeing and gesturing toward the Starburst. The therapist makes an in-the-moment decision to reinforce the next correct response with a Starburst.

MULTIPLE SCHEDULE
REINFORCER
ASSESSMENT

- Using the multiple schedule of reinforcement (B.10) to assess the most effective reinforcement contingency when two or more schedules of reinforcement are available for one behavior, with only one (signaled) schedule in effect at a time.

[USE FOR] Comparing the reinforcer effectiveness of different types of contingencies for the same behavior; comparing response-dependent contingencies (FR, VI schedules, B.10) vs. response-independent contingencies (FT, VT schedules, G.3).

[PROCEDURE]
1. Two or more possible schedules of reinforcement are established for one class of behavior, and discriminated with verbal or visual SDs.
2. The schedules of reinforcement can be response-dependent and/or time based (NCR, G.3).
3. An SD signals the schedule in effect at any given time (e.g., time of day, location, people present, visuals, visual/auditory timers, etc.).
4. The assessor switches between components of the multiple schedules.
5. The assessor records responding in each component to see which schedule produces the higher response rate.

**Example:** A teacher wanted to assess the effectiveness of different break options as reinforcers. On Monday, students were given a 10-minute break to the playground after completing math fluency drills. On Tuesday, students were given a 10-minute break on the computer after completing the same drills. They worked more quickly (and with higher accuracy) on Tuesday, which demonstrated that the computer was a more powerful reinforcer than the playground.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: PROGRESSIVE-RATIO SCHEDULE REINFORCER ASSESSMENT
body:
PROGRESSIVE-RATIO SCHEDULE REINFORCER ASSESSMENT

- Assesses the relative effectiveness of a stimulus as a reinforcer while response requirements are systematically increased, independent of client behavior.
THINK: How far will a reinforcer go?

[PROCEDURE]
1. Assessor establishes a target response and starting reinforcement criterion (i.e., FR 2).
2. The assessor starts with the initial reinforcement criterion, and gradually increases the response requirement (i.e., FR 3, FR 4, FR 5... FR 10, etc.).
3. The requirement is progressively increased until the client reaches a breaking point (when responding stops).
4. The breaking point and corresponding number of responses associated with each progressive ratio condition is compared, to assess the potency of a reinforcer.

Breaking point (or breakpoint): When a client stops responding because the current response requirements exceed the effectiveness of the reinforcer.

Example: Lee's parents gave him a $5 allowance for taking out the trash on trash day, which Lee is excited about. After two weeks, they add emptying the dishwasher to Lee's routine, without raising the allowance. That doesn't seem to bother Lee, who eagerly adds the new chore to his routine. Over the next few weeks, Lee's parents add folding laundry, picking up after the dog, vacuuming the family room, and dusting the entire house. To their surprise, a week after the last chore is introduced, Lee stops doing all his chores. Lee reached the breaking point. Five dollars can only go so far.

STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT VS. REINFORCER ASSESSMENT

PREFERENCE ASSESSMENT VS. REINFORCER ASSESSMENT

- Stimulus preference assessments are used to identify a client's preferred items and activities. THINK: What do they like? First step in identifying reinforcers.
- Reinforcer assessments are used to assess if preferred stimuli are effective as reinforcers, by looking at the changes in target behaviors that the preferred items are now contingent on. THINK: What will they work for? Most important step in identifying reinforcers.

body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

SUMMARY OF STIMULUS PREFERENCE AND REINFORCER ASSESSMENTS

STIMULUS PREFERENCE ASSESSMENTS

- ASK
  - Person.
  - Significant other.
  - Pre-task choice.

- FREE-OPERANT OBSERVATIONS
  - Naturalistic observation.
  - Contrived observation.

- TRIAL-BASED METHODS
  - Paired stimuli.
  - Multiple stimuli.
  - Single stimulus.

WHAT CLIENT LIKES

REINFORCER ASSESSMENTS

- Concurrent schedule.
- In-the-moment reinforcer analysis.
- Multiple schedule.
- Progressive ratio.

WHAT CLIENT WORKS FOR

Graphic: Preference and reinforcement assessments.

BCBA F.5 Design and evaluate descriptive assessments.

BCaBA F.5 Design and evaluate descriptive assessments.

COMMON FUNCTIONS OF BEHAVIOR

4 FUNCTIONS
- Escape
- Attention
- Tangible
- Automatic

- The source of reinforcement for any (wanted or unwanted) behavior.
- Functional Behavior Assessment (FBA) activities help attribute a maintaining consequence to the target behavior.
  [THINK: What's the function?]
- Knowing the function ensures appropriate, effective function-based interventions.

FOUR COMMON FUNCTIONS OF BEHAVIOR:
- Escape: Behavior results in escaping something aversive.
- Attention: Behavior results in social attention.
- Tangible: Behavior results in access to a tangible item.
- Automatic: Behavior results in self-mediated access or escape.
  [THINK: The analytic dimension of ABA. (A.5)]

DESCRIPTIVE ASSESSMENTS

- Direct observation of behavior, in naturally occurring conditions, used to identify the environmental events associated with a behavior.
- Correlational assessment to hypothesize the function of a target behavior.
- Should be conducted across multiple settings and times to show patterns of behaviors (e.g., assess behavior in home, school, community settings).
- Can be used to calculate the conditional probability of a behavior's occurrence.

[USE FOR] Gathering data-based info to hypothesize the function of behavior; identifying events that may be correlated with a target behavior; hypothesizing function for further assessment.

© 2012 - 2024, Pass the Big ABA Exam

title: DESCRIPTIVE
body:
DESCRIPTIVE
ASSESSMENTS
(Cont'd)

[pro]
- Safer than a functional analysis because it doesn't evoke (and reinforce) unwanted behavior.
- Way more evidenced-based than indirect FBA methods.

[con]
- Doesn't prove function of behavior.
- Can lead to false negatives for the escape function because caregivers often avoid placing demands to prevent challenging behavior.
- Can lead to false positives for the attention function, because attention can be available contingent on the behavior or not.
Example: When collecting data, while in the same room as the client, the observer's presence may serve as attention.

Conditional probability: The possibility of a behavioral event, based on a calculation of the proportion of times a target behavior is preceded by a specific antecedent, and/or followed by a specific consequence.

[THINK:] A formula to calculate the likelihood that a target behavior will occur under specific environmental conditions.

THREE VARIATIONS OF DESCRIPTIVE BEHAVIOR ASSESSMENTS:
- ABC continuous recording.
- ABC narrative recording.
- Scatterplots.

ABC CONTINUOUS
RECORDING
a.k.a. ABC checklist.

[HINT] Continuous and checklist both start with a C.

- A descriptive and direct assessment method.
- Requires direct observation during natural routines within a specified period of time (20 - 30 minutes).
- Observers record instances of target behavior and specific environmental events (specific antecedents and consequences) on CHECKLISTS.

[USE FOR] Assessment; data-based hypothesis of function; calculating conditional probability of behavior.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Create a data form (paper or electronic) to include which possible antecedents, behaviors and consequences are listed in each row for each column.
    - Checklist items are identified from information gathered during a behavioral interview or from ABC narrative recording.
2. Decide the time/intervals to observe the target behavior.
    - Observation periods should be a minimum of 20-30 minutes. Select times that will be most informative, based on previous interviews and assessments.

title: - Uses more precise measures than indirect FBAs.
body:
- Uses more precise measures than indirect FBAs.
- Data is less likely to yield false positives because data accounts for occurrence and nonoccurrence of behavior during specific conditions.

[pro]
Example: If a demand is placed, the demand box is checked, even if the target behavior didn't follow the antecedent event.
- Provides correlational info to predict causal relations between behaviors and antecedents and consequences, which is useful info for a functional analysis.

[con]
- Correlation ≠ Causation. The data only provides a hypothesized function.
- May be tough to discriminate what actually happened if there are multiple antecedents, behaviors, and consequences.
- Obtrusive process that can result in reactivity (D.3).

ABC NARRATIVE RECORDING
a.k.a. Anecdotal observation, ABC descriptive data, narrative data.

- A descriptive and direct assessment method.
- Requires direct observation during natural routines.
- Assessors provide accurate and detailed descriptions of behavior and related patterns in natural environments.
- Data are only collected when the behavior is observed on an open-ended blank ABC data sheet.

[THINK:] Narrate what you observed.

[USE FOR]
Calculating the conditional probability of behavior; data-based hypothesis of function; initial info for functional analysis; designing interventions.

| A | B | C |
|---|---|---|
| Little brother was loud and took client's toy. | Client began screaming and hit him. | Brother left, client stopped screaming and returned to playing. |

ABC chart: ABC narrative example.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Have a blank ABC data sheet on hand to record occurrences of the target behavior at any time.
2. For initial assessment, observations should be scheduled in 20-30-minute intervals.
3. Establish shorthand abbreviations/codes to make recording easier.
4. Any time the target behavior occurs, use the data sheet to:
- Describe what happened immediately before the behavior started.
- Describe everything the client does and says while the target behavior is occurring.

title: ABC NARRATIVE
body:
ABC NARRATIVE
RECORDING
(Cont'd)

- Describe anything and everything that happened after the target behavior, including the effective or ineffective consequence.
- Anything else of interest that happens to/by the client.
- Observers should be trained to:
    - Describe behavior that is seen or heard, not interpretations.
    - Record estimations of duration for each behavior.
    - Record onset and offset for each episode.
    - Identify and describe the antecedent(s) that preceded the behavior.
    - Identify and describe the consequence(s) that followed the behavior.
    - Be as unobtrusive as possible to prevent reactivity (e.g., reasonable distance, avoid eye contact, try to "blend in").
5. Conduct observations over several days so that the novelty of being observed wears off, and data will be more valid.
6. Conduct a sequence analysis: Assess data for a hypothesized function by calculating the following:
    - The number of behaviors preceded by a specific antecedent.
    - The number of behaviors preceded by a specific antecedent and followed by a specific consequence.
    - Calculate for all possible behavior, antecedent, consequence interactions.
7. Summarize data by ranking interactions from most to least likely.

ABC NARATIVE RECORDING DATA SHEET

ABC chart. ABC narrative recording data sheet.

[pro] - Takes less time than ABC continuous recording because there does not need to be a dedicated observation period.

[con] - Correlation ≠ Causation. The data only give a hypothesized function.
- Potentially low reliability.
- Data may yield false positives because it's only collected when the behavior occurs, and doesn't account for opportunities.
- May be tough to discriminate what actually happened if there are multiple antecedents, behaviors, and consequences.
- Observers may describe inferred states which threatens accuracy.
- Obtrusive process that can result in reactivity (D.3).

title: SCATTERPLOT RECORDING
body:
### SCATTERPLOT RECORDING

- A descriptive assessment method.
- Requires direct observation during natural routines in different environmental conditions (e.g., times, people, places, demand level).
- Assesses the timing patterns of target behaviors.
- Environmental conditions are evaluated for patterns such as: Higher rate of demands, diverted attention, a specific person present, etc.

[USE FOR] Assessing the extent to which a behavior occurs more or less often during different environmental conditions; analyze environmental/timing patterns typically associated with a target behavior; behavior assessment.

[CAUTION] The scatterplot is problematic because the data is correlational. Without information about antecedents and consequences, it's harder to see which environmental events actually occasion the behavior.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Data is recorded on cells in a specific grid that indicate a specific time interval (e.g., 20 minutes), and a column that indicates a specific day.
2. A code is used to indicate different rates of the target behavior (e.g., a square for high rate, a circle for low rate, blank for no occurrence).
3. During observations, assessors use the code to record occurrences of behavior.
4. Data is analyzed by visual inspection of the grid to identify times associated with zero, low, and high rates of problem behavior.
5. A pattern analysis is conducted to identify variations in the occurrence of the target behavior vs. relevant time frames and environmental conditions.

title: SCATTERPLOT
body:
SCATTERPLOT
RECORDING
(Cont'd)

- Only a hypothesis of function.
- Doesn't reflect how many times behavior occurred.
- Requires user know-how to create specific charting.
- [con] Accuracy hard to attain.
- Subjective determination of how often a behavior occurs
- Can be difficult to interpret.
- Does not include antecedents and consequences.
- Doesn't help identify replacement behaviors.

[BCBA] F.6 Design and evaluate functional analysis.

FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS
(FA)

a.k.a. Experimental
functional behavioral
assessment, analog
assessment, traditional
FA, extended FA, basic
FA.

- Originally developed by Iwata et. al.
- Antecedents and consequences that occur in a client's natural
environment are arranged and systematically manipulated so that
their individual effects on the target behavior can be observed and
measured.
THINK: Being able to turn behavior on and off = Functional control.
- Can be conducted in natural settings and contrived settings (i.e., lab).
- The only FBA method that allows you to make data-based claims
about the maintaining reinforcer (function) of challenging behavior.
- A multielement design is used for the visual analysis of FA results. (D.7)
- The pattern of behavior that emerges identifies the function(s).
- Typically conducted across multiple sessions.
[USE FOR] Confirming hypotheses about behavior functions.
- FAs should include any relevant/hypothesized test conditions and one
control condition.

CONDITIONS IN AN FA:
- Contingent attention (test).
- Contingent escape (test).
- Tangible (test) (not part of Iwata's original work).
- Alone (test).
- Free play (control).

[PROCEDURE]
1. Present the control condition:
- All sources of reinforcement are freely available (e.g., attention
and access to tangibles) and no demands are placed.
THINK: Enriched environment.
- Behavior is expected to be low in this condition and acts as a
comparison condition for the FA test conditions.
2. Once the behavior is at a low rate, the test conditions are
introduced sequentially for comparisons:
- Test and control conditions are presented one at a time with
systematic sequence alternations.

title: FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS
body:
FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS
(FA)
(Cont'd)

3. Each test condition should create a possible EO for the target behavior, with reinforcement available.
4. The occurrence of target behavior is measured in each test condition:
- The test condition with highest rates of the target behavior will demonstrate the function(s).
5. Graph and interpret results:
- Visually inspect graphed data.
  [THINK: Function(s) rise to the top.]
- Identify the conditions in which high rates of challenging behavior occur. Look for data paths that rise towards the top and are differentiated from other conditions.
  [THINK: Far away from the other data paths.]
- Target behavior can have more than one function (e.g., two functions, means two pathways rise towards the top).
- A target behavior that occurs in all (test and control) conditions (i.e., data paths look like a spider web) = Undifferentiated results = Suspected automatic reinforcement function.

[pro]
- A clear demonstration of variables that confirm the function of the target behavior.
  [THINK: Scientific evidence.]
- Standard to which all other forms of FBAs are evaluated.
- Enables valid development of effective function-based interventions.

[con]
- May temporarily strengthen/increase challenging behavior.
- Behavior may acquire new maintaining reinforcers/functions.
  Example: In an FA, elopement behavior is hypothesized to be maintained by negative reinforcement. During the demand condition the assessor is present to remove the demand, which results in unintentional attention, adding a new maintaining consequence for the target behavior.
- Requires funding, time, effort, informed consent, training and professional competency. (Code, 1.05)
- Low acceptability by clients and caregivers because of the potential to increase challenging behavior.
- Difficult to use for serious, low-rate behaviors (e.g., behaviors that occur once every six months).
  Example: A client's severe self-injurious behavior occurs approximately once every two months. In order to analyze the behavior, an assessor must contrive the test contingencies that evoke the behavior. This is not a good idea and should not be done.

title: THE ABCs OF FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS
body:
### THE ABCs OF FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS

| FA CONDITION | A | B | C | FUNCTION |
|:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |
| **Contingent attention.** | Attention diverted/EO for attention. | If challenging behavior occurs. | Attention delivered. | Positive reinforcement (attention). |
| **Contingent escape.** | Task demands presented/EO for escape. | If challenging behavior occurs. | Demands removed. | Negative reinforcement. |
| **Alone.** | Empty environment, no people, no stuff/EO for stimulation. | If challenging behavior occurs. | No response to behavior/ignored. | Automatic reinforcement. |
| **Tangible.** | Desired item withheld or removed. | If challenging behavior occurs. | Access is given. | Positive reinforcement (tangibles). |
| **Control/play.** | No demands, tons of attention and access to stuff/no EO. | If challenging behavior occurs. | No response to behavior/ignored. | Automatic reinforcement. |

*ABC chart: ABCs of functional analysis.*

title: CONTINGENT ATTENTION CONDITION
body:
### CONTINGENT ATTENTION CONDITION

- The contingent attention condition tests for a positive reinforcement function.

| | |
|:--- |:--- |
| **EO in test condition:** | Deprived of social attention. |
| **Tested function:** | Positive reinforcement (access to attention). |

*Table: Contingent attention.*

[HINT]: If taking attention away from the client turns the behavior on, and giving attention back turns it off, then the function of the behavior is attention.

[PROCEDURE]
1. Establish an EO for attention by removing or withholding attention (deprivation).
2. If/when the target behavior occurs, the assessor provides attention until the behavior stops. (Attention can be a mild reprimand, soothing statements in response to the behavior.)
3. Continue providing attention to re-establish the condition, then attention is removed again.
4. Each time the challenging behavior occurs, the attention is provided, the behavior stops, and attention is again removed.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

CONTINGENT ATTENTION CONDITION (Cont'd)

[EXAM TIP] If the attention data path rises to the top, then the function of the target behavior is positive reinforcement (attention).

CONTINGENT ESCAPE CONDITION

[HINT] If placing a demand turns the behavior on, and removing the demand turns it off, then the function of the behavior is escape.

- The contingent escape condition tests for a negative reinforcement function.

| EO in test condition: | Presentation of a demand. |
| --- | --- |
| Tested function: | Negative reinforcement (escape from demand). |

[PROCEDURE]
1. Establish an EO for escape by repeatedly presenting non-preferred demands (deprivation of relief).

[CAUTION: A demand does not just mean academic demand, like homework. A demand can be anything that a person finds aversive and wants to escape from (e.g., social interaction, toileting, eating vegetables, going in a car, etc.).]

2. If the challenging behavior occurs, remove the demands ("OK, we don't have to do this right now").
3. If the challenging behavior stops, reintroduce the demands after a predetermined break interval (e.g., 15 seconds) was provided as reinforcement.
4. Each time the challenging behavior occurs, repeat the steps of removing and reintroducing demands.
5. If the client does not respond to the demand or emits an incorrect response, provide a prompt to have the client respond correctly.

title: ALONE CONDITION (Cont'd)
body:
ALONE CONDITION (Cont'd)

[EXAM TIP]: If the alone data path rises to the top, then the function of the target behavior is automatic reinforcement.

FREE PLAY CONDITION (CONTROL)
- The free play condition is the control condition against which behavior in the test conditions is compared.
- Challenging behavior is expected to be low in this condition (because client has everything they want, so there is no EO).

| | |
|:--- |:--- |
| **EO in test condition:** | No EO in this condition, as there are no demands to escape, and nothing is being withheld. Everything is available. [THINK]: Disneyland. |
| **Tested function:** | Behavior is expected to be low in this condition. But if behavior does occur, then the function is likely to be automatic reinforcement. |

[PROCEDURE]
1. Clients are given free access to an environment that is free from demands, full of preferred stimuli, and with adult attention provided consistently (e.g., every 30 seconds). [THINK]: The world is your oyster.
2. Demands are not presented in this condition.
3. If the challenging behavior occurs at the 30-sec. mark, when attention is to be delivered, withhold attention until the challenging behavior stops.
4. No other consequences should be delivered for challenging behavior:
- If the target behavior consistently increases during this condition, the function of the target behavior is likely automatic reinforcement.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

FREE PLAY CONDITION (CONTROL) (Cont'd)

[EXAM TIP]
If the free play/control path rises to the top, then the function of the target behavior is likely automatic reinforcement.

CONTINGENT TANGIBLE CONDITION

[HINT]
If removing a tangible item from the client turns the behavior on, and giving the item back turns it off, then the function of the behavior is access to tangibles.

- The contingent tangible condition tests for a positive reinforcement function (access).
- Not an original Iwata FA condition.

| EO in test condition: | Deprivation/removal of a desired tangible item. |
| --- | --- |
| Tested function: | Positive reinforcement (access to tangibles). |

Table: Contingent tangible.

PROCEDURE
1. Present access to individualized, highly preferred items and activities for a set amount of time.
2. Establish an EO for tangibles by either removing the items or asking client to give them back.
3. If the challenging behavior occurs, return the tangibles or activity immediately, allow access for a set amount of time, and then remove them again.
4. Repeat previous steps for each instance of the target behavior.

FA: TANGIBLE FUNCTION

[Graph showing Number of Challenging Behaviors vs Sessions]

KEY:
- Escape
- Attention
- Tangible

Graph: Tangible function.

[EXAM TIP]
If the tangible condition path rises to the top, then the function of the target behavior is positive reinforcement (access).

UNDIFFERENTIATED PATTERN
- A pattern of responding during an FA, when a target behavior occurs at similar rates across all of the FA conditions or is highly variable with no clear differentiation of any path(s).
- Creates a graphic display of data paths running into each other.

title: UNDIFFERENTIATED PATTERN (Cont'd)
body:
UNDIFFERENTIATED PATTERN (Cont'd)

- Either this is an inconclusive result that does not indicate a clear representation of function (in which case the FA can be repeated for more conclusive results), or the function is automatic reinforcement.

FA: UNDIFFERENTIATED PATTERN AUTOMATIC FUNCTION

[EXAM TIP]: If the data paths of an FA overlap like a spider web, then either the FA results are inconclusive, or the function of the target behavior is automatic reinforcement.

FA ETHICS AND SAFETY

- Only BCBAs with appropriate training, supervision, experience, and competence can conduct FAs.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 1.05: Practicing within Scope of Competence: Behavior analysts practice only within their identified scope of competence. They engage in professional activities in new areas (e.g., populations, procedures) only after accessing and documenting appropriate study, training, supervised experience, consultation, and/or co-treatment from professionals competent in the new area. Otherwise, they refer or transition services to an appropriate professional.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard 2.13: Selecting, Designing, and Implementing Assessments: Before selecting or designing behavior-change interventions, behavior analysts select and design assessments that are conceptually consistent with behavioral principles; that are based on scientific evidence; and that best meet the diverse needs, context, and resources of the client and stakeholders. They select, design, and implement assessments with a focus on maximizing benefits and minimizing risk of harm to the client and stakeholders. They summarize the procedures and results in writing.

- Assess the risks and cost-benefit ratio prior to conducting an FA.
- Avoid the use of FAs for dangerous behaviors (e.g., punching, sexual assault); use a descriptive FBA or indirect FBA instead.
- If using an FA for severe behavior (e.g., hitting, SIB, PICA) is agreed upon, take important precautions:
    - Use a brief FA or a precursor FA.
    - Have medical staff present (e.g., nurses, doctors) if the client exhibits dangerous behaviors.

title: FA ETHICS AND SAFETY
body:
FA ETHICS AND SAFETY
(Cont'd)

- Staff should be trained and experienced in keeping everyone safe.
- Have additional staff on hand.
- Use protective equipment (e.g., helmets, gloves, goggles, etc.).
- Have termination criteria if behavior becomes dangerous.
- Use stimuli that don't present danger (e.g., soft toys).
- Rule out any medical concerns before initiating the FA. (Code, 2.12)

FA VARIATIONS

- Brief FA.
- Natural Settings FA.
- Trial-based FA.
- Latency-based FA.
- Precursor FA.
- Synthesized FA.

BRIEF FA

- An FA conducted over a shorter period of time.
- Includes one or two 5- to 10-minute sessions for each FA condition.

[USE FOR] Analyzing behavior when there are time restrictions or
the target behavior is too severe to evoke too many
times.

- If a clear functional relationship cannot be demonstrated, switch to
the basic FA.

[PROCEDURE]

1. Switch between conditions that evoke challenging behavior and
those that don't.
2. Contingency reversal: Reversing between conditions in which
reinforcers are contingent on challenging behavior, and conditions
in which reinforcement is made contingent on the occurrence of
replacement behaviors.

[CON] - Less effective in identifying functional relationships than a basic FA.

NATURAL SETTINGS FA

- An FA conducted in a natural setting, like the client's home or
classroom.

[USE FOR] Identifying the relevant stimuli that impact challenging
behavior in natural settings.

- When this method is problematic (often due to lack of experimental
control), a trial-based FA should be considered.

[CON] - Can be disruptive to natural routines (e.g., others in home or class).
- Tough for parents or teachers to manage while watching other
children simultaneously.

TRIAL-BASED FA

- An adaptation of a basic FA, but conducted using discrete trials.

[USE FOR] Developing function-based interventions.

title: DETERMINING THE NEED FOR BEHAVIOR-ANALYTIC SERVICES
body:
### DETERMINING THE NEED FOR BEHAVIOR-ANALYTIC SERVICES

- Assessment data can be used to determine the need for behavior-analytic services, or if another type of intervention would better suit a client's needs.
- Determine the need for services by asking the following questions:
    - Is the main beneficiary of services interested in receiving services? [THINK: Do they want the help?]
    - Does a behavior impact the client's safety and well-being?
    - Are members of the client's family and immediate community impacted by the client's behavior?
    - Have potential medical causes for the target behaviors been ruled out?
    - Would other non-ABA services be more beneficial for the client? (e.g., occupational therapy, mental health therapy, feeding therapy, speech therapy, parent training, academic support, occupational therapy, etc.).

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING:]
Code Standard 3.06: Consulting with Other Providers: Behavior analysts arrange for appropriate consultation with and referrals to other providers in the best interests of their clients, with appropriate informed consent, and in compliance with applicable requirements (e.g., laws, regulations, contracts, organizations and funder policies).

Code Standard: 3.13 Referrals: Behavior analysts make referrals based on the needs of the client and/or relevant stakeholders and include multiple providers when available. Behavior analysts disclose to the client and relevant stakeholders any relationships they have with potential providers, and fees or incentives they may receive for the referrals. They document any referrals made, including relevant relationships and fees or incentives received, and make appropriate efforts to follow up with the client and/or relevant stakeholders.

title: DETERMINING THE NEED FOR BEHAVIOR-ANALYTIC SERVICES (Cont'd)
body:
DETERMINING THE NEED FOR BEHAVIOR-ANALYTIC SERVICES (Cont'd)

- Does the challenging behavior prevent access to natural, least-restrictive environments? (e.g., mainstream classroom, district school, summer camp, etc.).
- Is the target behavior atypical when compared to same-aged, neurotypical peers? (Discrepancy analysis, F.4)

[BCBA] F.8 Interpret assessment data to identify and prioritize socially significant, client-informed, and culturally responsive behavior-change procedures and goals.

[BCaBA] F.3 Identify and prioritize socially significant, client-informed, and culturally responsive behavior-change goals.

SELECTING TARGET BEHAVIORS

- Assessment data should inform goal selection and intervention planning.
- Goal and treatment planning practices should be rooted in the behavior analyst's clinical expertise and their knowledge of a client's preferences and learning histories.
- Socially significant, client-informed, culturally responsive behavior analytic treatment, means that clients and/or stakeholders are active participants in goal and program planning.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard: 2.09 Involving Clients and Stakeholders: Behavior analysts make appropriate efforts to involve clients and relevant stakeholders throughout the service relationship, including selecting goals, selecting and designing assessments and behavior-change interventions, and conducting continual progress monitoring.

- Clients and relevant stakeholders are the experts in what is meaningful to them, their society, and their culture.
- When cultural preferences and norms are not considered in goal selection and treatment planning, service quality will be compromised.
- The ultimate goal of treatment is habilitation.

[PROCEDURE]: Habilitation (a.k.a. adjustment): When an individual's repertoire has been changed such that short- and long-term reinforcers are maximized and short- and long-term punishers are minimized.

- With habilitation, client-preference, and cultural responsiveness in mind, practitioners should consider:
  - Whose behavior is being assessed and changed, and why?
  - Is this being targeted to benefit the client, or to benefit others?
  - Will behavior change improve the quality of the person's life?
  - Do target behaviors have direct and indirect benefits to the client?

title: PRIORITIZING TARGET BEHAVIORS
body:
PRIORITIZING TARGET BEHAVIORS

DETERMINING THE RELATIVE PRIORITY OF TARGET BEHAVIOR:
1. Behaviors that pose a danger to the client or to others (#1 priority).
2. Behaviors that the client will use often (e.g., riding the bus, brushing teeth, feeding self, etc.).
3. Chronic long-lasting behaviors or skill deficits (e.g., ongoing vocal disruptions, limited mand repertoire, etc.).
4. Behaviors that will produce high rates of reinforcement (e.g., making purchases in a store, hygiene, job skills).
5. Behaviors that are needed for future skill development and independent functioning (e.g., prerequisite behaviors, self-help skills.).
6. Behavior that will reduce negative or unwanted attention from others (e.g., public self-touching, loud vocalizations).
7. Behaviors that will produce reinforcement for significant others (e.g., learning to flush the toilet, to help with household chores, or attending church).
8. Behaviors that are likely to be changed with intervention.
 - Consider behavior change proven effective in the literature, the expertise of the behavior analyst, the likelihood of a supportive environment, cultural significance, available resources, client buy in.

[CAUTION]: If your scope of comfort/competence compromises the effectiveness of services, refer out!

9. The behavior change is cost effective.
 - Consider cost and expected time commitment for behavior change.
 Cost shouldn't be a barrier if a behavior is in need of change.
 [THINK]: Cost-benefit ratio.

SOCIAL SIGNIFICANCE OF TARGET BEHAVIOR

[RELEVANCE OF BEHAVIOR RULE]: Chosen behaviors must be relevant to your client. This includes the consideration of a client's cultural values.

ASSESS THE RELATIVE SOCIAL SIGNIFICANCE OF TARGET BEHAVIORS: (10 QUESTIONS)
1. Will the behavior produce reinforcement in the client's natural environment after treatment ends?
2. Is the behavior a necessary prerequisite for a useful skill? (e.g., holding a writing utensil correctly is a necessary prerequisite to learning to write).
 - Consider cultural norms when assessing the "usefulness" of a behavior.
3. Will the behavior increase access to environments where other important behaviors can be learned and used?
 [THINK]: Mainstreaming.

title: SOCIAL SIGNIFICANCE OF TARGET BEHAVIOR (Cont'd)
body:
SOCIAL SIGNIFICANCE OF TARGET BEHAVIOR (Cont'd)

6. Is this an age-appropriate behavior? (E.g., driving, toileting, cutting food, reading, etc.)
    - Consider cultural norms and expectations for "age-appropriateness."
    - Especially important if the client's functional skills are significantly below typical performance.
7. If the proposed target behavior is to be reduced or eliminated, what adaptive behavior will replace it?
    - Take a constructional approach; If planning to eliminate a behavior, establish an adaptive replacement behavior and design a plan that ensures that the replacement behavior is learned. (H.3)

[PROCEDURE]: Constructional approach: The philosophy that replacement behaviors must be constructed for target behaviors that are being eliminated.

8. Does this behavior represent the actual problem or goal, or is it only indirectly related?
    Example: Teaching phonics, a prerequisite to reading, as a primary target wouldn't be sufficient. The real target is reading skills.
9. Is this just talk, or is it the real behavior of interest? (E.g., admitting you have a problem is not a behavior change.)
10. Is the goal of the behavior change program a behavior?
    Example: Passing the exam ≠ Behavior, but: Increasing fluency, studying, and answering questions correctly = Behavior.
    Example: Losing weight ≠ Behavior, but: An increase in healthy eating and exercise are behaviors that can be targeted.

COMPONENT BEHAVIOR VS. BEHAVIORAL CUSP VS. PIVOTAL BEHAVIOR

[COMPONENT BEHAVIORS]: The building block skills needed for the development of a more complex skill. Example: The necessary component skills for reading: Letter recognition, phonemic awareness, vocabulary comprehension.

[BEHAVIORAL CUSP]: A complete skill, once acquired, results in access to many different reinforcers. Example: Being able to read opens up a reader's world to history, entertainment, languages, news, social interaction, etc.

[PIVOTAL BEHAVIORS]: An acquired behavior that can lead to many new untrained responses. Example: Acquiring the pivotal response of choice-making in one environment, can generalize to different types and more sophisticated choice-making responses without formal training.

Graphic: Component behavior vs. behavioral cusp vs. pivotal behavior.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
Domain F: F.8

SOCIALLY SIGNIFICANT GOAL OBJECTIVES
- "Typical" performers can be used to identify and validate behavior change goals and target levels of performance.
  - THINK: Find some people who are already good at the specific needed skill.
- Objectives should be based on the performance levels necessary for optimal results.
  - THINK: How much skill is needed to meet the client's needs?
Example: After observing children in elementary classrooms, it was determined that seven-year-old peers typically engage in an average of 20 turn-taking responses per board or card game. This criteria was used for a client's social skills program, in which one of the ultimate goals was engaging in a turn-taking activity with a peer.

SOCIALLY SIGNIFICANT, CLIENT-INFORMED, AND CULTURALLY RESPONSIVE BEHAVIOR-CHANGE PROCEDURES
- Recommended procedures must be evidence-based, socially significant, client-informed, culturally responsive and utilize the least restrictive practices. (H.2)
- Behavior analysts must collaborate with clients and relevant stakeholders to choose the appropriate behavior-change procedures to address the goal objectives.

The potential of a procedure to be effective depends on several factors:
- The client's willingness to participate.
- Stakeholder willingness or ability to participate.
- Empirical evidence that a procedure has proved to be effective.
- Likelihood of public support within the individual's culture/community.
- The behavior analyst's scope of competence. (Code, 1.05)
- People most likely to be involved in implementing the program have the needed training, resources, buy-in, etc.

Socially appropriate and client-informed means:
- Clients and stakeholders understand the procedures.
- Clients and stakeholders agree that the procedures address their concerns. (Client opinions and concerns are also considered.)
- Clients and stakeholders are willing to implement the suggested procedures as described. (Client acceptability will enhance participation and buy-in.)
- Clients and stakeholders find the suggested procedures reasonable and appropriate, given the client's needs.
- There is an appropriate cost-benefit ratio for the clients and stakeholders to utilize the procedures.
- The procedures will be minimally disruptive to family or classroom dynamics.
- Clients and stakeholders like the proposed procedures. (Clients can choose between procedures.)
- Clients and stakeholders have weighed in on a client's likely discomfort as a result of procedures.

Please Do Not Duplicate
