title: BACKWARD CHAINING
body:
BACKWARD CHAINING
WITH LEAP AHEADS
(Cont'd)

Example: Mila is using backward chaining with leap aheads to teach Reva the behavior chain of opening her front door. Reva can already perform some of the steps, so Mila trains the last step and skips training for any steps that Reva knows.

Example: Reva has taught herself to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich by watching her dad do it for her. But she's confused on some of the steps, and she never ends up with a delicious sandwich. After watching to see what Reva can (and can't) do independently, Mila decides to use backward chaining with leap ahead to teach the missing steps so that Reva always ends with a delicious sandwich, and Mila will be able to bypass teaching the steps she already knows.

| | STEP 1 | STEP 2 | STEP 3 | STEP 4 | STEP 5 | STEP 6 | STEP 7 | STEP 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | Retrieve peanut butter & jelly | Retrieve knife & spoon | Lay out two slices of bread | Scoop PB onto bread | Spread PB onto bread | Scoop jelly onto bread | Spread jelly onto bread | Put slices together |
| BASELINE: | Reva | X | Reva | Reva | X | Reva | X | Reva |
| STEP 1: | Mila | Mila | Mila | Mila | Mila | Mila | (taught) | Reva |
| STEP 2: | Mila | Mila | Mila | Mila | (taught) | Reva | Reva | Reva |
| STEP 3: | Mila | (taught) | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva |
| STEP 4: | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva | Reva |

Table: Backward chaining, leap aheads.

[CAUTION]: There's a common misconception that known steps are skipped in the performance of the routine. That's not correct. It's the TRAINING of the mastered steps that is skipped. Clients must still perform all the steps in order, each time.

[USE FOR] Decreasing the duration of chaining procedures;
teaching clients who have some steps already in their repertoire; teaching clients when they acquire previous steps during the chaining process.

- pro • A flexible method that considers time spent on already acquired steps.
- con • Potential for passive client participation in the initial steps.
- • Skills can be acquired very slowly.

BEHAVIOR CHAIN
WITH A LIMITED
HOLD (LH) (Cont'd)

- A behavior chain method that incorporates specific timing criteria into the training of the routine.
- In this method, a behavior chain is not only taught to be performed correctly, but also to occur within a specified period of time.
- Using a limited hold would mean a time criteria would be added to ensure that the routine occurs within a reasonable amount of time. (Could be duration or IRT.)

[THINK]: There is a limited time to complete the routine.

title: PROBLEMATIC BEHAVIOR CHAINS
body:
## PROBLEMATIC BEHAVIOR CHAINS

[USE FOR] Teaching clients who can do the steps of the behavior chain but the entire process takes too long, and causes the routine to be ineffective.

Example: To effectively dial 911, it is important that all three numbers are dialed immediately, one after the other. When too much time elapses between numbers being pressed, 911 doesn't get dialed.

- When the chaining process results in an inappropriately formed chain, it is important to understand what went wrong in order to address it.
  Example: Despite what seems to have been an effective chaining procedure to teach Jimmy to get dressed, he still tends to put his jacket on before his shirt.

title: ASSESSING WHAT WENT WRONG:
body:
## ASSESSING WHAT WENT WRONG:

1. **Assess the S^Ds and response sequences for unintended reinforcers for the S^Ds within the chain.**
   Example: Jimmy's brother always laughs when Jimmy puts his jacket on before his shirt.
2. **Assess if similar S^Ds cue different responses.**
   Example: Both Jimmy's jacket and shirt are laid on his bed, and for some reason, putting the jacket on first has come under the control of the similar SD (laying on bed) to putting on his shirt.
3. **Assess the natural setting for relevant and irrelevant S^Ds; determine if the client can discriminate between the relevant combinations and variations, as well as the irrelevant ones.**
   Example: When Sergio practices his hand-washing routine, he is distracted by his Toy Story toothbrush, which makes musical sounds. When he sees it, he always picks it up and plays with it. This distraction has become part of the hand-washing routine, which typically ends with Sergio crying because the toothbrush is abruptly taken away.
4. **Assess if the S^Ds in the training environment differ from those in the natural environment.**
   Example: To prepare Shani for a trip to the dentist, her parents played a game called "Dentist" to teach Shani the steps of a dentist appointment. Shani and her parents took turns being the dentist and the patient. The dentist would welcome the patient, ask them to wait, bring them in, and sit them in the chair. Then, they would recline the chair and start to poke around in the patient's mouth, which they did with pixie sticks and Twizzler candy. Shani learned the routine. On the day of the real visit, she walked into the dentist's office, checked in, waited, climbed in the chair, let it recline, and then cried when the dentist took out his cold metal tools instead of Twizzlers or pixie sticks.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

PROBLEMATIC BEHAVIOR CHAINS (Cont'd)

[REFRESHER] Sometimes, it is not possible to replicate the natural environment in training settings. Ideally, the final phase of training includes the actual environment where the skill will be needed.
Example: High school driver's education classes use a simulated driving experience to teach students to drive. The final phase of learning includes completing the steps of the driving chain in an actual car, on an actual road. Without that step, students would have a hard time successfully learning to drive.

5. Assess novel environmental stimuli that may be impacting the completion of the behavior chain.
Example: Lili was able to do the entire dance combination at the studio, but made a lot of mistakes during the recital in the theater where there were bright lights, a huge audience, loud applause, and an auditorium full of shouting parents.

TASK ANALYSIS

- A task analysis is used to analyze the individual, discrete components of a routine in the order they must occur, to create an effective behavior chain.
- A breakdown of a complex behavior into small, teachable units that establish the behavior chain (series of steps and tasks presented in a specific order) as it will be taught.
- Used to assess the client's performance on each step of the sequence.

[CAUTION: A task analysis is not a behavior chain or a chaining method. It is an analysis of the target behavior to break it down into small, teachable units, which are used to devise the behavior chain for training.]

[USE FOR] Determining the exact sequence of behaviors that are necessary to complete a given behavior.

ESTABLISHING THE APPROPRIATE SEQUENCE OF STEPS:
- Individualization: Everyone is different and the needed steps to complete a specific routine are different for everyone.
- $S^D$s and responses: Identify the $S^D$s and responses that are needed to discriminate the conditions in which a given response must be performed.
- Generate a behavior chain by either doing the skill yourself, observing someone else perform the skill, or recruiting the help of an expert.

TWO METHODS TO ASSESS TASK ANALYSIS PERFORMANCE:
1. Single opportunity method: Used to assess if the client can perform each step in the task analysis, in the correct sequence.
- Most conservative method, because the assessment is discontinued at the first incorrect step.

PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

TASK ANALYSIS
*(Cont'd)*

[USE FOR] Assessing a client's skill level when there are time constraints.

[pro]
- Less chance that the client learns during the assessment.
- Less time consuming.

[con]
- Doesn't assess the client's skills on remaining steps.

[PROCEDURE]
1. List the necessary behaviors to complete the task in order.
2. Assess each step for mastery: Mark a (+) for correct response and (-) for an incorrect response.
3. If the client scores a (-) on a step, do not go any further and record a (-) for all the remaining steps.

Example: The chart below is an analysis of a client's ability to open the front door. As indicated, the client wasn't able to do step 3 on April 21st, therefore the analysis was terminated at that step and a (-) was recorded for the remaining (untested) steps. This process was repeated for the remaining assessment days.

TRIAL-BASED
PROCEDURES

DISCRETE-TRIAL TEACHING (DTT) a.k.a. discrete-trial training, discrete-trial instruction (DTI):
- A one-to-one structured teaching methodology that is presented in an organized and controlled environment.
  [THINK: Table-top.]
- Client's skills are assessed to establish an individualized target list.
- A discrete-trial is one sequence of a behavioral instructional routine (SD - Bx - C), in which the SDs are systematically planned.
  Example: "What color?", "Touch red," "Give me five," etc.
  [THINK: A single instructional unit (learn unit) is targeted with each trial.
- The critical components are an instruction (SD), the response, and the consequence.

Discrete, because each trial has a clear beginning (SD), middle (Bx) and end (C).

title: TRIAL-BASED PROCEDURES (Cont'd)
body:
TRIAL-BASED PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

- A response in a discrete trial is considered a discriminated operant because it is controlled by a restricted opportunity (SD is presented) to emit the response. (B.12)

[USE FOR] Promoting tightly controlled behavioral repertoires, responding in restricted conditions, acquiring new academic skills and verbal operants expanding verbal behavior, etc.

[pro] - Proven to be effective with clients with ASD.

[con] - Can result in rote, repetitive responding and prompt dependence.
- Doesn't naturally promote generalization.
- Instructor-directed SD signals the start of the trial.
- Relies on contrived motivation (e.g., praise, edible items, toys).

[PROCEDURE] Six components of a DTT trial:

1. Present the SD after placing at least one target stimulus in front of the client.
   Example: Three pictures are placed on the table (car, bowl, phone) and the trainer presents the SD, "touch car."
2. Prompting: Follow the client's individual prompting procedure (G7), either using time delay to allow independent responding, or errorless learning to ensure a correct response.
   Example: After the trainer says, "touch car," the car is moved slightly closer to the client.
3. Response: Client's behavior following the instruction.
4. Consequences: If correct, give predetermined reinforcement; if incorrect responses, provide a correction ("No, that is not the car").
   - The consequence closes the trial.
   - For incorrect responses, there are a series of error correction steps (e.g., re-present the SD with prompt, increasing prompt level if incorrect responding continues, etc.).

[*] The consequence (reinforcement or error correction procedures) is where the learning occurs!

5. Inter-trial interval: Trainer takes a brief pause between consecutive trials (:05 seconds).
6. Data collection:
   - Collected on a specific form (paper or electronic) for opportunity-based recording.
   - Record responses as: Correct (+); incorrect (-); or none (-).
   - Data are analyzed and (usually) reported as a percentage.
   - Mastery criterion is 80% - 100% correct responding.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

FREE-OPERANT
PROCEDURES
(Cont'd)

Five guiding principles for naturalistic teaching:
1. **Natural environment:** Skills are more likely to generalize and be maintained.
2. **Timing:** Trainers have to compose learning trials that take advantage of naturally occurring opportunities.
3. **Training loosely:** Instructions are presented in a variety of ways.
4. **Indiscriminable contingencies:** Mimics natural environment schedule of reinforcement.
5. **Natural MOs:** Finding natural learning opportunities for language development.
**Example:** Lin is completing a 100-piece puzzle and is almost finished, with the exception of the last piece. Her trainer waits patiently for her to use her language skills to ask for help.

**INCIDENTAL TEACHING:**
- A teaching methodology that takes place in a free-time setting, in which a child's initiations are learning opportunities.
- Expands on the client's current skill set.
- Training depends on what the client is doing rather than what the trainer wants the client to do.
- Teaches client to learn and use skills in their natural environment, with naturally occurring motivation, S^Ds, and reinforcers.
- Teaches client to discriminate the availability of adult attention(S^D) for language attempts (e.g., if an adult is attending, then a mand response will result in reinforcement; if an adult is not attending, then reinforcement is not available).
[THINK:] Only ask if the adult is looking at you.

[PROCEDURE]
1. A learning trial is initiated when the child shows an interest in something (e.g., points, gestures, touches, etc.).
2. The trial: The trainer approaches and presents a questioning look, which the child must discriminate as an S^D that signals the availability of reinforcement.
[THINK:] The look means reinforcement is available.

**Example:** Imagine going to a restaurant and ordering food before a waiter's body language signals that they are ready to take your order.

Prompts can be used (e.g., "What do you see?" or "What do you want?"), but should be faded so that spontaneous interactions can occur without prompting.

title: THREE GROUP CONTINGENCIES
body:
### THREE GROUP CONTINGENCIES

[HINT]

1. Dependent group contingency (a.k.a. hero procedure):
- A group procedure in which the reinforcement for the entire group is DEPENDENT on the behavior of one (or small group of) individual(s) within the group.
- THINK: Hero(es).
- THINK: It's on YOU!
- Example: A teacher tells her students that if "The Chosen One" finishes their math test before the bell rings, then everyone will not have to do homework for the entire week.

[USE FOR] Improving the behavior of one or a small group of individuals who respond well to peer influence and attention.

2. Interdependent group contingency:
- A group procedure in which reinforcement for the entire group is contingent on EVERYONE in the group meeting the pre-established criterion.
- THINK: It's on us.

[USE FOR] Promoting everyone in the group to perform at a certain level; facilitating group cohesiveness; decreasing challenging behavior and increasing prosocial behavior.

[3 GROUP CONTINGENCIES]
Dependent
Interdependent
Independent

title: GROUP CONTINGENCIES
body:
GROUP CONTINGENCIES
(Cont'd)

- Good behavior game:
  - An interdependent-group contingency that involves competition between two or more groups.
  - Teacher records occurrences of undesired target behavior in a prominent location.
  - The highest-scoring group receives reinforcement.
  - Highest score = The fewest marks.
  - [THINK: DRL.]
  - Promotes competition in a good way- students work as a team to earn for their team.
[USE FOR] Decreasing challenging behaviors in groups with a small number of individuals with disruptive behavior.
- Good student game:
  - [THINK: Good behavior game with group or individual self-monitoring.]
  - Used during independent in-seat activities when challenging behaviors typically occur.
  - Students in small groups record their own or group's performance.
  - The teacher chooses the target behaviors, establishes goals and reinforcers, and decides on group or individual monitoring.

ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: (Code, 2.14, 3.01)
- Using the dependent and interdependent group contingency, although known to be effective, can also do harm in certain environments. Make sure to know your group well enough to predict what losing access to a reinforcer can do to group members.
- Aggression can be an unwanted response of the dependent and interdependent group contingency, where some group members become aggressive to make sure others fulfill their end of the contingency or when the group contingency is unsuccessful. (H.4)

3. Independent group contingency:
- A group procedure in which reinforcement is only available for the individuals who meet the criterion.
- Can be combined with token economies and contingency contracts.
- Example: A teacher announces that the students who finish their math work before the bell rings will not have any assigned math homework for the rest of the week. The students who meet the goal escape the weekly math homework, while the students who don't, are assigned homework.
- Example: The Big exam. Those who score 400 or above pass, and those who don't, don't.

[WELCOME to the BIG ABA EXAM]

[USE FOR] Differentially reinforcing individual performance.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

[BCBA] G.15 Design and evaluate procedures to promote stimulus and response generalization.

[BCaBA] G.17 Develop and implement procedures to promote stimulus and response generalization.

PROMOTING GENERALIZATION
- A substantial positive outcome means that learned skills and behaviors generalize beyond the training setting, stimuli, people, and even behaviors.
- Achieving post-training stimulus and response generalization requires planning ahead and utilizing training methods that promote generalization.
- Choose behaviors that will produce reinforcement in the client's natural environment after treatment ends. (F.8)
- Identify all of the target behavior's desired variations as well as environments in which these behaviors should (and should not) occur.

[9 STRATEGIES TO PROMOTE GENERALIZATION]
- Common stimuli
- Loosely train
- Exemplars
- Mediation
- Management (self)
- Indiscriminable contingencies
- Negative examples
- General case analysis
- Behavior TRAP

NINE STRATEGIES TO PROMOTE GENERALIZATION (and their subtypes):

1. Program common stimuli:
- Program the same SDs in the instructional setting that exist in the generalization setting.
- Increases the probability that the correct response will be occasioned in the generalization setting.
- Example: If teaching someone to make a purchase in a store, include items typically found in a store in the instructional setting (e.g., rack, shopping bag, cash register, money exchange, etc.).
- [THINK:] Mock run or dress rehearsal.
- [USE FOR] Stimulus generalization.

2. Train loosely:
- Include a large variety of the non-critical aspects (e.g., training location, people, voice tone, carrier phrases, etc.) of the SD in the training setting.
- Example: Ask, "How are you?" in a high-pitched voice, a low-pitched voice, and a medium-pitched voice.
- Make minor changes to antecedent and environmental stimuli while training.
- Accept and reinforce a variety of responses that fall within criterion.
- Ensure that stimulus control is not too tightly focused on the instructional setting.
- [THINK:] Same target, different locations, or same target, different trainers.
- [USE FOR] Stimulus and response generalization.
qa_notes: Project owner confirms the transcript matches the scanned source; no page-specific QA note is recorded.

title: PROMOTING GENERALIZATION (Cont'd)
body:
PROMOTING GENERALIZATION (Cont'd)

3. Multiple exemplar training (two variations):
- Teach enough response examples:
    - Teach a variety of appropriate response topographies. The more examples utilized when teaching, the better for promoting generalized untrained responses.
Example: Various ways to ask for help (spoken, written, signed).
[USE FOR] Response generalization.
- Teach enough stimulus examples:
    - Teach responding to a variety of antecedent stimuli.
    - Give different stimulus examples and ensure that the client acquires untaught connections, as well.
    - The more trained examples, the more likely untrained generalizations will occur.
[THINK:] Exposure/generalization to different members of stimulus and response classes.
Example: Ask, "How are you?", "What's up?", "How are you doing?", etc.; accept a variety of responses ("I'm good," "Doing well," "Been better," thumbs-up, etc.).
[USE FOR] Stimulus generalization.

4. Mediation (two variations):
- Ask other people to reinforce behavior:
    - Teach those involved in client's life (parents, employers, teachers) to help maintain and generalize the new skills.
    - Inform key individuals in the natural setting to reinforce correct behavior.
Example: After Raju learns how to greet others, his parents and friends are asked to practice and reinforce this skill daily.
[USE FOR] Stimulus and response generalization.
- Contrived mediating stimulus:
    - Set up a stimulus or a person to help transfer the learned behavior from the training setting to the natural setting.
    - Bring the behavior under the control of the mediating stimulus during instruction to serve as a prompt in the generalized settings.
Example: Individuals, cue cards, visual activity schedules, self-operated prompting devices.
[USE FOR] Stimulus generalization.

5. Self-management:
- Cash in on the fact that the learner is present in both instructional and generalization settings.
- Teach self-management behaviors to enable managing (prompting and reinforcing) the target behavior on their own.

title: PROMOTING GENERALIZATION (Cont'd)
body:
PROMOTING GENERALIZATION (Cont'd)

[con] - Requires teaching two skills (self-management behavior and target behavior) and ensuring generalization for both.

- Three self-management variations:
    - Response variability:
        - Teach the client to improvise and problem-solve if the learned response doesn't produce the desired reinforcement.
        - Promotes flexibility and creativity.
        - Using lag-reinforcement contingency.

> **Lag-reinforcement:** Reinforcement is contingent on a response being different from a previously reinforced response or number of responses.

[USE FOR] Response generalization.
**Example:** When Oscar is asked what his favorite foods are, he says "chicken nuggets," even though he enjoys other foods. To help him vary his answers, Oscar must now answer differently each time he is asked the question. For each different response, he earns an extra two minutes of screen time before bed.

    - Recruit reinforcement:
        - Teach clients to recruit (ask for) reinforcement from caregivers instead of waiting for it.
        **Example:** A student asks a teacher, "How am I doing?" and the teacher provides praise.
        [USE FOR] Stimulus and response generalization.

[con] - Could result in extinction if reinforcement is not received when recruited.

    - Teach required levels:
        - Train target behaviors to meet the necessary performance criteria to contact reinforcement in the natural environment.
        - Increase the rate, accuracy, duration, latency, magnitude or topography of target behavior.
        **Example:** Timing yourself on a mock exam helps ensure that your timing is sufficient for you to be successful in completing the Big exam in time.
        [USE FOR] Stimulus and response generalization.

6. Indiscriminable contingencies:
- Reinforcement contingencies the client can't predict or discriminate.
- These types of schedules match the unpredictable contingencies of the generalization setting.
[THINK:] Schedule like the real world.

title: PROMOTING
body:
PROMOTING
GENERALIZATION
(Cont'd)

- Includes:
    - Intermittent reinforcement: During skill acquisition, use continuous reinforcement (CRF), then move to intermittent schedules.
    - All indiscriminable contingencies are intermittent, but not all intermittent schedules are indiscriminable.
    - Use VR and VI schedules to increase unpredictability and indiscriminability.
    - Delayed rewards: Rewards are not presented immediately after a correct response, and it is unclear which responses will produce reinforcement.

[USE FOR] Response generalization and maintenance.

7. Negative teaching examples:
    - Teach the client to discriminate the settings, times, and conditions in which it is not appropriate to display a certain behavior.
    - Teach the limits of a behavior: What is included and what is not included.
    [THINK:] Knowing when it's not OK to do that.
    Example: It may be OK to crack inappropriate jokes with your friends, but it is not OK to crack inappropriate jokes at work.
    [USE FOR] Response generalization and discrimination; increasing stimulus control.

8. General case analysis:
    - Teach all the different stimulus variations and response variations the learner may come across in the generalization setting.
    Example: To teach a client how to use a variety of laundry machines, we would work with different types of machines that exist (stimulus variations) and teach how to use each specific laundry machine (the response variations).
    [USE FOR] Stimulus and response generalization; teach the variations of an SD- and how responding might differ with different SDs.

9. Behavior trap:
    - Super effective contingency of reinforcement that's easy to enter; hard to leave!
    - When natural contingencies of reinforcement operate to promote and maintain generalized behavior changes. (Baer and Wolf, 1970).
    - Once the client is in a behavior trap, the trap creates generalized behavior change automatically.
    - Four elements:
        1. Client is baited with hard-to-resist reinforcers.
        2. Low response effort behavior is needed to enter trap.
        3. Connected contingencies of reinforcement motivate the client to acquire, extend, and maintain behavior.

**BCBA** G.16 Design and evaluate procedures to maintain desired behavior change following intervention (e.g., schedule thinning, transferring to naturally occurring reinforcers).

**BCaBA** G.20 Develop and implement procedures to promote maintenance of behavior change.

RESPONSE MAINTENANCE
- When a client continues to emit newly acquired behavior after services have been terminated.
- Progression to naturally occurring reinforcement schedules.
[THINK:] Results built to last.
- It is our ethical responsibility to produce outcomes that will maintain beyond treatment.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING:] Code Standard. 2.14: Selecting, Designing, and Implementing Behavior-Change Interventions. Behavior analysts select, design, and implement behavior-change interventions that: (1) are conceptually consistent with behavioral principles; (2) are based on scientific evidence; (3) are based on assessment results; (4) prioritize positive reinforcement procedures; and (5) best meet the diverse needs, context, and resources of the client and stakeholders. Behavior analysts also consider relevant factors (e.g., risks, benefits, and side effects; client and stakeholder preference; implementation efficiency; cost-effectiveness) and design and implement behavior-change interventions to produce outcomes likely to maintain under naturalistic conditions. They summarize the behavior-change intervention procedures in writing (e.g., a behavior plan).

Considerations for programming for maintenance:
1. Conduct weekly maintenance checks for approximately 3-6 weeks after mastery criterion has been met, to assess if a mastered skill is being maintained.
- Maintenance checks confirm and predict maintenance.

MAINTENANCE

2. Thin the reinforcement schedule used in training.
- Move to intermittent schedules by gradually increasing response requirements. (E.g., CRF to a VR 2 or VR 3.)
  - Thin the schedule in small increments.
  - Examine the client's progress to guide the thinning progression.

[EXAM TIP]
On exam questions, remember:
- Dense schedule = Frequent reinforcement.
- Thin schedule = Less frequent reinforcement.
- Schedule numbers increasing = Thinning schedule (e.g., from VR 4 to VR 6).
- Schedule numbers decreasing = Thickening schedule (e.g., from VR 6 to VR 4).

[CAUTION]
CAUTION: Extreme increases in ratio requirements going from denser to thinner schedules (e.g., FR 2 to FR 20) can result in ratio strain, in which case reduce the ratio requirements.

[CAUTION]
Ratio strain: When an abrupt increase in ratio requirements evokes a decrease in responding, avoidance, and/or aggression.

3. Move to variable schedules, which produce high rates of response without a post-reinforcement pause. Variable (VI and VR) schedules promote maintenance and generalization because they are more "natural," and therefore less predictable than fixed schedules. (B.9)
4. Program delays to reinforcement, which allow extra time for caregivers to deliver reinforcement.

[CAUTION]
CAUTION: If not planned carefully, delays to reinforcement can result in extinction which may result in a resurgence of challenging behavior. (H.5)

5. Use instructions (e.g., rules, directions, signs) to describe the schedule of reinforcement. (G.10)
- Helpful for making a smooth transition during the thinning process.
- When clients understand the schedule, interventions may be more effective.
- Only effective with learners who have more advanced verbal repertoires.
6. Program or progress to natural and intrinsic reinforcement.
7. Keep some components of the initial intervention in place (e.g., schedule, contingency contract, etc.).
8. High-level fluency promotes maintenance.
9. Involve stakeholders in behavior change procedures from the outset to establish reinforcement that is available in the natural environment. (Code, 2.09)

title: CONSIDERATIONS FOR USING PUNISHMENT:
body:
## CONSIDERATIONS FOR USING PUNISHMENT:

- **Immediacy:** Punishment should be delivered without any delay following the target behavior; even small delays can reduce the effectiveness.
- **Intensity:** Higher intensity punishers are more effective at decreasing behavior; should start at higher intensity and gradually decrease; the more intense at the onset, the more effective the punishment procedure; increasing intensity gradually has not proven to be effective.
- **Schedule:** Consistent and continuous schedules (e.g., FR 1) are most effective; intermittent schedules can be effective in some conditions.
- **Reinforcement for target behavior:** Reinforcement for challenging target behavior must be eliminated for punishment to be effective.
- **Alternative behavior:** Punishment is more effective when the target behavior isn't the only means of contacting reinforcement; most effective when paired with reinforcement for desired behavior.
- **Treatment integrity:** Especially important with punishment.

| pro | con |
|---|---|
| Quick impact on behavior. | Most aversive |
| | Can evoke emotional and elicited effects. |

POSITIVE PUNISHMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

[CAUTION]: This is a very controversial practice with a lot of ethical implications. We are not condoning it; we are merely including it here because it is a form of positive punishment.

2. Overcorrection: Client is required to engage in an effortful behavior that's directly related to the challenging behavior.
- Two types of overcorrection:
  - Restitutional overcorrection: A type of overcorrection in which, following a challenging behavior, the client is required to repair the damage caused by their behavior, and then engage in additional behavior to make the environment better than its original state. Example: After Jason spilled water while pouring himself a glass, his mother made him wash the basin and the entire kitchen floor.
  - Positive practice overcorrection: A type of overcorrection in which, following a challenging behavior, the client is required to repeatedly perform the correct form of the behavior for a certain amount of time or a certain number of repetitions. Example: After Jason spilled water all over the floor while pouring himself a glass of water, his mother made him practice by pouring water into every glass in the kitchen without spilling.

3. Reprimands: Negative or corrective feedback (e.g., "No!", "Stop," "Don't do that," etc.) delivered contingent on the occurrence of a target behavior. Most common form of punishment.

[CAUTION]: These same reprimands will act as positive reinforcement for attention-maintained behavior.

4. Response blocking: Physically intervening to prevent the response. Example: Wearing mittens over your hands to prevent nail biting (the mittens physically block the biting behavior).

5. Contingent exercise: A procedure in which the consequence for challenging behavior is physical exercise. Example: Marga's husband forgot to buy her flowers on their anniversary, so she told him to "Drop and give me 20." Push-ups aren't exactly related to his behavior, but Marga's husband hates push-ups and hasn't forgotten the flowers again.

6. Response interruption and redirection (RIRD): A positive punishment procedure in which demands or distractions are used to interrupt and redirect repetitive, stereotypic, and self-injurious behaviors.

NEGATIVE PUNISHMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

[pro]

2 TYPES OF RESPONSE COST
- Bonus
- Existing cache

Effective use of response cost:
- Describe/define the rules (which behavior will result in what response cost) before administering the procedure.
- Deliver fines immediately and consistently.
- Plan timing and amount of loss; make sure it's proportional to the severity of the behavior.
- Set rules for compliance concerns.
- Loss should be gradual to avoid bankruptcy and ensure enough of a reinforcer reserve.
- Avoid overuse.

[pro] - An effective least-restrictive punishment procedure; convenient.

- Two variations of response cost:
  - Bonus response cost: Additional noncontingent ("free") reinforcers are made available but removed contingent on challenging behavior.
  - Example: Students usually get 15 minutes of recess daily. But today, they're told that they can have a bonus 15 minutes, which can be lost contingent on challenging behavior.
  - Existing cache response cost (a.k.a. direct fine): Challenging behavior results in the direct loss of an existing collection of earned reinforcers.
  - Example: A client earned a bag of candy for completing his work on time. For each occurrence of a challenging behavior, he must give back a piece.

2. TIME-OUT FROM POSITIVE REINFORCEMENT (a.k.a. time-out):
- Procedure in which access to specific reinforcers is prohibited for a period of time following an occurrence of challenging behavior.

[pro]
[THINK:]
- Easy to implement, non-exclusionary forms are acceptable, works quickly, and can be combined with other programs.

The name of this procedure is "time-out from positive reinforcement," which means that the time-out is effective only if it removes access to the maintaining reinforcer.

- Effective use of time-out:
  - Define behavior on which time-out is contingent.
  - Set and explain rules.
  - Set the duration of time-out and set exit criteria.
  - Ensure legal and ethical compliance, permissions, etc.
  - Assess program's efficacy.
  - Set termination criteria.

[CAUTION] ETHICS DEVIL WARNING: A court ruling entitled, Hancock vs. Avery (1969) places limitations on the duration and conditions of time-out procedures.

title: NEGATIVE PUNISHMENT
body:
NEGATIVE PUNISHMENT
PROCEDURES
(Cont'd)

[CAUTION]: Time-out is often misused because it negatively reinforces the behavior of the person administering the procedure, and may do less to decrease future challenging behavior.

[BOX: 3 TIME-OUT PROCEDURES
Seclusion
Exclusionary
Non-exclusionary]

THREE VARIATIONS OF TIME-OUT:
1. Seclusion time-out: The client is placed in a time-out room for a period of time and locked in; most restrictive.
- Two types of seclusion time-out:
  - Required relaxation: Client is expected to lie down for a period of time.
  - Restrained time-out: The client's movement is suppressed and he is held in a therapeutic restraint; incredibly restrictive.

2. Exclusionary time-out: Immediate removal of the client from the reinforcing (time-in) space.
- Two types of exclusionary time-out:
  - Time-in setting removed: Location does not change.
    Example: Time-in is delivered as part of computer-based learning. Client gets an error screen or the computer turns off.
  - Removal from time-in setting:
    - Time-out room: Client is placed in a minimally furnished, secure, unlocked, and supervised space, close to the time-in setting for a period of time, without access to reinforcement.
    - Hallway time-out: Client is asked to leave the classroom and stay in the hallway outside of the room for a period of time.

3. Non-exclusionary time-out (a.k.a. inclusion time-out): Procedures in which the client is kept in the time-in space but is not allowed to participate in time-in activities, or contact reinforcement.
- Five types of non-exclusionary time-out:
  - Planned ignoring: Social reinforcers (attention, physical contact) are removed for a certain period of time; least aversive.
  - Withdrawal of a specific positive reinforcer (a.k.a. withdrawal of materials): Something preferred is taken away for a certain period of time (e.g., TV off).
  - Contingent observation: The client is removed from the instructional setting to another part of the room. They can observe the time-in setting, but not participate in the time-in activity.
  - Time-out ribbon: A ribbon on a child's wrist signals the availability of reinforcement. The removal of the ribbon signifies the loss of access to reinforcers, but not exclusion from the time-in environment.
  - Partition time-out: The client stays in the room, but their view of the time in space is restricted by a wall or partition.

[BCBA] G.18 Evaluate emotional and elicited effects of behavior-change procedures.

EMOTIONAL AND ELICITED EFFECTS OF BEHAVIOR-CHANGE PROCEDURES

- While the behavior change procedures that behavior analysts utilize are designed to promote positive and socially significant outcomes, there can be negative and unwanted emotional and elicited effects as well.
- Surprisingly, these outcomes are equally elicited by reinforcement, punishment, and extinction.

[REFRESHER] For the sake of a more organized and cohesive review of this topic, we combine TCO Domain G.18 with TCO Domain H.4, where we will detail the unwanted emotional and elicited effects of behavior-change procedures. See page 390.

EQUIVALENCE-BASED INSTRUCTION (EBI)

- A teaching method based on stimulus equivalence in which different combinations of taught relations result in other derived relations, which emerge without additional training.

- The client learns more than what was directly taught, which maximizes learning outcomes and generalization.

- Example: Without previous training, being able to generalize stimuli that are the same or opposites- such as stronger or weaker, louder or quieter, etc.

title: EQUIVALENCE-BASED
body:
EQUIVALENCE-BASED
INSTRUCTION (EBI)
(Cont'd)

- Requires conditional discrimination: The discrimination between the comparison stimuli is conditional upon the sample stimulus being present during each trial.
[THINK:] Two antecedent stimuli needed: The sample and the matching.
- Generalization occurs when client matches novel stimuli after having matched a few comparison stimuli to samples.

[ICON: STAR] This is known as generalized identity matching.

- Generalized matching-to-sample repertoires help to establish equivalent and non-equivalent relations between various stimulus classes and events.
[USE FOR] Teaching complex verbal relations (e.g., reading, math); attending and organization of different stimuli; used in pre-academic workbooks to introduce letter and number discrimination.

[PROCEDURE]
1. A visual sample stimulus is presented (e.g., a square).
2. Two or more comparison stimuli are presented (e.g., a square and a triangle; or a square, a triangle, a circle, and a heart).
3. One comparison stimulus (e.g., square) is identical to a sample stimulus, while the others are different.
4. The different stimuli are presented as the sample stimulus from trial to trial.
5. The correct comparison stimulus is conditional on which sample is present.
6. Consider procedural variations like presenting two sample stimuli to be matched to one comparative stimulus.
Example: Match a picture of a baby and the spoken word of baby to the written word of baby.
7. Differentially reinforce different match combinations.
Example: Matching a picture to an identical picture earns an M&M; or matching a picture to a written word earns a bag of M&Ms.

[ICON: STAR] Matching-to-sample alone is not enough and should be paired with reinforcement, modeling, error correction, and prompting procedures.

THREE TYPES OF MATCHING-TO-SAMPLE PROCEDURES:
1. Identity matching-to-sample: Sample and comparison stimuli are physically identical (e.g., matching a picture of a baby to an identical picture of a baby).

(Cont'd)

- A more complex type of conditional discrimination is one in which the comparison stimuli are not similar physically to the sample stimulus.
Example: Auditory-to-visual matching (e.g., receptive labeling) consists of the presentation of an auditory sample, such as dictated object names, with visual comparisons, such as an array of objects.

STIMULUS EQUIVALENCE

[4 PARTS OF STIMULUS EQUIVALENCE
Reflexivity
Symmetry
Transitivity
Stimulus
equivalence

Reach Students This
Spectacularly.]

- Defined by the emergence of correct responding to untrained and non-reinforced stimulus-stimulus relations, following the training of some correct stimulus-stimulus relations.
- Derived stimulus relation: A relation that is formed without direct training, indirectly acquired by making comparisons of sameness or difference, with two or more stimulus relations that were previously taught.
Example: Without previous training, being able to generalize stimuli that are the same or opposites, such as stronger or weaker, louder or quieter, etc.
THINK: Generalization.
- Requires a minimum of a three-member stimulus class, and the demonstration of the following: If A = B, and B = C, then A = C.

[PROCEDURE]

1. Select stimuli: Objects, pictures, spoken words, written words, numbers, quantities, symbols, etc.
2. Set predetermined accuracy criteria for each phase.
3. Choose effective consequences.
4. Present three different sample stimuli with three comparative stimuli to lead to nine different relations (e.g., with A, B, C, we have: A = A, B = B, C = C, A = B, A = C, B = A, B = C, C = A, C = B).
5. Client is taught an AB relation between (for example) a word (A) and an object (B) (e.g., A = B).
6. Client is then taught a BC relation between the same object (B) and a different stimulus (C) (e.g., B = C).
7. Then, there is a test for the emergence of an untrained relation (e.g., from A = B, and B = C, emerges A = C).

EMERGENT STIMULUS-STIMULUS RELATIONS:
1. Reflexivity (a.k.a. generalized identity matching):
- Identity matching-to-sample.
- Reflexive stimulus control.
- Matching two identical stimuli.

title: STIMULUS EQUIVALENCE
body:
### STIMULUS EQUIVALENCE
*(Cont'd)*

4. **Stimulus equivalence** (a.k.a. combined test for equivalence):
   - FINAL step for stimulus equivalence.
   - When every possible relation between the different stimuli has emerged.
   - Client is taught:
     > **A = B RELATION AND B = C RELATION.**
   - From which emerges the untaught relations:
     > **B = A (SYMMETRY) AND C = B (SYMMETRY).**
     > **A = C (TRANSITIVITY) AND C = A (SYMMETRY).**

#### Graphic: Stimulus equivalence triangle.

```
                    B
                  /   \
   SYMMETRY      /     \      SYMMETRY
 A = B: B = A  /       \   B = C: C = B
 <... UNTRAINED /         \ UNTRAINED...>
   -- TRAINED -->         <-- TRAINED --
              /             \
            A --------------- C
             <... UNTRAINED...
... UNTRAINED...>
```

**TRANSITIVITY: A = C**
**SYMMETRY: C = A**

**KEY:**
- ☐ Taught-relation
- ☐ Derived relation

---

- **If** **A PICTURE:** Baby = **B WRITTEN:** Baby **then,** **B WRITTEN:** Baby = **A PICTURE:** Baby
- **If** **B WRITTEN:** Baby = **C SPOKEN:** Baby **then,** **C SPOKEN:** Baby = **B WRITTEN:** Baby
- **If** **A PICTURE:** Baby = **C SPOKEN:** Baby **then,** **C SPOKEN:** Baby = **A PICTURE:** Baby

*Graphic: Stimulus equivalence.*

[*]
> The most important part of equivalence-based learning is the development of an equivalence class.

> **Equivalence class:** Consistent responding in the three categories of stimulus equivalence: Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity, without training or reinforcement history for many symbolic, arbitrary, and opposite relations.

title: RELATIONAL FRAME THEORY (RFT)
body:
### RELATIONAL FRAME THEORY (RFT)

- A behavior analytic approach to language which aims to connect and understand the relationship between language and derived stimulus relations.
- The theory hypothesizes that learned behavior is acquired through a combination of stimulus equivalence, naming, understanding, analogy, metaphor, rule-following, and other verbal behavior.
- In the course of our lives, we are able to derive many relations known as frames.

[THINK:]
Frame: A stimulus relation between two or more stimuli that function within that class. The behavior of making those relational connections (e.g., things that are like me, things not like me, good things, bad things, safe things, dangerous things, large things, small things).
THINK: An equivalence class.

- Framing behavior is learned through multiple exemplar training (G.15), which helps learners make abstract and concrete relationships between names and pictures, which can be expanded to other relations without additional training/shaping.
- Example: Learning that a baseball is smaller than a basketball is the formation of 'smaller than' as a frame for those two pairs. This can be generalized to novel pairs as well, such as a cherry is smaller than a watermelon and a kayak is smaller than a yacht (derived relations).

[USE FOR]
Complex human functioning; language skills; perspective-taking skills; academics.

- Symmetry relations: If a soccer ball (A) is smaller than a basketball (B), then a basketball (B) is bigger than a soccer ball (A).
- Transitivity relations: If a soccer ball (A) is smaller than a basketball (B) and a tennis ball (C) is smaller than a soccer ball (A), then a tennis ball (C) is smaller than a basketball (B).

Graphic: Symmetry relation.

Graphic: Transitivity relations.

- Example: A blue whale is bigger than an elephant. An elephant is bigger than a rhino. The trained relations = A blue whale is bigger than an elephant, and an elephant is bigger than a rhino. The derived relations = A blue whale is bigger than a rhino, and a rhino is smaller than a blue whale.

title: G.16 Develop and implement self-management procedures.
body:
### G.16 Develop and implement self-management procedures.

[Just in Case] Self-management is not part of the BCBA TCO, but it is part of the BCaBA TCO. We think it may be important for BCBA candidates as well, so don't skip it!

- Behavior-analytic procedures in which the target individual controls some or all aspects of his behavior change procedure.
- Interventions that are designed and used to change one's own behavior.
- Teaches an individual to engage in a behavior that will promote a reduction in a challenging behavior and/or an increase in a desired behavior.
- Controlling response: A self-managed behavior that promotes a behavior change in the target behavior (e.g., reminders, specific prompts, self-monitoring, etc.).
- Controlled response: The behavior targeted for change in the self-management protocol.
  Example: Setting an alarm is a controlling response that promotes the target response of waking up on time for work (the controlled response).
- Self-management means the target behavior is controlled.

[USE FOR] Improving life efficiency; breaking habits (e.g., negative self-talk); forming good habits; working toward difficult or long-term goals (e.g., quitting smoking, running a marathon, getting a professional certification), etc.

**CONSIDERATIONS FOR USING SELF-MANAGEMENT:**
- The targeted behavior and goal must be clearly defined.
- Collect behavior baseline data for goal criteria, and to assess effects of the procedure.
- Ensure strong contingencies for the desired behavior to compete with the contingencies that have maintained the challenging behavior.
- A public commitment or accountability partner can strengthen results.
- Consistently evaluate progress to make data-based adjustments as needed.

**FOUR TYPES OF SELF-MANAGEMENT PROCEDURES:**
1. **Self-monitoring (a.k.a. self-recording, self-observation):**
- A self-management procedure that involves recording data on one's own behavior.
- Has a positive reactive effect that motivates behavior change.
- Can be paired with feedback and reinforcement for accurate reporting (by self or others).

2. Self-evaluation (a.k.a. self-assessment):
- The act of assessing target behavior progress by comparing self-monitoring data to a predetermined criterion.
[THINK]: Assessing one's own behavior.
3. Self-administered consequences:
- Procedures that involve providing consequences for increasing or decreasing one's own behavior.
- Includes self-delivery of reinforcement and punishment, based on criteria that has been established.
4. Antecedent-based self-management procedures:
- Preventative or evocative self-management procedures.
  - Manipulating MOs: Contriving one's own state of deprivation or satiation to increase or decrease one's own behavior (e.g., eating before grocery shopping).
  - Response prompting: Prompting oneself to engage in the desired behavior: Any prompt form (e.g., visual, auditory) that will cue the correct behavior (e.g., calendar, phone alert, self-talk, finger string, to-do list, etc.).
[THINK]: Self-reminders.
  - Initiating the first step of a behavior chain: The first step acts as an SD for the rest of the necessary behaviors to complete the task (e.g., leave lunch by the door so you remember to take it to work, going to sleep in your workout clothes so that you go to the gym in the morning).
  - Arranging the environment to prevent behavior: Removing the environmental variables that evoke and/or maintain the target behavior (e.g., turn off cell at night, don't keep junk food at home).
  - Limiting challenging behavior to restricted conditions: Reducing the available opportunities for the behavior to occur. (E.g., restrict phone use to work hours only; eat junk food on vacation only; drink alcohol at restaurants, not at home; etc.)
[THINK]: Conditional discrimination. (G.6)
  - Assigning a specific environment for engaging in a desired behavior: Creating conditions that will support desired behavior (e.g., studying in the library, joining a gym).
  - Habit reversal: Identifying the events that precede challenging behavior and engaging in alternative behaviors instead.
[THINK]: Break the behavior chain. Do something else instead.
[EXAMPLE]: Instead of calling your ex, call your best friend. Place fruit where you used to keep chocolate.
  - Self-instruction: Self-directed verbal instructions (covert or overt) to (response) prompt desired behaviors (e.g., talking to oneself).
  - Self-directed systematic desensitization: (a.k.a. graduated exposure): Substituting a different behavior (e.g., muscle relaxation) for the challenging behavior.
  - Massed practice (a.k.a. negative practice): Repeatedly engaging in the challenging behavior to incite satiation.
[THINK]: Overdo it.

title: H.1 State intervention goals in observable and measurable terms.
body:
### H.1 State intervention goals in observable and measurable terms.

**MEASURABLE AND OBSERVABLE INTERVENTION GOALS**
- Goals describe desired behavioral changes.
- Behavior analysts take presenting concerns and convert them into measurable behavioral goals.
- Poses the question: How much does a behavior need to change to make a meaningful difference in the client's and stakeholder's lives?
- Once program goals have been agreed on, specific goal objectives must be established ahead of program initiation.
- Having set goals can prevent disagreements between those involved in evaluating a program's effectiveness.
- Established objective guidelines for continuing and terminating a treatment.
- Clients and stakeholders should participate in establishing and approving goal objectives to make sure they are meaningful to them.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard: 2.09 Involving Clients and Stakeholders: Behavior analysts make appropriate efforts to involve clients and relevant stakeholders throughout the service relationship, including selecting goals, selecting and designing assessments and behavior-change interventions, and conducting continual progress monitoring.

**6 GOAL OBJECTIVES**
Target behavior
Specific conditions
Non-conditions
Mastery criteria
Maintenance (and)
Generalization
Other Measures

- Goal objectives are the standard against which progress is assessed, and should include:
1. **Target behavior:** An operationally defined behavior for decrease or elimination; and/or skills for acquisition and improvement.
2. **Specific conditions in which the behavior will occur:** The settings, contexts, surroundings, materials, people, staff, timing, etc.
   [THINK]: Generalization.
3. **Specific conditions in which the behavior will NOT occur:**
   [THINK]: Discrimination.
4. **Mastery criteria:**
   - A measurable dimension (e.g., rate, frequency, percentage, etc.) for reaching a performance expectation, to signify when behavior change has occurred.
   - A rate/count criterion to indicate the length of time (or number of response opportunities) a behavior is expected to occur at that criterion before it is considered reliably mastered.
5. **Maintenance and generalization criteria:** Specify the additional (natural) conditions under which the mastered behavior must be tested (e.g., different people, places, settings, activities) to demonstrate maintenance and generalization of the skill.
6. **Criteria for other measurable dimensions:** For behaviors that require an additional dimension for mastery, like accuracy, latency, intensity and topography, etc.

### MEASURABLE AND OBSERVABLE INTERVENTION GOALS (Cont'd)

**Example:**
- **Target behavior:** Raising hand.
- **The specific conditions in which the behavior will occur:** During instructional time at school, Sunday school, baseball practice.
- **The specific conditions in which the behavior will NOT occur:** Free time at school, recess, home.
- **Mastery criteria:** 80% of opportunities, across 5 consecutive instructional sessions.
- **Generalization and maintenance criteria:** Three classroom teachers/aides, three academic subjects, three consecutive Sunday school meetings and three baseball practices.
- **A criteria for other measurable dimensions:** N/A.
- **Goal:** Darien will raise his hand instead of calling out during instructional time only, in at least 80% of opportunities across five consecutive instructional sessions at schools with three different classroom teachers/aides, three academic subjects, three consecutive Sunday school meetings and three baseball practices.

**Example:**
- **Target behavior:** Compliance to five simple instructions, (e.g., come here, sit down, stand-up, line up, stop).
- **The specific conditions in which the behavior will occur:** When specific known adults present instructions at school, at home, and in the community (e.g., street, bank, grocery store).
- **The specific conditions in which the behavior will NOT occur:** When strangers give instructions in any setting.
- **Mastery criteria:** 80% of opportunities.
- **Rate of criterion:** Five consecutive days in home and school setting.
- **Generalization and maintenance criteria:** Three consecutive community outings.
- **A criteria for other measurable dimensions:** With a response latency of no more than:06 seconds.
- **Goal:** Neema will comply with five simple instructions, delivered by familiar adults, within:06 seconds of delivery, in 80% of opportunities, across five consecutive school and home days, and three consecutive community outings.

title: BCBA H.2 Identify and recommend interventions based on assessment results, scientific evidence, client preferences, and contextual fit (e.g., expertise required for implementation, cultural variables,
body:
BCBA H.2 Identify and recommend interventions based on assessment results, scientific evidence, client preferences, and contextual fit (e.g., expertise required for implementation, cultural variables, environmental resources).

BCaBA H.2 Identify potential interventions based on assessment results and the best available scientific evidence.
H.3 Develop intervention goals and procedures based on risks and contextual fit (e.g., client preferences and values, cultural variables, social validity, environmental resources).

RECOMMENDING INTERVENTIONS
To make an appropriate recommendation for treatment means converting assessment results into interventions that are:
- Consistent with the assessment results.
- Supported with scientific evidence.
- In alignment with client preferences.
- A good contextual fit.

[ETHICS DEVIL WARNING]: Code Standard: 2.14 Selecting, Designing, and Implementing Behavior-Change Interventions: Behavior analysts select, design, and implement behavior-change interventions that: (1) are conceptually consistent with behavioral principles; (2) are based on scientific evidence; (3) are based on assessment results; (4) prioritize positive reinforcement procedures; and (5) best meet the diverse needs, context, and resources of the client and stakeholders. Behavior analysts also consider relevant factors (e.g., risks, benefits, and side effects; client and stakeholder preference; implementation efficiency; cost effectiveness) and design and implement behavior-change interventions to produce outcomes likely to maintain under naturalistic conditions. They summarize the behavior-change intervention procedures in writing (e.g., a behavior plan).

BASE INTERVENTION RECOMMENDATIONS ON
Assessment results
Scientific evidence
Client preference
Contextual fit

1. Depending on assessment results, look for specific strategies that are known to establish, increase, decrease, eliminate, maintain, and generalize behaviors. (Domain G.)
- Identify strategies for choosing socially significant replacement behaviors based on the function of a target behavior.
- Consider the less-intrusive environmental manipulations that can be made (e.g., placing a lock on the front door, dangerous items out of reach, etc.).
  - Manipulating antecedent variables (e.g., prompting).
  - Changing or eliminating the MOs (e.g., NCR).
  - Changing or eliminating the SDs (e.g., fading).
- Consider how the client's preferred items and potential reinforcers can be integrated into intervention.
- Consider manipulating and/or eliminating consequent variables (e.g., reinforcement, punishment, and extinction).
- Avoid using treatments that have been reported ineffective; use what has been historically effective.

title: RECOMMENDING INTERVENTIONS (Cont'd)
body:
RECOMMENDING INTERVENTIONS (Cont'd)

- In choosing interventions, think about how stakeholders' lifestyles will impact their program implementation, participation, time commitment and effort.
- Before choosing interventions, take time to assess stakeholders' stressors, triggers, strengths, supports, and resources.
- Select assessment methods with consideration of cultural factors, preferences and norms.
- Choose interventions that fit the cultural values, norms and preferences of the client (e.g., cultural differences in parental expectations, culturally specific parenting styles).

4. Consider contextual fit:
- Select interventions that are a good fit between the goal and the context in which the intervention will be implemented.
[THINK:] User-friendly interventions that fit the skill-sets, schedules, resources, and values of the behavior change agents (e.g., RBTs, school aides, group home staff, behavior interventionists, clinic staff, etc.).
- Increasing staff acceptability and buy-in means natural reinforcers for staff, procedural integrity, and intervention gains for the client. (It's a win-win!)

[BCBA] H.3 Select socially valid alternative behavior to be established or increased when a target behavior is to be decreased.

[BCaBA] H.4 Identify alternative behaviors to be established or increased when a target behavior is to be decreased.

SOCIALLY VALID ALTERNATIVE BEHAVIOR

- When target behaviors are being decreased or eliminated, there must be a plan to replace the behavior.
[THINK:] What need is the behavior serving?
- A replacement behavior is a more socially appropriate and effective way for the client to contact the consequences maintaining the challenging behavior.
- The target behavior becomes a less effective way for the client to meet their need(s) while the new replacement behavior contacts reinforcement.
Example: When a client is taught to raise his hand to ask questions instead of chronic shouting out, classroom staff are instructed not to call on him unless he raises his hand. Shouting out becomes an ineffective way to get questions answered, and the replacement behavior results in answered questions.

Since challenging behaviors serve a function, they should not be reduced or eliminated without:
1. Determining an incompatible and adaptive replacement behavior, and,
2. Developing a plan to ensure that the replacement behavior is learned.

title: SOCIALLY VALID
body:
SOCIALLY VALID
ALTERNATIVE BEHAVIOR
(Cont'd)

TWO CATEGORIES OF REPLACEMENT BEHAVIOR:
1. Functionally-equivalent behavior: Desirable behaviors that will contact the same reinforcement (meet the same need) as the challenging behavior.
   Example: If a client's aggressive behavior serves the function of access to tangibles, a functionally-equivalent replacement behavior would be using words to request for access to desired items.
2. Alternative behavior: Functionally inequivalent behavior that prevents the target behavior.
   Example: If a client elopes from his classroom during academic instruction, teaching him to ask for a break or to be excused could get in the way of meeting his academic goals. So, an alternative may be staying seated to receive the lesson and an intervention could be developed to increase sustained attention and/or tolerance of non-preferred academic activities.

[Graphic: CONSTRUCTIONIST APPROACH VS ELIMINATIVE APPROACH]

- Constructing replacement behaviors when a challenging behavior is eliminated.
  Example: Teach Andrea to clap her hands during a live performance instead of screaming and hitting herself.
- Eliminating behaviors without constructing anything to go in their place.
  Example: Forbidding Andrea to scream and hit herself during a live performance, without teaching an appropriate response.

Graphic: Constructionist approach vs. eliminative approach.

[BCBA] H.4 Plan for and attempt to mitigate possible unwanted effects when using reinforcement, extinction, and punishment procedures.

[BCaBA] H.5 Identify possible unwanted effects when using reinforcement, extinction, and punishment procedures.

UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES
Reinforcement procedures are known to impart a lot of positive behavior change. Nonetheless, practitioners utilizing reinforcement should be aware of - and prepared for - emotional and elicited effects, which can be planned for, avoided, or addressed with programming.

1. Emotional responding: The presentation of reinforcers results in emotional responses (e.g., excitement, laughter, screams) that interfere with the target response.

title: UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)
body:
# UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

2. **Adjunctive behaviors** (a.k.a. schedule induced behaviors): Behaviors that occur as a result of reinforcement schedules, at times when reinforcement isn't available. These behaviors are not related to the specific reinforcement yet tend to occur in the same conditions in which the reinforcement will be delivered.
   - THINK: Time-filling, while you wait, interim behaviors.
   - Example: While waiting for a zoom meeting to start, a person may doodle, whistle, or pace.
   - These become problematic if they are harmful to the individual (like drug and alcohol abuse, self-injury), or are difficult-to-quit behaviors (like smoking and nail biting), which can be insensitive to intervention.
   - Example: Cracking knuckles, snacking, drinking, hair playing, doodling, checking your phone, etc.

   [STARBURST] To mitigate: Teach alternative behaviors, manipulate the environment to evoke harmless time filling behaviors, reinforce the absence of harmful adjunctive behaviors.

3. **Target behavior is suppressed:** When powerful reinforcers evoke behavior that is not compatible with, and disrupts the target response or other functional responses.
   - Example: When a child is told that they will earn iPad time after completing a task, they may get so excited that it distracts them (walk toward iPad, look at it, touch it, ask questions about it) and completely interferes with the task that is being worked on.
   - Can also happen when the reinforcer isn't present (delayed).
   - Example: Parents tell the child that they will go out for ice cream after dinner, if they complete their morning routine independently. The anticipation of evening ice cream may compete with any further tasks that need to be completed that day.

   [STARBURST] To mitigate: Delay information about reinforcement, use token systems, teach tolerating delayed access to reinforcement, and reinforce alternative responses.

4. **Approach to reinforcing agent** (a.k.a. sign tracking): When a person who has received a lot of reinforcement tries to be physically near the reinforcing agent, a lot.
   - THINK: Clinging, holding on, hugging.
   - Interferes with appropriate behavior; can itself be socially inappropriate.

title: UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)
body:
UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

- The extent of approach depends on whether there are other sources of reinforcement available in a given situation. If the reinforcing agent is the primary source, approach to other sources will decrease.
Example: Ella is very clingy with her mother. When both of her parents are present, she ignores her dad and exclusively hangs on her mother. When her mother is not there, Ella tends to do the same thing with her dad.

[PROCEDURE] To mitigate: Ensure multiple sources of reinforcement, and program across different staff, teachers and family members.

5. Behavioral contrast: When behavior-change gains do not generalize and there are behavior changes in the opposite (undesired) direction in non-therapeutic contexts.
THINK: Multiple schedules of reinforcement.
- The use of reinforcement in a specific treatment condition can have the opposite impact on behavior when the client is in a non-treatment environment, even though nothing has changed in the non-treatment environment.
- Can result in relapses, regression and less progress outside of the therapeutic environment.
Example: A client receives a denser schedule of reinforcement for correct responding during his tacting program at school and tact responses increase. At the same time, the schedule of reinforcement for tacting in his ABA program stays unchanged, yet responses decrease.
Example: Boris is working on using his words to make requests at school and at home with his parents. His teacher recently increased the reinforcement contingencies for appropriate requests and, sure enough, Boris's behavior increased at school. Boris's parents haven't changed anything that they do, yet they see a decrease in functional communication at home.

[fyi] When the contrast effect results in an undesired decrease in behavior in a non-treatment setting, this is known as negative behavioral contrast. Typically associated with reinforcement as the treatment condition.

[PROCEDURE] To mitigate: Implement reinforcement procedures in all environments in which the behavior occurs, and program to generalize behavior change.

6. Response generalization: When reinforcement strengthens a behavior other than the target behavior, and the other behavior contacts the same consequence as the target behavior.
THINK: Do what it takes to get reinforcement.
Example: Melissa can have dessert if she eats her vegetables at dinner. On the days she doesn't want to eat her veggies, she hides them or feeds them to the dog. That also works to access dessert.

title: PTB ABA Exam Study Manual
body:
PTB ABA Exam Study Manual

UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

To mitigate: Ensure that non-target responses do not contact reinforcement.

7. **Aggressive responses:** When client's aggressive behavior prevents others from accessing reinforcement, and as a result prevents the reduction of available reinforcers (e.g., in a group contingency).
  THINK: Escape from the prospect of reinforcers becoming depleted.
  - Aggressive behavior is strengthened by negative reinforcement.
  - Can happen in interdependent and dependent group contingencies, when some members become aggressive to make sure others fulfill their end of the contingency.

To mitigate: Know the students, anticipate challenges, and use group contingencies wisely.

8. **Transient effects:** When the effects of a reinforcement procedure are short-lived and/or there is a reduction in response rate (even below baseline) following the removal of the procedure.
  - Attributed to a decrease in intrinsic motivation.
  THINK: Extrinsic rewards for the target response, can compromise intrinsic motivation.

To mitigate: Build natural consequences into programming, with less reliance on contrived reinforcers.

9. **Imitation:** When either:
  - A client inappropriately imitates the reinforcement delivery behavior of a therapist, or,
  - A person observes another person receiving reinforcement for a similar behavior and responds with a "me too" reaction, when the reinforcement is not the same for both people.
  **Example:** After watching her little brother receive M&Ms as reinforcers in ABA therapy, Sally brought M&Ms to school and used them to reward her friends for doing whatever she told them to do.

To mitigate: Program natural delivery of reinforcement, consider others when planning reinforcement schedules, educate stakeholders, model appropriate responses.

10. **Decrease in unreinforced behavior:** When the unreinforced members of a response class decrease because other responses are being reinforced.
  **Example:** A client may develop limited requesting carrier phrases if reinforcement is only given when the client says, "I want (desired object or activity)," and not given when he says, "Give me," or, "Can I have?"

title: UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)
body:
UNWANTED EFFECTS OF REINFORCEMENT PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Train loosely, differentially reinforce a larger response class, create discriminative contingencies for the target behavior vs. other responses in the same class.

11. **Excessive responding:** When the target behavior occurs at unnaturally/undesired high rates because the reinforcer is strong and/or the schedule is too dense.

**Example:** After being taught to request a break (instead of engaging in a tantrum to escape work), the student began requesting a break every time work was presented.

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Systematically set reinforcement criteria, thin schedules of reinforcement, and use differential reinforcement to lower response rates.

UNWANTED EFFECTS OF EXTINCTION PROCEDURES

The extinction procedure is known to result in decreases in challenging behavior, however practitioners utilizing this procedure should be aware of - and prepared to deal with - emotional and elicited effects, which can be planned for, avoided, or addressed with programming.

1. **Extinction burst:** An immediate and temporary increase in the rate of responding when an extinction procedure is first implemented.

[THINK:] The client has a negative reaction to not receiving the expected reinforcer, or think that they just have to "do more" to get the reinforcer.

**Example:** When extinction was used to reduce Kim's attention-maintained greeting behavior (repeatedly saying "hi" to the same person), her first response was a major increase in the rate of greetings.

- Should be anticipated, although it doesn't always occur.
- Potential sign that the correct maintaining consequence was identified.
- Can be the result of escape extinction.
- Can cause harm if the target behavior is dangerous, therefore extinction should be avoided with dangerous behaviors and in settings (e.g., public spaces, classrooms) that cannot handle a dangerous extinction burst.
- Discourages stakeholders from following through with the procedure.

[CAUTION: An extinction burst is much more likely when the target behavior has been maintained on a continuous reinforcement schedule.]

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Prepare stakeholders for the potential response, avoid reinforcing the burst, use NCR prior to extinction, or pair extinction with differential reinforcement.

title: UNWANTED EFFECTS

UNWANTED EFFECTS
OF EXTINCTION
PROCEDURES
(Cont'd)

2. **Increase in magnitude of behavior:** An extension of the extinction burst when there is a temporary magnitude increase (e.g., volume, duration, intensity).
   **Example:** When reinforcement was withheld for Katya's attention-maintained singing, she began to sing louder.

   [THINK:] To mitigate: See extinction burst.

3. **Extinction-induced response variability:** Novel behaviors (including new members of a response class, different forms of a response) emerge when the target response doesn't contact reinforcement during extinction.
   [THINK:] Client looks for new ways to contact reinforcement when the old way doesn't work anymore.
   - Can result in the emergence of new forms of challenging behavior.
   - **Example:** A child is not given a break when he asks, so he runs out of the class or says he doesn't feel good, so he can be sent to the nurse.

   Can be desirable if produces successive approximations of behavior that can be differentially reinforced to shape a desired response; or if appropriate behavior emerges.
   **Example:** A lag schedule of reinforcement (B.10) takes advantage of extinction to evoke novel responses, by withholding the reinforcer until a new/different response has been emitted.

   [THINK:] To mitigate: Include members of the complete response class in extinction procedures, or manipulate the environment to prevent other behaviors.

4. **Extinction-induced aggression:** The emergence of aggressive behavior as a result of reinforcement being withheld.
   [THINK:] An aggressive burst.
   - Can be the result of escape extinction.
   - A variation of extinction-induced behavior variability.
   **Example:** When extinction was used to reduce Kim's attention-maintained greeting behavior (i.e., repeatedly saying "hi" to the same person), her reaction was to push the person she was greeting.

   [THINK:] To mitigate: See extinction burst.

5. **Extinction-induced emotional behavior:** The client becomes agitated in the form of crying, attempting to escape, protest, etc. following the first phase of extinction.
   **Example:** When extinction was used to reduce Kim's attention-maintained greeting behavior (i.e., repeatedly saying "hi" to the same person), her reaction was to drop to the ground and begin screaming and crying.

UNWANTED EFFECTS OF EXTINCTION PROCEDURES (Cont'd)

- A variation of extinction-induced behavior variability.
- Makes extinction less acceptable to stakeholders.
- Can impact integrity with which caregivers implement the procedure.

[CAUTION: This should be considered an indicator that extinction is aversive and may increase escape or avoidance behavior and may not be the appropriate treatment.]

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Prepare caregivers for expected responses, avoid unintentional reinforcement, and teach alternative behaviors.

6. **Imitation:** When other students or siblings copy the challenging behaviors that are placed on extinction.
   **Example:** Classmates may imitate the client's attention-maintained disruptive behavior that is being ignored during the extinction procedure. Because why not?

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Educate others, recruit peer mediators, and model appropriate responses.

7. **Extinction of desired behaviors:** When withholding reinforcement for one behavior, mistakenly affects another behavior (typically in the same response class as the target behavior).
   **Example:** In hopes of lowering Will's vocal volume when he makes requests, requests that are shouted were placed on extinction (ignored). This resulted in the elimination of shouting AND the use of words to make requests.

[REFRESHER] To mitigate: Train loosely, establish discriminable contingencies for the target behavior vs. other responses in the same class.

8. **Behavioral contrast:** When behavior-change gains do not generalize to non-therapeutic contexts.
- The use of extinction in a specific treatment condition can have the opposite impact in a non-treatment environment, even though nothing has changed in the non-treatment environment.
- The rate of responding decreases on the extinction schedule and increases in the non-extinction setting.
   **Example:** Jack is interested in two women in his ABA program, Vicky and Sophia, who both give him the same amount of attention when he tries to talk to them. One day, Vicky pulls back on her attention (extinction), so now Jack talks to Sophia a lot more (increase in behavior in the unchanged condition).

[fyi] When the contrast effect results in an **undesired increase in behavior** in a non-treatment setting, this is known as **positive behavioral contrast**. Typically associated with extinction or punishment as the treatment condition.
